Hamlet's metaphysics stay unresolved, but his physiology is exact, and the graveyard is where the two finally meet.
themes.development: Abstract in the soliloquies of Acts I and III; literal from 3.4 onwards, and entirely material by 5.1, where death is a trade with tools and songs.

themes.name: Madness, real and performed
themes.summary: Hamlet announces in advance that he will pretend, which ought to settle the question and does not: the pretence gives him licence to say things that are far too accurate to be mad and far too wild to be safe. Ophelia's madness is not announced, not strategic and not interpretable, and the court's response to it is to keep watching.
themes.development: Declared in 1.5, diagnosed by Polonius in Act II, weaponised in 3.1, and set beside the real thing in 4.5.

themes.name: Memory and record
themes.summary: The Ghost's actual demand is 'Remember me', and Hamlet answers by treating his mind as a notebook to be wiped and rewritten. The play is full of records: tables, letters, commissions, songs, an old jester remembered by a skull. Its last act of business is arranging for the story to be told correctly.
themes.development: A vow in 1.5, a joke about writing it down moments later, and a formal commission to Horatio in 5.2 — the play ends by appointing its own narrator.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Hamlet has seven, and they do different jobs: self-disgust in 1.2, self-accusation in 2.2, abstract argument in 3.1, and in 4.4 a comparison with an army he can see from where he stands.

techniques.name: Metatheatre
techniques.definition: A play that draws attention to its own nature as performance.
techniques.bookDefinition: A play that draws attention to its own nature as performance.
techniques.inThisBook: A troupe of actors is hired, given a lecture on acting, and used to conduct an experiment on a spectator — inside a theatre, watched by spectators.

techniques.name: Foils
techniques.definition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character constructed to throw another's choices into relief by making different ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Laertes and Fortinbras are both sons of dead fathers who act at once. The play puts one in Act IV and the other in Act V so that Hamlet's hesitation is measured twice.

techniques.name: Prose against verse
techniques.definition: Shifting between metrical speech and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.bookDefinition: Shifting between metrical speech and prose to mark status, sanity or intimacy.
techniques.inThisBook: Hamlet drops into prose with the players, the spies and the gravediggers, and rises into verse when he is alone; Ophelia's madness arrives as prose broken by snatches of song.

techniques.name: Disease and rot
techniques.definition: A sustained figurative field that describes a political situation as a body's illness.
techniques.bookDefinition: A sustained figurative field that describes a political situation as a body's illness.
techniques.inThisBook: Denmark is rotten, an unweeded garden, an ulcer with a skin over it; the murder itself is a poison poured into a body, so the metaphor and the plot share a mechanism.

techniques.name: Hendiadys
techniques.definition: Joining two nouns with 'and' where grammar would expect one noun modifying another.
techniques.bookDefinition: Joining two nouns with 'and' where grammar would expect one noun modifying another.
techniques.inThisBook: 'The book and volume of my brain' and 'the expectancy and rose of the fair state' are typical: the figure doubles a thought instead of completing it, and the play's language keeps hesitating in the same way its hero does.

quotations.text: Seems, madam! nay it is; I know not 'seems.'
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: His first extended speech, answering Gertrude's question about why his grief looks so particular.
quotations.analysis: He objects to a verb, which tells you what kind of hero this is going to be. The irony is scheduled three scenes later, when he decides to put on an appearance deliberately, and the play never lets him have the word back.

quotations.text: O, that this too too solid flesh would melt Thaw and resolve itself into a dew!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The first soliloquy, immediately after the court has left the stage.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs of dissolving in a row, each one weaker than the last, so the wish loses force as it is spoken. Nothing here is about revenge or a ghost: the speech happens before he knows anything, which means the despair is prior to the plot rather than caused by it.

quotations.text: Frailty, thy name is woman!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the same soliloquy, on his mother's remarriage.
quotations.analysis: He generalises from one woman to half the species in five words, and the grammar does the work: an abstract noun is addressed directly, then given a name. The line is quoted as if it were the play's verdict, but it is spoken by a man who has just told us he cannot bear to think about it.

quotations.text: This above all: to thine ownself be true, And it must follow, as the night the day, Thou canst not then be false to any man.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: The end of a long farewell lecture to Laertes, who is trying to catch a ship.
quotations.analysis: The most quoted piece of wisdom in the play belongs to its most tiresome speaker, and he contradicts it within a scene by sending Reynaldo to lie about Laertes abroad. Read in context it is advice about self-interest rather than integrity, which is why the court repeats it and nobody follows it.

quotations.text: Something is rotten in the state of Denmark.
quotations.speaker: Marcellus
quotations.context: Watching Hamlet follow the Ghost away along the platform.
quotations.analysis: It is given to a minor soldier, not to the prince, which matters: the corruption is visible from the guard post before anyone at court admits it. 'Something' is doing a great deal of work — nobody on stage yet knows what, and the audience has not been told either.

quotations.text: My tables,--meet it is I set it down, That one may smile, and smile, and be a villain;
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone, minutes after the Ghost has gone.
quotations.analysis: He has just been told his uncle is a murderer and his response is to reach for a notebook. Writing it down converts unbearable testimony into a manageable proposition, and the stage direction that follows — he actually writes — makes the intellectual habit physical.

quotations.text: There are more things in heaven and earth, Horatio, Than are dreamt of in your philosophy.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has just been asked to swear on the sword while the Ghost calls from under the stage.
quotations.analysis: It is usually quoted as mysticism; in position it is an argument with a sceptic who has already seen the ghost and is still reasoning. Note the address: Hamlet uses his friend's name to make the rebuke personal, and the line's authority depends on a spirit shouting from beneath the floorboards.

quotations.text: How strange or odd soe'er I bear myself, As I perchance hereafter shall think meet To put an antic disposition on,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Swearing his friends to secrecy about anything they may see him do.
quotations.analysis: The madness is announced in advance, under oath, as a wardrobe decision — 'put on' is the verb used for clothes. That advance notice is what keeps the question alive for four acts: everything strange Hamlet does afterwards has been pre-authorised, so nothing he does can settle the matter.

quotations.text: Though this be madness, yet there is method in 't.
quotations.speaker: Lord Polonius
quotations.context: An aside during the conversation about words, words, words.
quotations.analysis: Polonius is right and cannot use it. He detects the design under the nonsense and then draws the wrong conclusion about what the design is for, which is the court's characteristic failure: good observation, bad inference. The line is spoken aside, so the audience is invited to grade his reading against theirs.

quotations.text: Denmark's a prison.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, moments after working out that they were sent for.
quotations.analysis: Three words of prose, offered as a flat statement of fact to two men who have just been hired as warders without quite realising it. The exchange that follows turns it into a philosophical game about thinking making it so, which is exactly how Hamlet avoids being pinned down by people fishing for symptoms.

quotations.text: What a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculty!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Explaining to the schoolfellows why he has lost all his mirth.
quotations.analysis: A textbook humanist celebration of mankind, delivered in prose to two informers, and finished a few lines later with dust. He is performing an orthodoxy in order to demonstrate that he no longer holds it — the praise is a set-up for the dismissal.

quotations.text: O, what a rogue and peasant slave am I!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Alone after the First Player's speech about Hecuba.
quotations.analysis: The trigger is not the murder but a professional actor crying about a woman dead for centuries. Hamlet's self-disgust is comparative and aesthetic: somebody else produced a convincing performance of grief and he has not, which is a strange thing to punish yourself for and a precise clue to what he thinks feeling is.

quotations.text: the play 's the thing Wherein I'll catch the conscience of the king.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The couplet that ends Act II, having just admitted the Ghost may be a devil.
quotations.analysis: It is the only plan in the play arrived at by argument, and it is a piece of experimental design: a stimulus, a subject, an observer. The rhyme gives it the confidence of a conclusion, and the flaw is buried in the verb — a conscience caught is a reaction, not a confession.

quotations.text: To be, or not to be, that is the question, Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles, And by opposing end them?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Spoken while Claudius and Polonius are hidden, having placed Ophelia in his path.
quotations.analysis: The speech contains no first-person pronoun and names nobody: it is written as a general problem in ethics, not a private confession. That is worth noticing because two men are listening for symptoms and hear philosophy instead — the most intimate speech in the play is also the most carefully depersonalised.

quotations.text: Thus conscience does make cowards of us all; And thus the native hue of resolution Is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: The close of the same soliloquy, before he sees Ophelia.
quotations.analysis: 'Conscience' here means consciousness as much as moral scruple, and the metaphor is a complexion: thought spreads over resolve like an illness over a face. It is the play's own diagnosis of its hero, offered by the hero, which is one reason the diagnosis has never quite been improved on.

quotations.text: O, what a noble mind is here o'erthrown!
quotations.speaker: Ophelia
quotations.context: Alone on stage after Hamlet's exit, before the watchers come out.
quotations.analysis: She is the only character who mourns Hamlet as a loss rather than assessing him as a problem, and she does it in a formal lament built from three-part lists — eye, tongue, sword. The speech also establishes what he was like before the play began, information the audience has no other way of getting.

quotations.text: The lady protests too much, methinks.
quotations.speaker: Queen Gertrude
quotations.context: Watching the Player Queen swear she will never remarry.
quotations.analysis: Asked to judge a play about a widow's promise, Gertrude gives a critic's verdict on the acting rather than a wife's answer to the charge. Whether that is composure or blindness is the closest the play comes to telling us what she knows, and it declines to decide.

quotations.text: O, my offence is rank it smells to heaven;
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Alone, trying to pray, immediately after the play has broken up.
quotations.analysis: This is the moment the audience stops needing the Ghost: the confession comes from the murderer, unprompted, with nobody listening. Shakespeare gives the proof to the theatre and withholds it from Hamlet, who walks in forty lines later and sees only a man at his devotions.

quotations.text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below: Words without thoughts never to heaven go.
quotations.speaker: King Claudius
quotations.context: Rising from his knees, seconds after Hamlet has left without killing him.
quotations.analysis: The couplet is a joke at Hamlet's expense that Hamlet never hears: he spared a man whose prayer was not working. The chiastic arrangement of words and thoughts — up, below, words, thoughts — makes the failure sound like a law of physics rather than a moral judgement.

quotations.text: How all occasions do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge!
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: On a plain in Denmark, watching Fortinbras's army march towards Poland.
quotations.analysis: 'Inform against' is legal language for turning informer, so Hamlet describes the world as a witness giving evidence against him. It is his last soliloquy, and the resolution it reaches is immediately undercut by the fact that he is being escorted onto a ship to England as he speaks it.

quotations.text: Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio: a fellow of infinite jest, of most excellent fancy:
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: In the churchyard, holding a skull the gravedigger has identified.
quotations.analysis: It is the first death in the play he can speak about without a theory, and the reason is that he has a name and a memory to attach to the bone. The scene is in prose, and the joking goes on around him: the play's most affecting moment about mortality is set in a workplace where corpses are routine.

quotations.text: There's a divinity that shapes our ends, Rough-hew them how we will,
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Telling Horatio how he found and rewrote the sealed commission on board ship.
quotations.analysis: He credits providence in the middle of an account of his own forgery, seal and all. The Hamlet of Act V explains his actions after he has taken them rather than before, and the change in tense is the change in the man: less deliberation, more report.

quotations.text: the readiness is all: since no man has aught of what he leaves, what is't to leave betimes?
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: To Horatio, who has offered to call off the fencing match.
quotations.analysis: Set this against 'To be, or not to be': the same question about dying, answered now in prose, in one sentence, with no metaphors. He has stopped arguing, and the calm is not peace but a kind of exhaustion that the plot immediately exploits.

quotations.text: Which have solicited. The rest is silence.
quotations.speaker: Hamlet
quotations.context: Dying, having given his vote for the succession and told Horatio to report the circumstances.
quotations.analysis: His last act is administrative: a vote, a request for an accurate account, and then nothing. 'The rest' means both what remains to be said and what remains of him, and the man who could not stop talking hands the talking over and stops.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Close in date to Julius Caesar, which the play itself remembers when Polonius says he once played Caesar.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: The short First Quarto. A longer Second Quarto followed in 1604/5, and the Folio text in 1623.

atAGlance.label: Three early texts
atAGlance.note: Each preserves material the others lack, so no edition can print all of Hamlet without choosing.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Two of the five acts pass before Hamlet takes any action against Claudius at all.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as a problem of character
criticalViews.summary: The reading that dominated the nineteenth century and shaped most since: the play is the study of a particular temperament, and the delay is explained by something in the man — reflectiveness, melancholy, a will paralysed by thought.
criticalViews.counter: It has to treat Elsinore as scenery. A court that hires spies, opens letters and stages entrapments gives Hamlet practical reasons for caution that have nothing to do with temperament.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as a play about proof
criticalViews.summary: On this account the delay is rational. The only evidence is a ghost of uncertain origin; Hamlet designs a test, gets a reaction rather than a confession, and has to decide what a reaction is worth.
criticalViews.counter: It struggles with 3.4, where he kills a concealed listener without checking who it is — a man careful about evidence has just behaved as carelessly as possible.

criticalViews.position: Hamlet as three plays, not one
criticalViews.summary: Because Q1, Q2 and the Folio differ substantially, textual criticism since the late twentieth century has argued that editors who conflate them produce a play no early audience ever saw.
criticalViews.counter: Readers and actors still need a text to work from, and the conflated tradition has shaped four centuries of performance, which is itself a fact about the play.

essayQuestions.question: Is Hamlet's delay a failure of character or a problem of evidence?
essayQuestions.focus: Revenge, proof and the status of the Ghost
plan: Establish what Hamlet actually has at the end of Act I: unverifiable testimony from a spirit whose nature he says he cannot classify.
Trace the design of the Mousetrap in 2.2 and 3.2 as an experiment, and ask precisely what Claudius's reaction proves.
Turn the argument at 3.3: the refusal to kill a praying man is a theological calculation, not hesitation — and the audience knows the prayer failed.
Test the counter-case with 3.4, where he stabs a concealed listener without identifying him.
Close on Act V, where the killing finally happens under conditions Hamlet did not arrange and cannot control.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use watching and being watched in Hamlet?
essayQuestions.focus: Surveillance, privacy and the court
plan: Open with Reynaldo in 2.1: the court's method stated in its purest form, applied by a father to his own son.
Map the arranged scenes — 3.1 with two men concealed, 3.2 with the whole court watching a king watch a play, 3.4 with a listener behind the arras.
Show how Hamlet adopts the method rather than rejecting it: the play, the rewritten commission, the friends he tests.
Consider what the play makes private: the soliloquies, Claudius's prayer, and the fact that the audience is always the extra watcher.
Decide whether the arrival of Fortinbras ends the surveillance or simply changes who is doing it.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Ophelia and Gertrude.
essayQuestions.focus: Constraint, silence and what the play declines to tell us
plan: Count what each is allowed to say, and note how much of it is answering a question put by a man.
Read 1.3 and 3.1 as a sequence in which Ophelia is instructed, positioned and then abused for being where she was told to stand.
Examine 4.5: madness as the first occasion on which she speaks first, at length, and without being interrupted.
Weigh Gertrude's silences — her refusal to answer directly in 3.4, and the strangely detailed drowning speech in 4.7.
Assess two readings: a play that exposes the constraints on these women, or one that shares them.

essayQuestions.question: 'Hamlet is a play about acting.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Performance, theatre and the antic disposition
plan: Begin with 1.2, where Hamlet rejects 'seems', and 1.5, where he schedules a performance of madness.
Use the players in 2.2: a professional weeping for Hecuba shames a son who cannot produce feeling on demand.
Take the advice to the players in 3.2 as the play's own theory of acting, then watch it applied to an audience of one.
Set Claudius beside Hamlet as a rival performer whose public manner never slips until he is alone in 3.3.
Conclude with Act V, where Hamlet stops performing, and ask what he loses and gains by it.

discussionQuestions: The Ghost's account of the murder has no other witness. What would it take for Hamlet to know it is true?
Hamlet announces his madness before he performs it. Does that settle the question of whether any of it is real?
Is Claudius a good king? Consider how he handles Norway, the rebellion and the succession.
Why does Shakespeare keep Hamlet offstage for so much of Act IV?
Horatio is told to stay alive and report what happened. Do you trust the account he would give?

timeline.label: Saxo Grammaticus writes the Amleth story into the Gesta Danorum
timeline.detail: Composed around the turn of the thirteenth century: feigned madness, a murdered father and a dangerous uncle are all already there.

timeline.label: Belleforest retells Amleth in the Histoires tragiques
timeline.detail: The French version that carried the Danish story into sixteenth-century print and, in some form, to Shakespeare.

timeline.label: The Globe opens on Bankside
timeline.detail: The playhouse the Lord Chamberlain's Men built for themselves, and the theatre Hamlet was written for.

timeline.label: Hamlet most likely completed
timeline.detail: Usually dated to about 1599-1601, close to Julius Caesar and Twelfth Night.

timeline.label: Entered in the Stationers' Register by James Roberts
timeline.detail: The entry precedes the first printing by a year.

timeline.label: The First Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Published by Nicholas Ling and John Trundle. Much shorter than the later texts, and differently ordered in places.

timeline.label: The Second Quarto printed
timeline.detail: Printed by James Roberts for Nicholas Ling, and advertised as enlarged; the longest of the early versions.

timeline.label: The First Folio text
timeline.detail: Prints material the Second Quarto lacks and omits material it has, so the two are witnesses rather than drafts.

timeline.label: Thomas Betterton plays Hamlet after the theatres reopen
timeline.detail: The beginning of the long tradition in which the part is treated as the measure of an actor.

timeline.label: Sarah Bernhardt plays Hamlet
timeline.detail: A reminder that the role has never been securely fixed to one kind of body or voice.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Heavily cut, and the first Shakespeare film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh films a full-text Hamlet
timeline.detail: A four-hour screen version that keeps the material most productions have to lose.

places.name: Kronborg Castle, Helsingør
places.note: The fortress on the sound that gave Shakespeare his Elsinore, guarding the narrowest crossing into the Baltic.

places.name: The Øresund
places.note: The strait the battlements overlook, and the water Hamlet is shipped across towards England.

places.name: Wittenberg
places.note: The university Hamlet and Horatio come from, and which Claudius will not let him return to.

places.name: Paris
places.note: Where Laertes goes, and where Reynaldo is sent to spread useful slander about him.

places.name: London
places.note: England, where the sealed commission sends Hamlet to die — and where the play was first performed.

related.why: The opposite case: a tragedy of soliloquy in which the hero acts far too quickly and thinks about it afterwards.
Written within a few years, and equally concerned with what happens when a court stops being able to tell truth from performance.
The play Hamlet remembers when Polonius says he once played Caesar, and another study of a political killing argued out in advance.
The next of the great tragedies, and the clearest contrast: a hero destroyed by accepting evidence too quickly.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller textual, critical and performance material on the three early texts.

books.title: Henry V
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: England and northern France, 1414-1420
books.lengthNote: Around 3,200 lines in the Folio — the quarto of 1600 is barely half that
books.openingLine: O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend The brightest heaven of invention
books.summary: A king takes an army across the Channel on a claim that churchmen have built for him, sacks a town by threatening its children, and wins a battle he had no business winning. Shakespeare frames it with a Chorus who describes a national epic, and then writes scenes that will not quite fit inside it: a soldier who asks whose fault it will be if the cause is bad, a boy who would trade his fame for a pot of ale, an epilogue that hands the conquest straight back.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Henry V
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, in which each act's Chorus is numbered as scene 0. The 1600 quarto contains none of the Chorus speeches.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A claim assembled to order
structure.summary: Two bishops discuss a bill that would strip the Church of its land and agree that a French war would be a useful distraction. Canterbury then delivers a sixty-line genealogy proving Henry's right to France, and takes the sin of it on his own head when the king asks. The Dauphin's gift of tennis balls turns a legal argument into a personal one.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The Chorus apologises for the stage and asks the audience to supply the horses, the fleet and the two kingdoms.

scenes.title: The bishops
scenes.summary: Canterbury and Ely count the cost of a parliamentary bill and the value of the king's new piety.

scenes.title: Salic law and tennis balls
scenes.summary: The claim is argued at length; the French ambassadors deliver an insult; Henry promises widows.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Old friends cut away
structure.summary: Henry traps Cambridge, Scroop and Grey into demanding severity for a drunkard and then hands them their own arrest warrants. In Eastcheap, Falstaff dies offstage and is given an obituary by a hostess who cannot manage the word. The men who knew the king when he was a prince pack up and follow the army to France as looters.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The Chorus reports a country arming, and warns of treason paid for by France.

scenes.title: Eastcheap
scenes.summary: Nym and Pistol quarrel over the hostess; word comes that Falstaff is dying.

scenes.title: Southampton
scenes.summary: The three conspirators argue for harshness and are condemned out of their own mouths.

scenes.title: Falstaff's death
scenes.summary: The Hostess describes the death; Pistol, Nym and Bardolph leave for France.

scenes.title: The French court
scenes.summary: The French king takes the invasion seriously; the Dauphin does not; Exeter delivers the ultimatum.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Harfleur, and what a siege requires
structure.summary: The breach speech makes an exhausted army into a company of fathers and sons. When the town still holds, Henry stands at the gates and describes in detail the rape and infanticide that will follow if he has to attack again — and the town surrenders, so the audience never learns whether he meant it. Katharine begins learning English; the army begins to get sick.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The fleet crosses; the Chorus tells the audience to imagine the siege guns.

scenes.title: The breach
scenes.summary: 'Once more unto the breach': the most famous exhortation in English drama.

scenes.title: Behind the breach
scenes.summary: Bardolph, Nym and Pistol hang back; the Boy sizes them up; four captains of four nations argue.

scenes.title: The gates
scenes.summary: Henry threatens the townspeople of Harfleur; the governor yields.

scenes.title: The English lesson
scenes.summary: Katharine learns the parts of the body from Alice, and finds two of the words obscene.

scenes.title: The French react
scenes.summary: The French nobility are appalled to be beaten in the field by an army they despise.

scenes.title: Bardolph hanged
scenes.summary: Fluellen reports the execution of a thief; Henry confirms it without a pause.

scenes.title: The French camp
scenes.summary: Noblemen pass the night before the battle praising their own horses.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The night, and the battle
structure.summary: Disguised in a borrowed cloak, Henry argues with two soldiers about whether a king answers for the souls of the men he leads, loses the argument in substance, and prays alone about his father's usurpation. In the morning he turns a shortage of men into the Crispin's Day speech. The victory is followed immediately by an order to kill the prisoners.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: The Chorus's night-piece: two camps, the hum of either army, and a little touch of Harry in the night.

scenes.title: The argument in the dark
scenes.summary: Henry in disguise debates responsibility with Bates and Williams, quarrels over a glove, and prays.

scenes.title: The French mount
scenes.summary: The French ride out confident of an easy morning.

scenes.title: Saint Crispin's Day
scenes.summary: Answering a wish for more men, Henry makes scarcity the point of the speech.

scenes.title: Pistol takes a prisoner
scenes.summary: A Frenchman is ransomed through a boy interpreter; the comedy runs beside the killing.

scenes.title: French despair
scenes.summary: The French lords resolve to die rather than live shamed.

scenes.title: The order
scenes.summary: Told the French have rallied, Henry commands that every soldier kill his prisoners.

scenes.title: The boys in the camp
scenes.summary: Fluellen and Gower report the killing of the luggage-boys; Henry says he was not angry until this instant.

scenes.title: The reckoning
scenes.summary: The dead are counted, the disparity is enormous, and Henry credits God.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: A leek, a treaty and a marriage
structure.summary: Fluellen makes Pistol eat a leek, which is the last the play sees of Eastcheap. Burgundy describes a France gone to weeds while the two courts negotiate, and Henry courts Katharine in the plain-soldier manner of a man who has already been promised her in the treaty. The Chorus then returns to say that their son lost everything.

scenes.title: Prologue
scenes.summary: London greets the king; the Chorus glances at a general expected home from Ireland.

scenes.title: The leek
scenes.summary: Fluellen beats Pistol and makes him eat the leek he mocked.

scenes.title: Troyes
scenes.summary: Burgundy pleads for peace; Henry woos Katharine; the treaty makes him heir of France. The Epilogue undoes it.

characters.name: King Henry V
characters.summary: He can produce whatever voice a situation requires — legal, terrifying, fraternal, awkwardly amorous — and the play never lets the audience behind all of them at once. The one scene in which nobody knows he is the king is the one in which he is contradicted and cannot answer, and it is followed immediately by a prayer about his father's stolen crown.
characters.clue: He asks a bishop whether his claim is lawful, threatens a town with the murder of its infants, and borrows a cloak so that he can hear what his soldiers really think.

characters.name: The Chorus
characters.summary: It appears before every act to apologise for the theatre and to recruit the audience into supplying what the stage cannot. Its Henry is a mirror of all Christian kings moving through a clean epic; the scenes that follow are consistently more complicated, and the gap between the two is the play's method.
characters.clue: It begs pardon for the wooden stage, tells the audience to imagine the horses, and promises a king the following scenes do not quite deliver.

characters.name: The Archbishop of Canterbury
characters.summary: He opens the play worrying about a bill that would confiscate Church lands and closes his first scene proposing to fund a French war. His genealogical argument takes sixty-two lines, and when Henry asks whether the claim is honest he offers to carry the sin himself, which is not the same as saying yes.

characters.name: Katharine
characters.role: Princess of France, later Queen of England
characters.summary: She learns English from her waiting-woman two scenes after Harfleur falls, and the lesson collapses into laughter at two words that sound obscene in French — a comic scene about a woman preparing to be handed over with a country. In the last scene she asks whether it is possible to love the enemy of France, and never quite answers.
characters.clue: She learns the words for hand, fingers and neck from her waiting-woman, and is embarrassed by two of them.

characters.name: Fluellen
characters.summary: He talks constantly about the disciplines of the wars and tests every event against a classical precedent, which makes him funny; he is also the only officer who reports the killing of the boys as a breach of the law of arms. The comic accent and the moral accuracy belong to the same character and the play does not separate them.
characters.clue: A captain who compares Monmouth to Macedon because both have a river, and who makes a braggart eat a leek.

relationships.label: serves, and is claimed as a countryman by

characters.name: Michael Williams
characters.summary: He states the case against the war more precisely than anyone else in the play: if the cause is bad, the reckoning belongs to the man who ordered it. Henry answers him at length about the souls of individual soldiers, which is not the question he asked, and the disguise means he never knows he has been debating the king.
characters.clue: He tells a stranger by the fire that legs and arms chopped off in battle will cry out at the latter day, and exchanges gloves with him.

characters.name: Pistol
characters.summary: He speaks in fragments of old plays and treats the campaign as a business opportunity, ransoming a terrified Frenchman he cannot understand. What is left of Falstaff's world goes to France and comes back as a man planning to pass off his beating as war wounds.

characters.name: The Boy
characters.role: Servant to Pistol, Bardolph and Nym
characters.summary: He gives a clear-eyed account of the three men he works for, decides that their swaggering is not for him, and would trade all his fame for a pot of ale and safety. He is with the luggage when the French attack the camp, and the play does not show his death.
characters.clue: He would give all his fame for a pot of ale and safety, and is left minding the baggage.

characters.name: Exeter
characters.summary: He carries the ultimatum to Paris and returns with the tennis balls' reply, and it is he who tells the French king that the coming widows and orphans will be laid at his door. He functions as the war's clear voice: no argument about the claim, only a statement of what refusing it will cost.

characters.name: The Dauphin
characters.summary: He sends the tennis balls, spends the night before Agincourt praising his own horse, and is the play's argument that aristocratic confidence is a military weakness. His contempt for the English is the engine of the first act and the reason the French lose the fourth.

themes.name: What a king is for
themes.summary: The play asks repeatedly what the crown actually consists of, and the answer Henry reaches alone at night is ceremony: a set of forms that buys obedience and costs sleep. Nothing in the victory revises that answer; it is simply not spoken of again once there are people watching.
themes.development: Set out in the bishops' account of the reformed prince in 1.1, tested in the dark in 4.1, and closed off by an Epilogue that reduces the whole reign to a short time greatly lived.

themes.name: Whether the war is just
themes.summary: The claim is manufactured in Act I by men with a financial motive, blessed by a churchman who offers to bear the sin, and never examined again by anyone at court. It is a common soldier, in the dark, who asks the question the archbishop was paid to settle.
themes.development: Canterbury's genealogy in 1.2; Williams's objection in 4.1; the order to kill the prisoners in 4.6, which nobody on stage condemns.

themes.name: One army, four countries
themes.summary: The English army contains a Welshman, an Irishman and a Scot who cannot agree on anything except that they are fighting the French, and the play both laughs at their accents and takes their professionalism seriously. On the French side, Katharine's English lesson makes the conquest audible as a problem of language.
themes.development: The captains' quarrel in 3.2, the lesson in 3.4, Fluellen's leek in 5.1 and Henry's claim in 4.7 that he is Welsh himself.

themes.name: Persuasion as a weapon
themes.summary: Henry's speeches are not decoration; they are the mechanism by which a tired, outnumbered army agrees to fight. The play stages the same skill turned in four directions — law, terror, fellowship and courtship — so that the audience can see it working and notice that it is a technique.
themes.development: Legal argument in 1.2, terror at Harfleur in 3.3, fellowship at Agincourt in 4.3, and a deliberately clumsy plainness at Troyes in 5.2.

themes.name: Ceremony and the private man
themes.summary: Stripped of recognition by a borrowed cloak, Henry discovers that the difference between a king and a soldier is a set of observances that cannot cure a fever or buy an hour's sleep. The speech is delivered to nobody, and the play never returns to it in company.
themes.development: 4.1: the disguise, the argument, the soliloquy on ceremony and the prayer about his father's crown, all in one unbroken scene.

themes.name: How a victory is remembered
themes.summary: The Crispin's Day speech is about the future tense: old men forgetting, names remembered with advantages, a story taught to a son. The play is interested in the making of the legend as much as in the battle, which is why it ends by pointing out that everything won here was lost within a generation.
themes.development: The Chorus builds the legend across five acts; 4.3 predicts its transmission; the Epilogue's sonnet takes it all back in fourteen lines.

techniques.name: The Chorus
techniques.definition: A narrator who addresses the audience directly between the acts.
techniques.bookDefinition: A narrator who addresses the audience directly between the acts.
techniques.inThisBook: Uniquely in Shakespeare, a Chorus appears before every act and returns at the end. It supplies scale, apologises for the stage, and consistently describes a more heroic play than the one being performed.

techniques.name: Anaphora
techniques.definition: Beginning successive clauses with the same word.
techniques.bookDefinition: Beginning successive clauses with the same word.
techniques.inThisBook: The battle speeches run on it — 'Once more... once more', 'mock out of their dear husbands; Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down' — and the repetition does the work of an argument the speeches never actually make.

techniques.name: Juxtaposition of scenes
techniques.definition: Placing two scenes side by side so that each comments on the other.
techniques.bookDefinition: Placing two scenes side by side so that each comments on the other.
techniques.inThisBook: The breach speech at 3.1 is followed at once by Bardolph and Nym refusing to go through it; the reckoning of the dead at 4.8 comes minutes after the order to kill the prisoners.

techniques.name: Dialect and broken English
techniques.definition: Regional speech written phonetically.
techniques.bookDefinition: Representing national or foreign speech in the spelling of the line.
techniques.inThisBook: Fluellen, Macmorris and Jamy are written phonetically, and Katharine's lesson turns English into a set of sounds to be got wrong. The nation the play assembles is audibly made of several.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud.
techniques.inThisBook: Henry has only one of real substance, and it comes at four in the morning after he has lost an argument with a private soldier. Everything else he says is performed for somebody.

techniques.name: The sonnet epilogue
techniques.definition: A fourteen-line rhymed poem used to close a play.
techniques.bookDefinition: A fourteen-line rhymed poem used to close a play.
techniques.inThisBook: The Epilogue is a sonnet, and it spends its last six lines explaining that Henry's son lost France and bled England — the tightest form in English used to cancel five acts of triumph.

quotations.text: O for a Muse of fire, that would ascend The brightest heaven of invention, A kingdom for a stage, princes to act And monarchs to behold the swelling scene!
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The opening lines of the play.
quotations.analysis: The play begins by wishing it were a different play, performed by actual kings in an actual kingdom. 'A kingdom for a stage' reverses Richard III's famous bargain, and the wish is impossible by design: everything the Chorus asks for is precisely what the theatre cannot supply, which is how the audience gets recruited.

quotations.text: can this cockpit hold The vasty fields of France? or may we cram Within this wooden O the very casques That did affright the air at Agincourt?
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Prologue, apologising for the theatre.
quotations.analysis: The question is rhetorical and the answer is no, which is the point: the play will do it anyway, and the audience will have agreed to let it. 'Wooden O' describes the playhouse the first spectators were standing in, and the word for helmets, casques, is doing the work of an entire army.

quotations.text: And let us, ciphers to this great accompt, On your imaginary forces work.
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: Asking the audience to supply what the stage cannot.
quotations.analysis: A cipher is a zero, worth nothing alone and everything in the right column, and the actors are cheerfully calling themselves nothings. 'Forces' is the play's first use of a military word, and it is applied to the audience — the invasion of France begins with the people watching being conscripted.

quotations.text: May I with right and conscience make this claim?
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: After Canterbury's long genealogical argument for the French crown.
quotations.analysis: It is the right question, asked of the one man in England with a financial interest in the answer. Canterbury does not say yes: he says 'The sin upon my head, dread sovereign', which offers to take the blame rather than to remove it — and Henry accepts the offer without pressing further.

quotations.text: for many a thousand widows Shall this his mock mock out of their dear husbands; Mock mothers from their sons, mock castles down;
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Replying to the Dauphin's present of tennis balls.
quotations.analysis: He is answering an insult, and he answers it by itemising the dead in advance: widows, then mothers, then buildings, in descending order of grief. 'Mock' is used five times in three lines, so a joke about tennis turns into the word for the whole war — and the responsibility is carefully assigned to the man who made the joke.

quotations.text: for his nose was as sharp as a pen, and a' babbled of green fields.
quotations.speaker: Hostess
quotations.context: Describing Falstaff's death to Pistol, Bardolph and Nym.
quotations.analysis: The greatest comic character in English drama dies offstage, between scenes, in a hostess's muddled prose, and is given one unforgettable image by a woman who is not trying to be eloquent. Eastcheap is being closed down: within forty lines the survivors are on their way to France to steal what they can.

quotations.text: Once more unto the breach, dear friends, once more; Or close the wall up with our English dead.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: At Harfleur, rallying an assault that has already failed once.
quotations.analysis: The two alternatives offered are to go forward or to become masonry, and the second is presented as an equally good outcome. 'Once more' admits that this has already been tried and failed, which is the fact the speech has to convert into a reason — and the whole of the rest of it is about ancestry, because the present tense is not helping.

quotations.text: But when the blast of war blows in our ears, Then imitate the action of the tiger; Stiffen the sinews, summon up the blood, Disguise fair nature with hard-favour'd rage;
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The continuation of the breach speech.
quotations.analysis: 'Imitate' and 'disguise' are theatre words: he is asking his soldiers to act ferocity rather than to feel it, and giving them stage directions for the face. The speech assumes that fair nature is what men are actually made of, which makes the ferocity a costume — and raises the question of what is underneath Henry's own.

quotations.text: The game's afoot: Follow your spirit, and upon this charge Cry 'God for Harry, England, and Saint George!'
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The last lines of the breach speech.
quotations.analysis: The order of the three names is worth noticing: the king comes before the country, and the saint comes last. 'The game's afoot' turns a siege into hunting, which is the register the whole speech has been reaching for — greyhounds in the slips, straining at the start.

quotations.text: Would I were in an alehouse in London! I would give all my fame for a pot of ale and safety.
quotations.speaker: Boy
quotations.context: Behind the breach, with Pistol declining to advance.
quotations.analysis: Ten lines after the most famous call to arms in the language, a child says he would sell the whole thing for a drink and not being killed. The play puts the two speeches in consecutive scenes on purpose, and gives the honest one to the youngest person on stage.

quotations.text: The gates of mercy shall be all shut up, And the flesh'd soldier, rough and hard of heart, In liberty of bloody hand shall range With conscience wide as hell, mowing like grass Your fresh-fair virgins and your flowering infants.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: At the gates of Harfleur, demanding surrender.
quotations.analysis: The threat is framed grammatically as something that will happen rather than something he will do — the soldiers range, the hand is bloody, and the king is a bystander to his own army. He then tells the townspeople the fault will be theirs, which is the same transfer of blame Canterbury performed for him in Act I.

quotations.text: The poor condemned English, Like sacrifices, by their watchful fires Sit patiently and inly ruminate The morning's danger
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The night before Agincourt.
quotations.analysis: 'Condemned' and 'sacrifices' are the Chorus's own words for an army it otherwise celebrates, and the tone of the fourth Prologue is quite unlike the first. It is the one place where the narrator's version and the play's version agree — and the scene that follows immediately puts the king among those fires in a borrowed cloak.

quotations.text: I am afeard there are few die well that die in a battle; for how can they charitably dispose of any thing, when blood is their argument?
quotations.speaker: Williams
quotations.context: To a stranger by the fire, who is the king.
quotations.analysis: The objection is not about the politics of the claim but about dying unprepared, which in 1599 was a real and specific fear. 'Blood is their argument' compresses the case: men killing cannot also be settling their affairs, and someone has put them in that position — which is the sentence Henry spends the next forty lines not answering.

quotations.text: Every subject's duty is the king's; but every subject's soul is his own.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The conclusion of his long reply to Williams and Bates.
quotations.analysis: It is a clean and quotable separation, and it answers a question nobody asked: Williams had raised the guilt of the man who ordered the battle, not the state of each soldier's conscience. The neatness is the evasion, and the prayer that follows a hundred lines later shows that Henry knows it.

quotations.text: Upon the king! let us our lives, our souls, Our debts, our careful wives, Our children and our sins lay on the king! We must bear all.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after the soldiers leave.
quotations.analysis: He is mimicking his subjects' voices, piling their possessions onto himself in a list that starts with lives and ends with sins. The pronoun slips from 'us' to 'we' without settling whose side he is arguing from, which is the closest the play comes to showing the man inside the office losing track of the boundary.

quotations.text: And what art thou, thou idle ceremony? What kind of god art thou, that suffer'st more Of mortal griefs than do thy worshippers?
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The centre of the soliloquy on what a king has that a private man has not.
quotations.analysis: He addresses ceremony as a person and then as a deity, and finds it a god that suffers more than the people who pray to it. The speech is an audit: rents, comings in, place, degree and form on one side, and a slave's untroubled sleep on the other, with the balance clearly against the crown.

quotations.text: Not to-day, O Lord, O, not to-day, think not upon the fault My father made in compassing the crown!
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Praying alone before the battle.
quotations.analysis: The prayer is not for victory but for a postponement, and the fault he names is his father's deposition of Richard II — the event that makes his own title questionable. He then lists the chantries and the tears and the five hundred poor on his payroll, and ends by admitting that all of it is worth nothing, which is the most honest sentence he speaks.

quotations.text: That he which hath no stomach to this fight, Let him depart; his passport shall be made And crowns for convoy put into his purse: We would not die in that man's company That fears his fellowship to die with us.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Answering Westmoreland's wish for ten thousand more men from England.
quotations.analysis: The offer of a passport and travelling money is safe to make because nobody can now accept it, which is the trick of the whole speech: he converts a shortage into a privilege before naming the day. Note that he does not say such a man is a coward — only that he would be poor company to die with.

quotations.text: From this day to the ending of the world, But we in it shall be remember'd; We few, we happy few, we band of brothers; For he to-day that sheds his blood with me Shall be my brother
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: The Saint Crispin's Day speech, before the battle.
quotations.analysis: The tense is the engine: almost the whole speech is in the future, describing old men in flowing cups remembering a day that has not happened. Brotherhood is offered as payment, and the play tests it immediately — Williams, who was promised gentling, spends the next scenes in a quarrel over a glove with the man who promised it.

quotations.text: The French have reinforced their scatter'd men: Then every soldier kill his prisoners: Give the word through.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: In the middle of the battle, on hearing an alarm.
quotations.analysis: Three lines, no argument, no soliloquy, and the audience is given no chance to decide what it thinks before the next scene starts. Shakespeare places the order before the report of the murdered luggage-boys rather than after it, so it cannot be read as retaliation — a sequence the 1600 quarto and several famous productions have quietly rearranged or cut.

quotations.text: Yes, captain; but with this acknowledgement, That God fought for us.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Permitting Fluellen to announce the casualty figures.
quotations.analysis: The numbers just read out are wildly lopsided, and the king's response is to forbid any English explanation of them. It is genuine piety and excellent policy at once: attributing the victory to God removes it from the reach of anyone who might ask harder questions about the campaign that produced it.

quotations.text: I speak to thee plain soldier: If thou canst love me for this, take me: if not, to say to thee that I shall die, is true; but for thy love, by the Lord, no; yet I love thee too.
quotations.speaker: King Henry V
quotations.context: Courting Katharine at Troyes, in prose.
quotations.analysis: The man who has produced perfect verse on demand for four acts spends the courtship insisting he has no eloquence, which is itself the most calculated performance in the play. The honesty is real in one respect: he will not claim he would die for her, and the sentence about love arrives after the treaty has already awarded her to him.

quotations.text: Small time, but in that small most greatly lived This star of England: Fortune made his sword; By which the world's best garden be achieved, And of it left his son imperial lord.
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The Epilogue, spoken after the betrothal.
quotations.analysis: 'Fortune made his sword' quietly withdraws the credit that Act IV gave to God and Act III to Henry's own rhetoric. The Epilogue is a sonnet, and it uses its turn to move from the garden achieved to the garden lost, which is the tightest possible form for undoing five acts.

quotations.text: Henry the Sixth, in infant bands crown'd King Of France and England, did this king succeed; Whose state so many had the managing, That they lost France and made his England bleed:
quotations.speaker: Chorus
quotations.context: The last four lines before the appeal to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The final word on the conquest is that it did not last, and the audience is reminded that they have already seen the sequel — the Henry VI plays were written and staged years earlier. The play ends by pointing backwards in the theatre and forwards in the history, which leaves the victory suspended between the two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The fifth Chorus imagines a general returning in triumph from Ireland, which points to the months of the Earl of Essex's expedition.

atAGlance.label: Early texts
atAGlance.note: The quarto has no Choruses and much less of the night before Agincourt. Editions follow the Folio.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.value: Holinshed, Hall and an older play
atAGlance.note: The anonymous Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth had already put the same career on the London stage.

atAGlance.label: The battle
atAGlance.note: Saint Crispin's Day, which Henry turns into a bond between everyone who survives it.

criticalViews.position: The play as national epic
criticalViews.summary: The oldest and most durable reading takes the Chorus at its word and the Crispin's Day speech at face value: a study of successful leadership and the making of a nation out of four quarrelling countries.
criticalViews.counter: It has to work around the bishops' motives in Act I, the threat at Harfleur, the order in 4.6 and an Epilogue that says the whole thing was undone within a generation.

criticalViews.position: The play as an interrogation of the war
criticalViews.summary: A reading that has dominated British theatre since the 1960s treats the heroic scenes as the surface and Williams, the Boy, Bardolph's hanging and the prisoners as the evidence underneath it.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed too far it makes the Crispin's Day speech unplayable, when the play plainly wants an audience to be moved by it before it asks them to think again.

criticalViews.position: The play as an argument about theatre
criticalViews.summary: A third approach starts from the Chorus: a play that keeps saying it cannot show what it describes is also a play about how national stories are manufactured and who agrees to believe them.
criticalViews.counter: It risks treating the war as a metaphor, when Harfleur and the prisoners are staged as events rather than as figures of speech.

essayQuestions.question: Does Henry V celebrate its king or put him on trial?
essayQuestions.focus: Heroism, evidence and the structure of the play
plan: Establish the Chorus's version first — mirror of all Christian kings — so that the later scenes have something to be measured against.
Set the breach speech in 3.1 beside the threat at the gates in 3.3: the same voice, ten minutes apart, doing two entirely different things.
Use 4.1 as the play's own cross-examination, and note that Williams is never answered on the point he actually raised.
Weigh 4.6 carefully: the order comes before the killing of the boys, not after it.
Conclude with the Epilogue, which is a sonnet, and which gives the last word to loss rather than to Agincourt.

essayQuestions.question: What does the Chorus do to the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, imagination and unreliability
plan: Describe the Chorus's stated job: apologising for the stage and recruiting the audience's imaginary forces.
Show the pattern of contradiction — a heroic prologue followed by bishops counting money, or by Pistol refusing to advance.
Identify the fourth Prologue as the exception, where narrator and play agree on condemned men by their fires.
Consider the 1600 quarto, which has no Choruses at all, and what a performance without them would be like.
Decide whether the Chorus is propaganda, nostalgia, or an invitation to notice how national stories get made.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play present the ordinary soldier?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, responsibility and the cost of the campaign
plan: Begin with the Eastcheap survivors in Act II and what they say they have come to France for.
Use the Boy's speech at 3.2 as the deliberate reply to the breach speech that precedes it.
Read the Williams and Bates exchange in 4.1 as a genuine argument rather than a lapse in morale, and track what Henry concedes.
Follow the glove quarrel through to 4.8, and ask what the gentling promised in the Crispin's Day speech actually amounts to.
Close with the killing of the luggage-boys and the fact that the play never shows the Boy's death.

essayQuestions.question: 'A play about language as much as about war.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Rhetoric, dialect and translation
plan: Set out Henry's four registers: the legal argument of 1.2, the terror of 3.3, the fellowship of 4.3 and the plainness of 5.2.
Examine the captains' scene at 3.2 as an attempt to make one army out of four kinds of English.
Read Katharine's lesson in 3.4 as conquest happening in vocabulary before it happens in the treaty.
Use Pistol's borrowed theatrical rant as the play's example of rhetoric with nothing behind it.
Return to the Chorus, whose whole function is to say that words must do the work the stage cannot.

discussionQuestions: Canterbury offers to take the sin of the war on his own head. Does that settle anything?
Henry orders the prisoners killed before he hears about the boys in the camp. Does the order of those scenes change how you read him?
Williams argues with a man he does not know is the king, and is never told he won. What would change if he were?
The Epilogue spends its last lines explaining that everything won here was lost. Why end a triumph that way?
Olivier's 1944 film cuts the Harfleur threat and the prisoners. Is a production that keeps them telling the truth, or making a different argument?

timeline.label: Henry V succeeds his father
timeline.detail: Henry IV had taken the crown from Richard II in 1399, which is the fault the king prays about before Agincourt.

timeline.label: The Battle of Agincourt, 25 October
timeline.detail: Fought on Saint Crispin's Day after the siege of Harfleur and a long, sick march towards Calais.

timeline.label: The Treaty of Troyes
timeline.detail: Henry was recognised as heir to the French crown and married Katharine of Valois.

timeline.label: Henry dies; his infant son succeeds
timeline.detail: Henry VI was not yet a year old, which is the fact the Epilogue closes on.

timeline.label: Holinshed's Chronicles reissued
timeline.detail: Shakespeare's principal source for the campaign, alongside Edward Hall.

timeline.label: The Famous Victories of Henry the Fifth printed
timeline.detail: An anonymous earlier play covering the same career, which had already made the wild prince and the tennis balls familiar.

timeline.label: Henry V written and first performed
timeline.detail: The fifth Chorus's general returning from Ireland is almost certainly the Earl of Essex, who left in March and came home disgraced in September.

timeline.label: The first quarto
timeline.detail: About half the length of the Folio text, with no Chorus speeches and far less of the night-time debate among the soldiers.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The fuller text, and the basis of modern editions.

timeline.label: Laurence Olivier's film
timeline.detail: Made during the Second World War, and shaped throughout by that purpose: the Harfleur threat and the order to kill the prisoners are not in it.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: A muddier, more exhausted Agincourt, which restored much of what the 1944 version had removed.

places.name: London
places.note: The council chamber of Act I, the Eastcheap of Act II, and the city that welcomes the king home in the fifth Prologue.

places.name: Southampton
places.note: Where the fleet gathers and the three conspirators are exposed and executed.

places.name: Harfleur
places.note: The town besieged in Act III, and the gates at which Henry describes what a sack would look like.

places.name: Azincourt
places.note: The village in Picardy that gave its name to the battle of 25 October 1415.

places.name: Calais
places.note: The English-held port the exhausted army was marching towards when the French cut them off.

places.name: Troyes
places.note: Where the treaty of Act V was made and the marriage agreed.

places.name: Monmouth
places.note: Henry's birthplace, and the town Fluellen compares to Macedon on the grounds that both have a river.

related.why: The prince before the crown, and Falstaff alive — the play whose promises this one collects on.
Ends with the rejection of Falstaff, which is the decision Henry V spends its second act paying for.
The deposition that made the Lancastrian title doubtful, and the fault Henry prays about before Agincourt.
The sequel Shakespeare had already written: France lost, exactly as the Epilogue says.
Written in the same year, and equally interested in how a public speech turns an audience into an army.

books.title: Jane Eyre
books.author: Charlotte Brontë
books.setting: Five houses in the north of England — Gateshead, Lowood, Thornfield, Moor House and Ferndean — with Jamaica and Madeira offstage
books.lengthNote: Thirty-eight chapters, published in three volumes and usually printed straight through
books.openingLine: There was no possibility of taking a walk that day.
books.summary: An orphan with no money, no family willing to own her and no beauty to trade on argues her way to the terms she will accept. The novel is subtitled an autobiography and behaves like one: it is told entirely from inside Jane's judgement, it addresses the reader directly at the decisive moments, and it refuses both the men who want her until the arrangement is one she can hold without losing herself.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Jane Eyre
sourceText.note: References give the chapter, numbered straight through from 1 to 38. The original three-volume division is not marked in this text, so it is not used in references here.

structure.label: Chapters 1–4
structure.title: Gateshead and the red-room
structure.summary: A ten-year-old dependent is struck by her cousin, blamed for it, and locked in the room where her uncle died. The opening is a lesson in how a household decides who counts, and Jane's first act of rebellion is verbal: she tells her aunt the truth about herself and feels the power of it.

scenes.summary: Hidden behind a window curtain with Bewick's birds; John Reed throws the book at her head.
The red-room: cold, grand, unused since her uncle's death, and the place where her reason first says the word unjust.
Brocklehurst interviews her about hell; she tells Mrs Reed exactly what she thinks of her and is sent away.

structure.label: Chapters 5–10
structure.title: Lowood, Helen Burns and eight years
structure.summary: A charity school run on cold water, burnt porridge and public humiliation, where Jane meets two answers to injustice: Miss Temple's practical decency and Helen Burns's doctrine of endurance. A typhus epidemic kills half the school and shames the management into reform.

scenes.summary: Helen, beaten for untidiness, explains why she does not resent it; Jane says she could not do the same.
Brocklehurst orders the girls' hair cut off while his own daughters stand by in velvet and false curls.
Typhus empties the school; Helen dies of consumption in Jane's arms, unmourned by the institution.
Eight years on, Jane advertises for a situation and receives one reply, from Thornfield.

structure.label: Chapters 11–20
structure.title: Thornfield, and the laugh on the third storey
structure.summary: Governess to a French child in a comfortable house with one door nobody opens. Jane's restlessness on the leads produces the novel's most direct statement about what women are permitted; then a man falls off a horse in a lane, a bed catches fire at night, and a guest is stabbed in the dark.

scenes.summary: Pacing the third-storey corridor, Jane argues that women feel as men feel; a strange laugh interrupts her.
In Hay Lane, a dog and a horse out of Bessie's ghost stories turn out to be Pilot and Mr Rochester.
Jane wakes to smoke, puts out a fire in Rochester's bed and is told to tell nobody.
Mason is attacked upstairs; Jane holds a sponge and a candle for hours and is told nothing.

structure.label: Chapters 21–27
structure.title: The proposal, the interruption and the flight
structure.summary: Mrs Reed dies confessing that she hid a letter from Jane's uncle. Rochester proposes in the orchard and the chestnut tree is split by lightning that night. At the altar a solicitor produces a marriage register from Spanish Town, and Jane is taken upstairs to be shown what is in the attic.

scenes.summary: The orchard: Jane's speech about being poor, obscure, plain and little, and about spirits standing equal.
The wedding is stopped; Rochester takes the whole party up to see Bertha Mason.
Rochester's account of Jamaica and his offer of the south of France; Jane leaves before dawn with nothing.

structure.label: Chapters 28–35
structure.title: Moor House, money and St John Rivers
structure.summary: Jane begs on the moor, nearly dies at a door, and is taken in by the three people who turn out to be her cousins. An inheritance makes her independent; she divides it four ways. Then St John asks her to marry him and go to India, not because he loves her but because she would be useful.

scenes.summary: Village school-teaching, and Jane's discomfort at how far she has fallen in her own estimation.
The inheritance from John Eyre of Madeira, and the discovery that the Rivers family are her cousins.
St John tells her she is formed for labour, not for love, and claims her for his Sovereign's service.
She is close to consenting when she hears a voice calling her name across the moor.

structure.label: Chapters 36–38
structure.title: Ferndean
structure.summary: Thornfield is a blackened shell: Bertha set it alight and jumped from the roof, and Rochester lost a hand and his sight getting the servants out. Jane finds him in a damp house in a wood, and this time she has money, family and the right to choose. The last chapter reports ten years of marriage in the first person plural.

scenes.summary: The innkeeper's account of the fire, the woman on the roof and the pavement below.
Jane arrives with a tray of candles and water, and declines to explain herself quickly.
Reader, I married him: a quiet wedding, St John's death in India, and ten years of being somebody's life.

characters.name: Jane Eyre
characters.summary: Small, plain, penniless and entirely unwilling to be grateful. Her defining habit is argument: she wins the red-room scene, the orchard scene and the Moor House scene by reasoning out loud, and the novel's structure follows her refusals rather than her attachments.
characters.clue: She is locked in a red room at ten, teaches a French child to sing, and walks out of a house at dawn with nothing rather than take a name she has no right to.

relationships.label: governess to his ward, later his wife

characters.name: Edward Fairfax Rochester
characters.summary: A man who tells Jane an enormous amount and withholds the one thing that matters, and who conducts his courtship partly by dressing up as a fortune-teller. The novel likes him and does not excuse him: his account of Jamaica is at once the most sympathetic and the least trustworthy passage in the book.
characters.clue: He falls off a horse on ice, keeps a secret on the third storey, and loses a hand and his sight trying to get a woman off a burning roof.

characters.name: Bertha Mason
characters.role: Rochester's wife, kept on the third storey
characters.summary: Everything the reader learns about her arrives through people with reasons to be believed: her husband, her brother, her keeper. She has no dialogue. What she does have is a series of actions — the fire in the bed, the torn veil, the attack on Mason, the burning of the house — that read as purpose when they are not being described as madness.
characters.clue: She is heard before she is seen, tears a wedding veil in two, and takes a house down with her from the roof.

characters.name: St John Rivers
characters.summary: The novel's hardest test, because he is not a villain. He gives Jane a home, a school and a fortune, and then asks for her whole life on the grounds that she is fitted for work rather than affection. He is in love with someone else and has decided that this disqualifies him from wanting her.
characters.clue: He is handsome as a Greek statue and about as warm, loves a woman he will not marry, and wants a wife chiefly as an instrument.

relationships.label: cousin, benefactor and would-be husband of

characters.name: Helen Burns
characters.summary: She offers the doctrine of endurance in its most attractive form: forgive, look past the body, live in calm looking to the end. Jane finds it magnificent and unusable. Helen's death is the novel's argument that patience is a real answer and not, for Jane, the available one.
characters.clue: She is beaten for untidiness, reads Rasselas at a window, and tells her friend that life is too short for registering wrongs.

characters.name: Mrs Reed
characters.role: Jane's aunt by marriage, of Gateshead
characters.summary: She promised her dying husband to bring the child up and has kept the letter of it for ten years while hating the child throughout. Her deathbed is remarkable for what it does not contain: she confesses to hiding a letter from Jane's uncle and still will not be reconciled.
characters.clue: She keeps a promise to a dead man without any of the warmth that would have made it worth keeping, and dies still refusing to be forgiven.

characters.name: Mr Brocklehurst
characters.role: Treasurer and manager of Lowood School
characters.summary: He preaches mortification of the flesh to eighty half-starved girls and orders their hair cut off while his own daughters wait in velvet and ostrich plumes. Brontë makes him a study in a particular hypocrisy: not a man who disbelieves his doctrine, but one who has never imagined it applying to himself.
characters.clue: He is a black pillar of a man who asks a ten-year-old how she will avoid the pit, and preaches plain living to girls he is underfeeding.

relationships.label: brands as a liar before the school
presides over the school that kills

characters.name: Miss Temple
characters.summary: The one adult in the first half of the book who behaves decently and has the authority to act on it: she orders bread and cheese for the girls, writes to a doctor to clear Jane's name, and tells the truth about it publicly. Her marriage and departure are what finally make Jane restless enough to leave.
characters.clue: She feeds the school at her own expense after a burnt breakfast and quietly obtains the evidence that clears a child publicly accused.

characters.name: Adèle Varens
characters.summary: A French child fond of dresses and performance whom Rochester describes with a coolness the novel does not endorse. Jane's treatment of her is one of the quiet tests in the book: she teaches her, defends her against the charge of being merely frivolous, and looks after her placement at the end.
characters.clue: She sings a grown woman's song about betrayal without understanding it, and is told her guardian is not her father.

characters.name: Grace Poole
characters.role: The servant who keeps the third storey
characters.summary: Paid two hundred a year to sit with a woman nobody names, and blamed for everything that happens on her watch. She is the household's explanation for the unexplainable noises, and the fact that everyone accepts the explanation says more about the house than about her.
characters.clue: She sews at an upper door, drinks when she should not, and is the name given to every noise nobody wants to investigate.

themes.name: Independence and equality
themes.summary: Jane's demand is not for love but for standing. The orchard speech puts it in terms of souls at God's feet, and the last movement of the novel puts it in terms of money: she cannot accept Rochester until she has her own income, her own relatives and no obligation to be grateful to him.
themes.development: Refusing Mrs Reed's authority at ten, refusing the south of France at nineteen, refusing St John's Sovereign's service at twenty, and arriving at Ferndean able to say she is her own mistress.

themes.name: Three religions
themes.summary: Brontë sets out three versions of Christian conduct and tests each against Jane. Brocklehurst preaches mortification he does not practise; Helen Burns practises forbearance Jane cannot manage; St John offers a self-abolishing usefulness that Jane recognises as a slower death. What she keeps is the law she says was given by God and sanctioned by man.
themes.development: Each is embodied in a house: Lowood's hypocrisy, Helen's deathbed, Moor House's vocation. Jane refuses all three arrangements and none of the belief.

themes.name: Passion and self-command
themes.summary: The novel's own imagery is fire and ice, and its position is that both can destroy. Jane's feeling for Rochester is described in terms as strong as anything in Victorian fiction, and the argument of Chapter 27 is that laws and principles exist for exactly the moment when feeling makes them inconvenient.
themes.development: The red-room's cold rage, the burning bed, the split chestnut tree, and then the deliberate iciness of Moor House — the book moves between temperatures as a way of measuring self-control.

themes.name: Rooms, locks and confinement
themes.summary: Jane is shut in the red-room at ten and taken to the third storey at nineteen, and the book plainly links the two: a woman put out of sight because she is inconvenient. The difference is that Jane can argue and be let out.
themes.development: Gateshead's locked door, Lowood's walls, the Thornfield attic, and Jane's own habit of pacing corridors because there is nowhere further to walk.

themes.name: Class, money and the governess
themes.summary: A governess is educated enough to teach a gentleman's children and poor enough to be a servant, which places her precisely nowhere. Jane feels the position in every scene with Blanche Ingram, and the novel solves it with an inheritance rather than with an argument, which readers have been objecting to ever since.
themes.development: From a dependent child at Gateshead to a salaried governess at Thornfield to a woman with twenty thousand pounds who gives three-quarters of it away.

themes.name: Jamaica, Madeira and what is offstage
themes.canonicalName: Jamaica, Madeira and what is offstage
themes.summary: The two turns of Jane's fortune both come from outside England: Rochester's marriage was arranged in Spanish Town for thirty thousand pounds, and Jane's inheritance comes from an uncle in the wine trade at Funchal. The novel's English settlement is paid for in colonies it barely describes.
themes.development: Bertha arrives as a rumour, then a register, then a body; John Eyre's letter arrives at Gateshead and is hidden for years before it finally frees Jane.

techniques.name: Address to the reader
techniques.definition: The narrator speaking straight out of the page to whoever is holding the book.
techniques.bookDefinition: The narrator speaking straight out of the page to whoever is holding the book.
techniques.inThisBook: Used at the hinges rather than for decoration: 'Reader, I married him' announces the marriage as Jane's action, with her as the subject of the verb and Rochester as its object.

techniques.name: Gothic inheritance
techniques.definition: Bells, darkness, apparitions, graves and locked rooms used to produce dread.
techniques.bookDefinition: Great houses, locked doors, night noises, interrupted weddings and secrets on an upper floor.
techniques.inThisBook: Brontë uses the machinery and then insists on explanations: the Gytrash in the lane is a dog, the laugh is a person, and the terror on the third storey is a marriage settlement.

techniques.name: Fire and ice
techniques.definition: A pair of opposed images used consistently to measure feeling.
techniques.bookDefinition: A pair of opposed images used consistently to measure feeling.
techniques.inThisBook: Rochester's world burns — the bed, the house — and St John's freezes; Jane has to find a temperature she can live at, and the novel tracks it in hearths, frost and weather.

techniques.name: Objects and omens
techniques.definition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
techniques.bookDefinition: Things in the narrative that carry a meaning the characters half-register.
