atAGlance.note: The Hero plot belongs to a European story family found in Ariosto and in Bandello; Beatrice and Benedick are Shakespeare's own.

atAGlance.label: Title
atAGlance.note: The two words sounded close in early modern English, and almost every turn of the plot depends on somebody noting — watching, overhearing or reporting.

criticalViews.position: The play belongs to Beatrice and Benedick
criticalViews.summary: On this reading the inherited slandered-bride plot is the frame and the invented couple are the picture: the comedy's real subject is two intelligent people arguing themselves out of a defence.
criticalViews.counter: It leaves Act IV hard to account for, since the church scene is the longest and most serious writing in the play and Hero is at the centre of it.

criticalViews.position: A comedy about evidence
criticalViews.summary: Criticism has long noticed that nothing here is learned first-hand. The same technique — a scene staged for a watcher — makes one marriage and nearly destroys another, which turns the play into an argument about how societies decide what is true.
criticalViews.counter: The resolution comes from a confession rather than from anybody reasoning better, so the play may be less confident about evidence than the reading suggests.

criticalViews.position: A play about what men are permitted to do
criticalViews.summary: Recent stage practice and criticism have concentrated on Claudio's public shaming of Hero, Leonato's readiness to believe it, and Beatrice's fury that revenge is a man's office. The comedy is then held open rather than closed by the second wedding.
criticalViews.counter: Hero herself is given no scene in which to judge Claudio, which makes it difficult to say what the play thinks the right ending would be.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare use deception in Much Ado About Nothing?
essayQuestions.focus: Overhearing, evidence and the two plots
plan: Establish the pattern: nobody in this play learns anything except by watching or being told.
Compare the two gulling scenes, 2.3 and 3.1, and note that each accuses its target of the fault they most fear.
Set Don John's window scene against them, and observe that Shakespeare never stages it.
Add the Friar's false report of Hero's death as a third kind of lie, used as medicine.
Conclude on the watch: the truth arrives from the people nobody bothered to listen to in 3.5.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of Beatrice.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, anger and the limits of comedy
plan: Begin with 1.1, where she asks after Benedick before admitting she has any interest in him.
Read her wit as defence rather than temperament, using her hint at an earlier hurt.
Use the rhymed verse of 3.1.113 to show how completely the trick works, and how much she concedes in the image of the tamed bird.
Turn to 4.1: the repeated wish to be a man, and the demand that Benedick act because she cannot.
Close by asking whether the last scene's discovered sonnet restores the comedy or simply puts the armour back on.

essayQuestions.question: Is Claudio forgivable?
essayQuestions.focus: Reputation, repentance and the second wedding
plan: Note how he falls in love: by report, through a proxy, with a woman he has spoken to scarcely at all.
Show that the denunciation at 4.1.29 is staged rather than impulsive — he waits for the altar and an audience.
Weigh the mourning of 5.3 against the fact that he agrees to marry an unseen cousin the next morning.
Consider what the play withholds: Hero never accuses him, and no character demands that he explain himself.
Decide whether the comedy asks for forgiveness, or simply moves on and lets the audience decide.

essayQuestions.question: What is the function of Dogberry and the watch?
essayQuestions.focus: Class, language and who gets believed
plan: Set out the joke first: a constable who reverses his words and instructs his men to avoid arresting anyone.
Show that the watch nevertheless overhear the confession that solves the plot, in 3.3.
Make 3.5 the centre of the argument — Leonato is in a hurry and will not listen, and the wedding proceeds.
Read the 'write me down an ass' joke as a grievance about record and testimony as well as a gag.
Conclude on the reversal: the gentlemen read signs badly and the fools take statements accurately.

discussionQuestions: Both love plots are begun by a lie. Does the play think that matters?
Shakespeare never shows the scene at Hero's window. What does the play gain by keeping it offstage?
'Kill Claudio' usually gets a laugh. Should it?
Leonato believes the accusation against his own daughter before anyone else does. Is he forgiven too easily?
Don Pedro ends the play without a partner. What should a production do with him in the final dance?

timeline.label: Ariosto's Orlando Furioso first published
timeline.detail: Its story of Ginevra, falsely accused after a maid is seen at her window in her mistress's clothes, is the closest analogue to the Hero plot.

timeline.label: Bandello's Novelle
timeline.detail: Another version of the slandered bride, set in Messina, which brings the story to the city Shakespeare uses.

timeline.label: Sir John Harington translates Orlando Furioso
timeline.detail: The English verse translation makes the Ginevra episode available to readers and playwrights in London.

timeline.label: The play is most likely written
timeline.detail: Composition is usually placed in 1598 or 1599, at the end of the decade of comedies.

timeline.label: First Quarto
timeline.detail: Printed by Valentine Simmes for Andrew Wise and William Aspley; its title page links the play to the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

timeline.label: Performed at court
timeline.detail: Recorded among the plays given during the celebrations for the marriage of Princess Elizabeth.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: Printed among the comedies, with some of the quarto's confusing speech prefixes regularised.

timeline.label: Peggy Ashcroft and John Gielgud at Stratford
timeline.detail: The pairing that began the modern tradition of the play as a vehicle for two major actors.

timeline.label: Judi Dench and Donald Sinden for the RSC
timeline.detail: One of the best remembered of the company's many Beatrice and Benedick pairings.

timeline.label: Kenneth Branagh's film
timeline.detail: Shot at the Villa Vignamaggio in Tuscany, with Emma Thompson as Beatrice; one of the most commercially successful Shakespeare films.

timeline.label: Iqbal Khan sets the play in contemporary Delhi
timeline.detail: An RSC production with Meera Syal as Beatrice, staged as part of the World Shakespeare Festival.

timeline.label: Kenny Leon's Public Theater production is filmed
timeline.detail: An all-Black cast in a contemporary American political setting, recorded for broadcast.

places.name: Messina
places.note: The whole play: Leonato's house, its orchard and garden, a church and a prison.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Benedick's city, named in the first scene along with the reputation that precedes him.

places.name: Florence
places.note: Claudio's city; the first scene introduces him as a young Florentine who has fought beyond the promise of his age.

places.name: Zaragoza
places.note: Chief city of Aragon, the kingdom Don Pedro is prince of and the source of the company's rank.

places.name: London
places.note: Where the 1600 quarto was printed and where the Lord Chamberlain's Men first played it.

related.why: The next of the great comedies, and the other one in which a joke played on a self-important man goes too far to be laughed off.
Written within a year or two, and the closest comparison for two people talking themselves into love in prose.
The same accusation of a faithful woman, taken seriously enough to kill a child and to need sixteen years to mend.
The slandered-wife plot again, with the malicious deceiver given a full part and no comic constables to stop him.
Shakespeare's other comedy of people made to love on someone else's instruction, with the trickery done by magic instead of gossip.

books.title: Othello
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Venice for one act, then a garrison on Cyprus from which nobody can leave
books.lengthNote: Around 3,200 lines; the Folio prints roughly 160 that the quarto lacks, including the Willow Song
books.openingLine: Tush! never tell me; I take it much unkindly
books.summary: A general marries a senator's daughter without asking anyone, defends the marriage before the Venetian state, and wins. Then the war he was sent to fight is cancelled by a storm, and his ensign spends one long scene in a garden converting a handkerchief into evidence. The play is less about jealousy than about what a man will accept as proof when the person offering it has never once been wrong.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Othello
sourceText.note: The Globe numbering follows a conflated text. The 1622 quarto and the 1623 Folio differ in oaths, stage directions and several substantial passages.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A marriage is put on public trial
structure.summary: Iago begins the play complaining about promotion and ends it with a plan, and in between a private marriage becomes a matter of state. Brabantio accuses Othello of witchcraft before the Senate; Othello answers with an account of courtship and Desdemona answers with a statement of divided duty. They win, and the reward is a posting to a war.

scenes.title: Under the window
scenes.summary: Iago and Roderigo wake Brabantio with the most racially loaded language in the play.

scenes.title: Arrest in the street
scenes.summary: Othello meets an armed party with a joke about dew and rust, and is summoned by the Duke.

scenes.title: The Senate
scenes.summary: Othello and Desdemona defend the marriage; Cyprus is threatened; Iago tells Roderigo to fill his purse.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: The storm removes the war and seals the island
structure.summary: The Turkish fleet is destroyed by weather before a shot is fired, which strands a garrison with nothing to do. Iago uses the holiday to get Cassio drunk, start a brawl and have him stripped of his lieutenancy — then offers, as a friend, to help him get it back by asking Desdemona.

scenes.title: Landfall
scenes.summary: Separate ships arrive through the storm; Iago watches Cassio take Desdemona's hand.

scenes.title: The proclamation
scenes.summary: A herald announces feasting to celebrate a war that never happened.

scenes.title: The watch
scenes.summary: Drink, a stabbing, a cashiered lieutenant, and a piece of advice that starts the plot.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: One long scene manufactures certainty
structure.summary: In about five hundred lines Iago moves Othello from 'I do love thee' to a demand for a wife's death, without producing a single fact. The handkerchief drops by accident, is picked up by Emilia and planted; by the end of the act it has stopped being cloth and become a document.

scenes.title: The musicians
scenes.summary: Cassio arranges his approach to Desdemona through Emilia.

scenes.title: The fortifications
scenes.summary: Eleven lines of routine business that keep Othello offstage and the audience waiting.

scenes.title: The garden
scenes.summary: Insinuation, repetition, a dropped handkerchief and a demand for ocular proof.

scenes.title: The handkerchief
scenes.summary: Othello asks for it, invents or reports its history, and will not hear about Cassio.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: Othello watches the scene Iago directs
structure.summary: Iago stages a conversation about Bianca and lets Othello overhear it as a conversation about Desdemona. Othello falls into a fit, then strikes his wife in front of a Venetian envoy. The act ends in a bedroom with two women talking honestly about marriage while one of them prepares the bed she will be killed in.

scenes.title: The overhearing
scenes.summary: A staged conversation, the handkerchief produced by the wrong woman, and a blow struck in public.

scenes.title: The brothel scene
scenes.summary: Othello interrogates Emilia, then Desdemona, treating his own house as a whorehouse.

scenes.title: The Willow Song
scenes.summary: Desdemona remembers her mother's maid; Emilia sets out the case for wives.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The murder is performed as justice, then exposed
structure.summary: Roderigo is finally spent and killed; Cassio is wounded in the dark. Othello comes to the bedchamber with a speech about cause and light, and kills his wife as though carrying out a sentence. Emilia takes the whole structure apart in about forty lines, and pays for it.

scenes.title: The street
scenes.summary: Iago's last improvisation: two attacks in the dark and a witness silenced.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: The killing, Emilia's testimony, Iago's silence, and Othello's last account of himself.

characters.name: Othello
characters.role: A general in the service of Venice
characters.summary: Indispensable to the state and never quite of it, he is the most controlled speaker in the play until the middle of Act III and one of the least controlled afterwards. What destroys him is not credulity in general — he defends himself brilliantly against Brabantio — but a standard of proof that he hands over to somebody else.
characters.clue: He answers a charge of witchcraft with a story about his life, and later demands to be shown something he can see.

characters.name: Desdemona
characters.summary: She marries against her father, argues her own case before the Senate, and then finds that every quality she showed in Act I is used against her: constancy becomes persistence, generosity becomes appetite. Her worst mistake is a piece of ordinary decency — pressing Cassio's suit because she believes he has been wronged.
characters.clue: She defends her own marriage before the Venetian Senate, and with her last breath says nobody killed her.

characters.name: Iago
characters.summary: He gives more reasons for what he does than any other Shakespearean villain and none of them holds: the promotion, the rumour about Emilia, the claim that he too loves Desdemona. What is consistent is method. He almost never lies outright; he times, he hesitates, he declines to say things, and lets other people finish his sentences for him.
characters.clue: He is called honest by nearly everyone in the play, and his last decision is to stop speaking.

characters.name: Emilia
characters.summary: She hands her husband the handkerchief without asking why, and spends the last act making up for it. Her long speech in 4.3 is the only sustained argument in the play against the sexual double standard, and it is spoken by a woman who has been married to Iago for years and has clearly learned it from him.
characters.clue: She picks up a handkerchief to please her husband, and later tells the truth about it knowing what he will do.

characters.name: Michael Cassio
characters.summary: Promoted over Iago's head and entirely unequipped to survive him. He cannot drink, he is courteous to women in a way that can be made to look like something else, and his idea of a disaster is the loss of a reputation. The play never suggests he has done anything wrong, which is why the plot works.
characters.clue: One cup of wine costs him his commission, and he then asks the general's wife to get it back.

characters.name: Roderigo
characters.role: A Venetian gentleman in love with Desdemona
characters.summary: Iago's purse and his rehearsal space. Every technique used on Othello is tried first on Roderigo, who is told to sell his land, follow the wars and wait — and does. He is the only character who accuses Iago to his face before Act V, and he is killed in the dark for it.
characters.clue: Told to put money in his purse, he sells his land, follows an army he has no business with and is stabbed by the man who advised him.

characters.name: Brabantio
characters.summary: He has entertained Othello at his house for years and still cannot imagine his daughter choosing him, so he reaches for witchcraft. Defeated in the Senate, he leaves with a warning that Iago will be quoting in effect for the rest of the play: a daughter who deceived her father may deceive a husband.
characters.clue: He calls a general a thief and a sorcerer in front of the Senate, then hands over a daughter he says has already deceived him.

characters.name: Bianca
characters.role: A woman of Cyprus, attached to Cassio
characters.summary: She is given the handkerchief to copy, brings it back in a jealous temper, and thereby supplies the visible object Othello has been demanding. The play lets her be openly in love and openly angry, and then uses her reputation to discredit her in front of the men who need a witness.
characters.clue: Asked to take out the work on a piece of embroidery, she throws it back in the street at exactly the wrong moment.

themes.name: Jealousy
themes.summary: The play distinguishes between suspicion and jealousy with some care. Iago names jealousy before Othello feels it, describes it as a self-feeding animal, and thereby installs the idea in advance. What follows is not the growth of a doubt but the operation of a machine that supplies its own fuel and cannot be shown counter-evidence.
themes.development: Named by Iago in 3.3 before it exists, mimicked in 3.4, staged as farce with Bianca in 4.1, and finally spoken of by Othello in 5.2 as though it were a judicial cause.

themes.name: Proof and evidence
themes.summary: Othello asks for ocular proof and is given a scene to watch with the sound arranged. The tragedy turns on a category error that anyone might make: he treats interpretation as sight. Nothing Iago produces would survive a question, and the play makes sure the audience notices that nobody ever asks one.
themes.development: Demanded in 3.3, fabricated with the handkerchief in 3.4, performed in 4.1, and dismantled by Emilia in 5.2 with a single fact about who found the cloth.

themes.name: Reputation and name
themes.summary: Cassio calls reputation the immortal part of himself; Iago tells him it is an idle imposition, and twenty lines later tells Othello it is the immediate jewel of the soul. The contradiction is the point. In a garrison, where office depends on public trust, what people say about you is not a reflection of your standing but its substance.
themes.development: Lost by Cassio in 2.3, weaponised by Iago in 3.3, and destroyed for Desdemona in 4.2, where her husband uses the language of the brothel about his own house.

themes.name: Race and belonging
themes.summary: Venice needs Othello and does not consider him one of its own, and the play stages that contradiction without resolving it. Iago's most violent racial language comes before Othello has spoken a line, so the audience meets the prejudice first. Iago does not invent it; he uses material the society has already prepared.
themes.development: Shouted under a window in 1.1, argued in the Senate in 1.3, internalised by Othello in 3.3, and returned to by Emilia in 5.2 with the word devil.

themes.name: Marriage, duty and women
themes.summary: Three marriages and an attachment run in parallel: Othello and Desdemona, Iago and Emilia, Cassio and Bianca. Each is a different arrangement of trust and property, and all three women are described by men as something other than what the audience has seen them be.
themes.development: Publicly defended in 1.3, privately corroded through Act III, and analysed by Emilia in 4.3 in the only scene where two women talk to each other at length.

themes.name: Honesty
themes.summary: The word appears more often in this play than in any other by Shakespeare, and almost always attached to Iago. It means truthful, it means chaste when applied to women, and it means socially reliable when applied to a subordinate. The tragedy uses all three meanings at once and never lets any character notice the slippage.
themes.development: A compliment in Acts I and II, a lever in 3.3, an accusation about Desdemona in Act IV, and in 5.2 a word Othello uses about Iago one line before the truth arrives.

techniques.name: Soliloquy and aside
techniques.definition: Speech directed past the other characters, to the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: Speech directed past the other characters, to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Iago has more of them than anybody, and uses them to recruit: he explains the next move before making it, so the audience watches the trap being built and cannot warn anyone.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.bookDefinition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: Sustained for four acts by the word 'honest'. Every time Othello calls Iago honest, the phrase means one thing on stage and another in the auditorium, and the gap is the tension.

techniques.name: The stage property
techniques.definition: An object handled on stage that accumulates meaning as it changes hands.
techniques.bookDefinition: An object handled on stage that accumulates meaning as it changes hands.
techniques.inThisBook: The handkerchief passes through five pairs of hands and is never once examined. Its power is entirely a function of who is holding it and when it is seen — Iago's argument made portable.

techniques.name: Breaking verse
techniques.definition: Metrical collapse used to register a mind losing order.
techniques.bookDefinition: Metrical collapse used to register a mind losing order.
techniques.inThisBook: Othello begins in long, balanced periods and ends 4.1 in broken prose — 'noses, ears, and lips' — before recovering the grand manner one last time for his final speech.

techniques.name: Animal imagery
techniques.definition: Language that reduces people to beasts and appetite.
techniques.bookDefinition: Language that reduces people to beasts and appetite.
techniques.inThisBook: Iago introduces it under Brabantio's window with rams and horses, and by Act IV Othello has adopted it — goats and monkeys — which is how the play shows the infection taking.

techniques.name: Double time
techniques.definition: Two incompatible timescales running at once, one fast enough for the plot and one long enough for the accusations to be possible.
techniques.bookDefinition: Two incompatible timescales running at once, one fast enough for the plot and one long enough for the accusations to be possible.
techniques.inThisBook: The Cyprus action takes about thirty-six hours, which leaves Desdemona no opportunity to be unfaithful; yet Iago speaks of a thousand times and nights together. Audiences do not notice, and that is the trick.

quotations.text: I follow him to serve my turn upon him:
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Explaining to Roderigo, in the street at night, why he still works for Othello.
quotations.analysis: 'Follow' and 'serve' are the vocabulary of loyal service, and he uses both against their meaning in a single line. The plan is announced in the play's first fifty lines, so nothing Iago does later is a surprise to anyone except the people on stage.

quotations.text: But I will wear my heart upon my sleeve For daws to peck at: I am not what I am.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: The end of his account of the two kinds of servant.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is a flat contradiction that cannot be unpacked into sense, which is exactly its function: he tells the truth about himself in a form that guarantees nothing follows from it. It also inverts the formula God gives Moses, and the audience is left holding a confession no character has heard.

quotations.text: Even now, now, very now, an old black ram Is topping your white ewe.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Shouted up at Brabantio's window in the dark, before Othello has appeared.
quotations.analysis: The audience is given the marriage as an image of livestock before it meets either partner, and the colour contrast is doing the work of an argument. Iago is anonymous in the dark here, which lets the play introduce the prejudice as a voice from the street rather than the view of a named character.

quotations.text: Rude am I in my speech, And little bless'd with the soft phrase of peace:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Beginning his defence before the Duke and the senators.
quotations.analysis: A claim to be a poor speaker, made in perfectly balanced verse at the opening of the most persuasive speech in the play. The modesty is a rhetorical device with a long pedigree, and its success in this scene is what makes Act III so painful: he can handle a senate but not an insinuation.

quotations.text: She loved me for the dangers I had pass'd, And I loved her that she did pity them.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Ending his account of how the courtship happened, over dinners at her father's house.
quotations.analysis: The couplet balances two lines and two verbs and quietly reveals an asymmetry: she loves a story, he loves being listened to. That is a real marriage and a fragile one, and Iago's whole campaign consists of offering Othello a different story about himself.

quotations.text: I do perceive here a divided duty: To you I am bound for life and education;
quotations.speaker: Desdemona
quotations.context: Asked by her father, in front of the Senate, where she owes most obedience.
quotations.analysis: She answers a question about love with an analysis of obligation, and the structure of the speech — father first, husband second, precedent from her own mother — is legal rather than romantic. It is the most politically skilful thing anyone says in the scene, and she is about twenty.

quotations.text: Look to her, Moor, if thou hast eyes to see: She has deceived her father, and may thee.
quotations.speaker: Brabantio
quotations.context: His parting shot as the Senate breaks up.
quotations.analysis: A father's last piece of spite, delivered in a rhyming couplet so that it sticks. Iago never has to make this argument himself: it has already been said in public by a senator, and Othello recalls it in the middle of Act III as though it were evidence.

quotations.text: The Moor is of a free and open nature, That thinks men honest that but seem to be so, And will as tenderly be led by the nose As asses are.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act I, working out his plan.
quotations.analysis: It is an accurate character reference and a plan of attack in the same sentence: the quality he names is generosity, and he treats it as an exploit. The animal simile arrives at the end of the thought rather than the beginning, so the insult lands after the compliment has been accepted.

quotations.text: Reputation, reputation, reputation! O, I have lost my reputation! I have lost the immortal part of myself, and what remains is bestial.
quotations.speaker: Cassio
quotations.context: Drunk and disgraced, moments after the brawl that costs him his lieutenancy.
quotations.analysis: Five uses of the word in three lines, in prose, from a man too drunk to vary his vocabulary — and the content is theologically serious. Iago answers by calling reputation an idle imposition, then tells Othello the opposite in 3.3, which is the clearest evidence that he believes neither.

quotations.text: Excellent wretch! Perdition catch my soul, But I do love thee! and when I love thee not, Chaos is come again.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: As Desdemona leaves the garden, seconds before Iago begins.
quotations.analysis: He phrases his love as a condition on which the order of the world depends, and does it minutes before the world is dismantled. The construction is a hostage to fortune and the play collects: within four hundred lines he will love her not, and the noun he chose is the one that arrives.

quotations.text: Good name in man and woman, dear my lord, Is the immediate jewel of their souls: Who steals my purse steals trash;
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Refusing, at length, to say what he is thinking.
quotations.analysis: He argues for the sanctity of reputation as a reason not to speak, which makes the withholding look like scruple rather than technique. The same man told Cassio in 2.3 that reputation was an idle imposition; the contradiction is never noticed on stage because each speech is exactly what its hearer needs.

quotations.text: O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; It is the green-eyed monster which doth mock The meat it feeds on;
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Warning Othello against a feeling he has not yet described.
quotations.analysis: A warning that functions as an instruction: the word is placed in Othello's mind under cover of protecting him from it. The image is of something that plays with its food rather than eating it, which is a fair description of what Iago is doing for the rest of the scene.

quotations.text: Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ:
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Alone, having just taken the handkerchief from Emilia.
quotations.analysis: He states his epistemology out loud and it is correct: once a man is jealous, weight of evidence stops mattering and any object will do. The comparison with scripture is precise — proof that cannot be questioned because questioning it is already the offence.

quotations.text: Farewell the tranquil mind! farewell content! Farewell the plumed troop, and the big wars, That make ambition virtue!
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Rounding on Iago, having accepted that his wife is unfaithful.
quotations.analysis: Told that his marriage is over, he says goodbye to his career. The list is entirely military — troops, banners, drums — because his occupation and his sense of himself are the same thing, and Iago has just removed the domestic foundation the whole structure stood on.

quotations.text: Villain, be sure thou prove my love a whore, Be sure of it; give me the ocular proof:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Seizing Iago by the throat in the middle of the garden scene.
quotations.analysis: The demand sounds rigorous and is already a defeat: he has accepted the charge and is asking only to be shown it. Note the word order — 'my love a whore' assumes the conclusion inside the request — and note that what he is eventually given to see is a conversation about another woman.

quotations.text: Like to the Pontic sea, Whose icy current and compulsive course Ne'er feels retiring ebb, but keeps due on
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Rejecting Iago's suggestion that he may change his mind.
quotations.analysis: He describes his own resolve as a current that cannot turn, using a geographical fact about the Black Sea to make a psychological claim. The passage appears in the Folio and not in the 1622 quarto, so some early readers met an Othello who never said it.

quotations.text: But I do think it is their husbands' faults If wives do fall: say that they slack their duties, And pour our treasures into foreign laps,
quotations.speaker: Emilia
quotations.context: Undressing Desdemona for bed, after a conversation about whether any woman would betray her husband.
quotations.analysis: The argument is causal rather than moral: she is not defending adultery but explaining it as a response. Coming at the end of an act in which Desdemona has been struck and called a whore, it is the play's only sustained analysis of marriage from inside one, and it is spoken by the woman who lost the handkerchief.

quotations.text: It is the cause, it is the cause, my soul,-- Let me not name it to you, you chaste stars!-- It is the cause.
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Entering the bedchamber with a light, Desdemona asleep.
quotations.analysis: Three statements and no object: he cannot say what the cause is, and the refusal is addressed to the stars rather than to himself. 'Cause' is a legal word, and he uses it to convert a murder into a sentence — the speech is the machinery by which he becomes, in his own account, a judge.

quotations.text: Put out the light, and then put out the light:
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: Standing over the bed with a taper in his hand.
quotations.analysis: The same six words twice, meaning a candle and then a life, and the difference between them is the whole of the following seven lines: the lamp can be relit, she cannot. He is working out the metaphor while holding the object, which is why the line can only be understood in performance.

quotations.text: Nobody; I myself. Farewell Commend me to my kind lord: O, farewell!
quotations.speaker: Desdemona
quotations.context: Asked by Emilia who has done this deed.
quotations.analysis: Her last act is to lie to protect the man who has just killed her, and the adjective she chooses for him is 'kind'. Whether this is love, self-abnegation or a final failure of the play to let her speak for herself has been argued for four centuries, and the text supplies no stage direction to settle it.

quotations.text: O, the more angel she, And you the blacker devil!
quotations.speaker: Emilia
quotations.context: Hearing Othello admit that he killed Desdemona, and that she died denying it.
quotations.analysis: She reaches for the colour vocabulary the play has been circling since the first scene, and turns it on Othello at the moment he is least able to answer. It is also the first time anyone in Cyprus contradicts him to his face, and the whole exposure of Iago follows from a servant refusing to be quiet.

quotations.text: Demand me nothing: what you know, you know: From this time forth I never will speak word.
quotations.speaker: Iago
quotations.context: Asked why he has ensnared Othello's soul and body.
quotations.analysis: The one thing an audience wants at the end of this play is an explanation, and he withholds it deliberately, in a couplet, having talked more than anyone else for five acts. The silence is his last piece of control: no motive can now be checked against the deeds.

quotations.text: Speak of me as I am; nothing extenuate, Nor set down aught in malice: then must you speak Of one that loved not wisely but too well;
quotations.speaker: Othello
quotations.context: His last speech, before the concealed dagger.
quotations.analysis: He commissions his own obituary and then dictates it, which is not quite the same as accepting judgement. The phrase 'loved not wisely but too well' is a considerable piece of editing by a man who smothered his wife on the word of an ensign, and the play lets him have it without endorsing it.

atAGlance.label: First recorded performance
atAGlance.note: The Revels accounts record a play of the Moor of Venice at Whitehall.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: A quarto printed by Nicholas Okes for Thomas Walkley, nearly twenty years after the court record.

atAGlance.label: Source
atAGlance.note: An Italian prose tale supplies the Moor, the ensign, the wife and the handkerchief; Shakespeare supplies the names and the motives.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: One act in Venice, four on an island, and a single scene — 3.3 — in which the whole tragedy is arranged.

criticalViews.position: A domestic tragedy
criticalViews.summary: The reading that stresses scale: no state falls, no succession is disputed, and the catastrophe happens in a bedroom between four people who all work for the same employer. On this account the play's power comes from its ordinariness.
criticalViews.counter: It underplays Act I. The marriage is tried before a senate, and Othello's standing as an outsider indispensable to Venice is the condition of everything that follows.

criticalViews.position: A play about race
criticalViews.summary: Criticism and performance since the mid-twentieth century have made the play's racial language central: Iago's plot succeeds because the society around him already supplies the terms, and Othello's isolation is structural rather than temperamental.
criticalViews.counter: The difficulty is the play's own vocabulary, which productions cannot simply endorse; casting and staging decisions do at least as much interpretive work as the text.

criticalViews.position: Iago's motive as the play's real problem
criticalViews.summary: He offers promotion, a rumour about Emilia and a claimed desire for Desdemona, and drops each in turn. One tradition takes the incoherence as characterisation — a man who improvises reasons afterwards — and another takes it as evidence of a figure closer to allegory than to psychology.
criticalViews.counter: Both readings have to account for 5.2, where he refuses to speak at all: the play withholds the answer rather than offering competing ones.

essayQuestions.question: What actually persuades Othello?
essayQuestions.focus: Proof, evidence and the handkerchief
plan: List what Iago produces across 3.3: hesitation, a refusal to speak, a recollection of Brabantio's warning, and a dream he says he overheard.
Show that the demand for ocular proof in 3.3 marks the point at which Othello has already conceded the charge.
Track the handkerchief through 3.3, 3.4 and 4.1 and note that nobody ever asks Emilia a question about it.
Analyse 4.1 as theatre: Othello is given a scene to watch with the sound arranged and the subject changed.
Conclude with 5.2, where Emilia dismantles four acts of evidence with one fact about who found the cloth.

essayQuestions.question: How does Shakespeare present Iago?
essayQuestions.focus: Motive, method and the audience's complicity
plan: Separate his stated motives — the lieutenancy, the rumour about Emilia, his own claimed desire — and note where each is dropped.
Examine method instead: timing, withholding, letting other people complete his sentences, and almost never lying outright.
Use the soliloquies to show how the play makes the audience his confidant, and what that does to our position as watchers.
Consider the word 'honest' as the play's most sustained piece of dramatic irony.
Close on his silence in 5.2 and what it denies the audience.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss the presentation of women in Othello.
essayQuestions.focus: Desdemona, Emilia and Bianca
plan: Begin with Desdemona's speech to the Senate in 1.3: a woman arguing her own case in public, and winning it.
Trace how the same qualities are reinterpreted — her advocacy for Cassio becomes persistence, her warmth becomes appetite.
Read 4.3 as the play's only scene of women talking to each other, and weigh Emilia's argument on its own terms.
Use Bianca to test the play's social range: she is candid, in love, and dismissed because of what she is assumed to be.
Assess the ending: Emilia's testimony is decisive, and both women die within fifty lines of speaking plainly.

essayQuestions.question: 'Othello is destroyed by Venice, not by Iago.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Race, service and the state
plan: Set out Othello's position in Act I: indispensable in war, and put on trial for a marriage.
Note that the play's most violent racial language is spoken before Othello appears, and by more than one character.
Examine 3.3, where Othello reaches for Brabantio's warning and for his own difference as explanations.
Consider Cyprus: an outpost with no war left to fight, where Venetian authority is present only as an envoy with a letter.
Weigh the counter-case — Iago's plot requires particular people in particular rooms, and works on Roderigo and Cassio too.

discussionQuestions: Iago gives at least three reasons for what he does. Does the play want us to believe any of them?
Desdemona's last words blame nobody. Is that a final act of love or a final silencing?
The Turkish fleet is destroyed offstage before the second act begins. Why does Shakespeare cancel the war?
Emilia hands over the handkerchief without asking why. How far does the play hold her responsible?
Othello's last speech arranges how he will be remembered. Should we let him?

timeline.label: Cinthio's Hecatommithi published

timeline.detail: The island Shakespeare's garrison defends had been Ottoman for a generation by the time the play was written.

timeline.label: Knolles's General History of the Turks
timeline.detail: Evidence of how current Ottoman affairs were in London when the play was taking shape.

timeline.detail: The Revels accounts place the Moor of Venice at court on 1 November.

timeline.detail: Often connected with the Folio text's removal of oaths that the quarto prints.

timeline.detail: Around 160 lines longer than the quarto, including the Willow Song and the Pontic sea speech.

timeline.detail: Restoration records associate the part with the first appearance of a woman on the English public stage.

places.name: Venice
places.note: The republic that needs Othello's generalship and cannot quite accept his marriage.

places.name: Famagusta, Cyprus
places.note: The Venetian stronghold on the island; the walled port a garrison would have held against the Ottoman fleet.

places.name: Rhodes
places.note: The feint in the Senate scene — the Turkish fleet steers for it in order to be somewhere else.

places.name: Aleppo
places.note: The city Othello names in his last speech, in the story about the turbaned Turk.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where the earliest recorded performance took place, on 1 November 1604.

related.why: The tragedy immediately before it, and the opposite problem: a hero who will not act until the evidence is sound.
Another play in which a credulous man destroys the person who loves him on the strength of a fabrication.
The other tragedy in which a marriage is the engine of the plot, and in which one partner talks the other into it.
The same city, and the same question about who Venice will use and who it will accept.
The expanded Astor edition, with fuller material on the quarto and Folio texts, criticism and stage history.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: Jane Austen
books.setting: Hertfordshire, Kent, London and Derbyshire, in the years of the militia camps
books.lengthNote: Sixty-one chapters, first issued in three volumes
books.openingLine: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
books.summary: A family of five daughters, an estate entailed away from all of them, and a neighbourhood that treats every new arrival as an opportunity. Elizabeth Bennet is the best reader of character in the book and gets the two most important readings wrong, and Austen builds the plot so that correcting them costs her something. The comedy never lets go of the arithmetic underneath it: who has money, who will inherit, and who can afford to refuse.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Pride and Prejudice
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously from 1 to 61, as in the Standard Ebooks text; first editions divide the same chapters across three volumes.

structure.label: Chapters 1–12
structure.title: Netherfield taken, and everybody measured
structure.summary: A single man with four or five thousand a year moves into the neighbourhood and the Bennets begin calculating. The Meryton assembly fixes Darcy’s reputation in one overheard sentence, and Jane’s convenient illness keeps Elizabeth at Netherfield long enough for the two of them to start sparring in earnest.

structure.label: Chapters 13–23
structure.title: The heir, the officer and the practical marriage
structure.summary: Mr Collins arrives to inspect the estate he will inherit and the cousin he intends to marry; Wickham arrives with a grievance that flatters Elizabeth’s judgement. Within three days Collins is refused, Charlotte Lucas accepts him, and the Bingleys leave for London taking Jane’s prospects with them.

structure.label: Chapters 24–34
structure.title: Hunsford, Rosings and a proposal nobody wanted
structure.summary: Elizabeth visits Charlotte’s parsonage and sees what a comfortable home actually costs. Lady Catherine presides, Colonel Fitzwilliam lets slip that Darcy separated Bingley from Jane, and Darcy proposes in terms that make refusing him easy and enjoyable.

structure.label: Chapters 35–42
structure.title: The letter, and a second reading
structure.summary: Darcy hands over a letter and walks away, and the novel changes direction without a single event taking place. Elizabeth reads it twice, reconstructs Wickham from the beginning, and arrives at the only self-accusation in the book that is not comic.

structure.label: Chapters 43–50
structure.title: Pemberley, and the news from Brighton
structure.summary: A house, a housekeeper and a set of grounds supply the evidence about Darcy that conversation could not. Then Lydia runs off with Wickham, and the family’s standing, which has been a joke for forty chapters, becomes something that can actually be destroyed.

structure.label: Chapters 51–61
structure.title: What the settlement cost, and who paid it
structure.summary: Lydia returns married and unembarrassed, and the reader learns before Elizabeth does who bought the marriage. Lady Catherine’s attempt to extract a promise produces the opposite of the one she wants, and the last chapters distribute incomes as carefully as affections.

characters.name: Elizabeth Bennet
characters.role: Second of the five Bennet daughters
characters.summary: Quick, funny and justly confident in her own judgement, which is exactly why the novel arranges for her to be wrong about the two men she is most certain of. Her wit is a form of courage in a household where nobody else will say anything true.
characters.clue: She refuses two proposals, walks three miles through mud to nurse her sister, and only discovers her own vanity by reading a letter twice.

relationships.label: closest friend, and a test of her principles

characters.name: Fitzwilliam Darcy
characters.summary: Ten thousand a year and no talent for a room full of strangers. Austen gives him the novel’s worst opening sentence and then spends fifty chapters showing that his conduct has always been better than his manner, which is not quite the same as saying he was right.
characters.clue: He insults a woman within her hearing at a country dance, proposes to her against his own better judgement, and later pays a blackguard to marry her sister without telling anyone.

characters.name: Jane Bennet
characters.summary: Her determination to think well of everybody is presented as a moral achievement and a practical disaster: it makes her unreadable to Bingley, unreadable to Darcy, and defenceless against Caroline Bingley. The novel likes her and does not recommend her method.
characters.clue: She catches cold riding to dinner in the rain because her mother wanted her to stay the night, and forgives everyone involved.

characters.name: Charles Bingley
characters.summary: Amiable, rich and so willing to be guided that his friend can detach him from the woman he loves with a few words about her family. He is the novel’s evidence that good nature without judgement is a kind of weakness.
characters.clue: He takes a house for the shooting, falls in love at the first assembly, and is talked out of it by a friend and a sister in a single winter.

characters.name: George Wickham
characters.summary: He tells Elizabeth a story about Darcy within an hour of meeting her, and she believes it because it is well told and because she wants to. His charm is a working method rather than a temperament, and the militia’s presence in Meryton is what gives it a market.
characters.clue: The steward’s son who was left a living in a will, sold it for ready money, and then complained for the rest of the book that he had been robbed of it.

relationships.label: elopes with, and is paid to marry
slanders and is bought off by

characters.name: Mr Collins
characters.role: Clergyman of Hunsford, heir to Longbourn
characters.summary: He proposes to two women in three days and is not embarrassed by either outcome, because the proposal was never about a person. Everything he says is addressed upwards to his patroness, even when he is standing in somebody else’s parlour insulting their daughter.
characters.clue: He offers his hand as a favour to the family he will dispossess, and numbers his reasons for marrying like items in a sermon.

characters.name: Charlotte Lucas
characters.summary: Twenty-seven, without fortune, and the only character who states the terms of the marriage market out loud without either joking or complaining. Her parsonage is arranged so that she sees as little of her husband as the house allows, which is the closest the novel comes to a verdict on the bargain.
characters.clue: She accepts in three days the man her closest friend refused, and explains that she asks only a comfortable home.

characters.name: Lydia Bennet
characters.summary: Fifteen, unsupervised and encouraged, she does exactly what her upbringing has trained her to do, and the novel is careful to spread the blame across her mother’s indulgence and her father’s amused neglect. Her elopement is the one plot event that could not be undone by an explanation.
characters.clue: She is delighted to be married before her elder sisters and cannot understand why the family is not delighted too.

characters.name: Mr Bennet
characters.summary: He retreats to his library and treats his family as a source of entertainment, and the novel charges him for it: the daughter he never bothered to check runs away, and his best line about making sport for our neighbours is spoken just before he finds out what that costs.
characters.clue: He tells his least favourite daughter that one parent will refuse to see her again whichever way she answers a proposal.

characters.name: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
characters.summary: She gives orders about other people’s carriages, shelves and marriages with the same confidence, and is the only character who states the class objection to the match in plain words. Her one decisive action in the plot is the one that brings the marriage about.
characters.clue: She drives to a small Hertfordshire village to demand a promise, and is told that she has no right to ask for one.

characters.name: Mrs Bennet
characters.summary: Ridiculous and not wrong. Her single subject is getting five daughters married before her husband dies, and the entail means that the alternative is genuine poverty, so the novel laughs at her method rather than her motive.
characters.clue: Her nerves are her oldest companions, and she can turn a wet evening into an engagement if the house is far enough from home.

themes.name: First impressions and judgement
themes.summary: The discarded title is still the working one. Almost every character forms a verdict in a single evening and then spends the book defending it, and Austen makes the reader do the same thing so that the correction lands on both at once.
themes.development: Fixed at the Meryton assembly, hardened by Wickham’s story, dismantled by a letter in Chapter 35, and formally re-examined at Pemberley.

themes.name: Marriage and money
themes.summary: Every attachment in the novel is quoted with a figure attached, from Bingley’s four or five thousand a year to the hundred a year Mr Bennet is asked to promise for Lydia. Austen does not treat this as vulgar; she treats it as the arithmetic within which affection has to operate.
themes.development: Stated as a joke in the first sentence, argued seriously by Charlotte in Chapter 22, and paid in cash by Darcy in the last volume.

themes.name: Rank and connection
themes.summary: The obstacle between Elizabeth and Darcy is not money on her side but relations on hers: an uncle in trade, an aunt in Cheapside, a mother who cannot be taken anywhere. The novel dismantles the objection by making the Gardiners the most sensible adults in it.
themes.development: Voiced by Caroline Bingley, formalised by Darcy’s first proposal, and shouted by Lady Catherine in the last volume after it has stopped being true for anyone the reader trusts.

themes.name: Entail and female security
themes.summary: Longbourn passes to Mr Collins, so five daughters must find husbands or find lodgings. The legal fact sits under every comic scene, and it is why Charlotte’s calculation is a calculation rather than a failure of feeling.
themes.development: Explained early and never forgotten: it makes Mrs Bennet’s campaign rational, Collins’s proposal a favour in his own eyes, and Lydia’s ruin a threat to four other women.

themes.name: Reputation and family conduct
themes.summary: Character in this novel is public property. A sister’s elopement is treated as a defect in every other sister, and Mary’s moralising about a woman’s irretrievable ruin is contemptible and, within the world of the book, accurate about the consequences.
themes.development: From the embarrassment of the Netherfield ball, through Darcy’s letter about Jane’s family, to the Brighton crisis where reputation becomes something that must be bought back.

themes.name: Self-knowledge
themes.summary: Both leading characters have to revise not an opinion but a habit of mind. Elizabeth discovers that she was flattered into belief; Darcy discovers that being brought up on good principles is not the same as being taught to apply them.
themes.development: Elizabeth’s reckoning comes in Chapter 36, Darcy’s is reported in Chapter 58, and the novel makes the two confessions echo each other’s grammar.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Narration that takes on a character’s vocabulary and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narration that takes on a character’s vocabulary and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.inThisBook: The narrative sits so close to Elizabeth that her errors arrive as facts; the reader distrusts Darcy on her evidence and has to re-read the first half after the letter.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.bookDefinition: Saying one thing in a form that invites the opposite judgement.
techniques.inThisBook: The famous first sentence states a truth nobody in the book holds and everybody acts on: it is the mothers, not the single men, who are in want of anything.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written documents inserted into a narrative as evidence and as plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Written documents inserted into a narrative as evidence and as plot.
techniques.inThisBook: Darcy’s letter is the structural hinge, and Austen distinguishes her characters by their prose: Collins pompous, Jane over-careful, Lydia unpunctuated and untroubled.

techniques.name: Dialogue as exposure
techniques.definition: Letting characters convict themselves in their own speech rather than describing their faults.
techniques.bookDefinition: Letting characters convict themselves in their own speech rather than describing their faults.
techniques.inThisBook: Mr Collins numbers his reasons for marrying and Lady Catherine interrogates a stranger about her sisters’ accomplishments; neither needs a word of narrative comment.

techniques.name: Epigram
techniques.definition: A generalisation compressed into a single balanced sentence.
techniques.bookDefinition: A generalisation compressed into a single balanced sentence.
techniques.inThisBook: Characters reach for maxims when they are least reliable — Mary on vanity and pride, Charlotte on happiness in marriage, Mary again on a woman’s ruin.

techniques.name: Parallel courtships
techniques.definition: Running several versions of the same situation so that each comments on the others.
techniques.bookDefinition: Running several versions of the same situation so that each comments on the others.
techniques.inThisBook: Five marriages are set side by side — Jane’s, Charlotte’s, Lydia’s, Elizabeth’s and the Bennets’ own — so that the reader can see what each one was bought with.

quotations.text: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
quotations.context: The opening sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The sentence claims to report a consensus and names nobody who holds it; the passive construction hides the mothers who are the actual subject. Read strictly it is also false in the book that follows, where the single men are in want of nothing and the women are in want of an income.

quotations.text: You mistake me, my dear. I have a high respect for your nerves. They are my old friends. I have heard you mention them with consideration these twenty years at least.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Answering his wife’s complaint that he has no compassion on her nerves.
quotations.analysis: The joke depends on treating an ailment as an acquaintance, and it establishes the marriage in a line: he has been amusing himself at her expense for two decades and has changed nothing. Twenty years is also the age of the eldest daughter, which quietly dates the arrangement.

quotations.text: She is tolerable; but not handsome enough to tempt me; and I am in no humour at present to give consequence to young ladies who are slighted by other men.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At the Meryton assembly, refusing Bingley’s suggestion that he dance with Elizabeth, who is sitting close enough to hear.
quotations.analysis: Eight words decide the first half of the book. The grammar is the insult: she is graded, then found insufficient for a purpose, with no verb that admits she is a person in the room. Elizabeth’s response is to repeat it as a comic story, which is how a wound is kept fresh.

quotations.text: I could easily forgive his pride, if he had not mortified mine.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Discussing Darcy’s behaviour at the assembly with Charlotte Lucas and her family.
quotations.analysis: She names the mechanism of her own prejudice and does not notice she has done it. The two pronouns are balanced against each other across the comma, which is the shape the whole novel will take: two kinds of pride meeting and neither able to see the other’s.

quotations.text: Vanity and pride are different things, though the words are often used synonymously. A person may be proud without being vain. Pride relates more to our opinion of ourselves, vanity to what we would have others think of us.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: Mary offering the company the benefit of her reading.
quotations.analysis: The distinction is sound and the novel uses it: Darcy is proud and Wickham is vain, and the difference is exactly the one Mary draws. Austen’s joke is that the book’s dullest speaker supplies its most useful definition, and nobody in the room listens.

quotations.text: My good opinion once lost is lost forever.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: At Netherfield, admitting to a resentful temper during an evening of sparring with Elizabeth.
quotations.analysis: He says this as a confession of a fault and plainly regards it as a standard. The novel then spends fifty chapters disproving it about him, since his good opinion of Elizabeth survives her refusal and her family; the line is a self-portrait that has stopped being accurate.

quotations.text: That will do extremely well, child. You have delighted us long enough. Let the other young ladies have time to exhibit.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Stopping Mary’s second song at the Netherfield ball.
quotations.analysis: A father humiliates a daughter in public and the sentence is constructed so that the cruelty travels inside a compliment. It is the clearest instance of the habit Elizabeth will later have to judge: her father’s wit is aimed at his own children and costs him nothing.

quotations.text: My reasons for marrying are, first, that I think it a right thing for every clergyman in easy circumstances (like myself) to set the example of matrimony in his parish.
quotations.speaker: Mr Collins
quotations.context: Proposing to Elizabeth, having secured her mother’s permission but not her attention.
quotations.analysis: He begins a proposal with an enumerated list and the first item is professional example. The woman is not in the sentence at all; she appears later, as the third reason, on the recommendation of somebody else. Austen lets the syntax do the whole characterisation.

quotations.text: An unhappy alternative is before you, Elizabeth. From this day you must be a stranger to one of your parents. Your mother will never see you again if you do not marry Mr. Collins, and I will never see you again if you do.
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Called in by Mrs Bennet to force Elizabeth to accept Collins.
quotations.analysis: He supports his daughter by pretending not to, which lets him defeat his wife and stay amusing at the same time. The sentence is perfectly balanced around the two parents, and the balance is the point: Elizabeth’s rescue arrives as a joke, and the same detachment will let Lydia go to Brighton.

quotations.text: I am not romantic you know. I never was. I ask only a comfortable home; and considering Mr. Collins’s character, connections, and situation in life, I am convinced that my chance of happiness with him is as fair, as most people can boast on entering the marriage state.
quotations.speaker: Charlotte Lucas
quotations.context: Telling Elizabeth that she has accepted Mr Collins.
quotations.analysis: She asks only for a house and states her odds like an actuary, and the novel never corrects her arithmetic. Set against the first sentence of the book, this is the same proposition with the irony taken out, spoken by the person whom the marriage market has priced most accurately.

quotations.text: In vain have I struggled. It will not do. My feelings will not be repressed. You must allow me to tell you how ardently I admire and love you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The first proposal, at the Hunsford parsonage, while Elizabeth is re-reading Jane’s letters.
quotations.analysis: Four short sentences, three of them about his own resistance, and the declaration arrives only in the fourth. ‘Struggled’ and ‘repressed’ treat his feeling as an enemy position, so that by the time he reaches ‘admire and love’ he has already told her what the offer costs him.

quotations.text: I had not known you a month before I felt that you were the last man in the world whom I could ever be prevailed on to marry.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Darcy, after he has asked why he is rejected with so little civility.
quotations.analysis: The superlative is a hostage to fortune and Austen collects on it twenty-six chapters later. Note the precision of ‘a month’: she dates her verdict exactly, which is what makes it possible for the novel to show her the evidence she had not yet seen.

quotations.text: Be not alarmed, Madam, on receiving this letter, by the apprehension of its containing any repetition of those sentiments, or renewal of those offers, which were last night so disgusting to you.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: The opening of the letter handed to Elizabeth in the park at Rosings.
quotations.analysis: He hands over the one form of speech she cannot interrupt, and opens by disclaiming any renewal of the offer, which is how he makes the document readable. From here the novel’s evidence arrives in writing, and its turning point involves no event at all — only a second reading.

quotations.text: But vanity, not love, has been my folly. Pleased with the preference of one, and offended by the neglect of the other, on the very beginning of our acquaintance, I have courted prepossession and ignorance, and driven reason away, where either were concerned. Till this moment, I never knew myself.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Alone, having read Darcy’s letter twice and reconstructed everything Wickham told her.
quotations.analysis: She does not accuse herself of loving the wrong man but of a fault in method: she was pleased by one and slighted by the other, and let that do her thinking. ‘Vanity, not love, has been my folly’ applies Mary’s distinction from Chapter 5 to herself, thirty chapters after it was laughed at.

quotations.text: I have never had a cross word from him in my life, and I have known him ever since he was four years old.
quotations.speaker: Mrs Reynolds
quotations.context: The Pemberley housekeeper showing the house to Elizabeth and the Gardiners.
quotations.analysis: The testimony that changes Elizabeth’s mind comes from a servant with twenty years of observation and no reason to flatter a stranger. Austen makes the evidence economic rather than romantic: landlord and master are job titles, and Darcy is being assessed on how he treats people who cannot answer back.

quotations.text: In what an amiable light does this place him!
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Standing in the Pemberley gallery, hearing the housekeeper describe Darcy’s care of his sister.
quotations.analysis: ‘This place’ is doing double duty: the phrase means this circumstance, and she is standing in the house itself. The estate is functioning as evidence — grounds, portraits, accounts of conduct over years — where conversation had produced only impressions.

quotations.text: Unhappy as the event must be for Lydia, we may draw from it this useful lesson; that loss of virtue in a female is irretrievable⁠—that one false step involves her in endless ruin⁠—that her reputation is no less brittle than it is beautiful⁠—and that she cannot be too much guarded in her behaviour towards the undeserving of the other sex.
quotations.speaker: Mary Bennet
quotations.context: To Elizabeth, while the family waits for news of Lydia.
quotations.analysis: The consolation is monstrous and the description is correct, which is the difficulty the novel will not dissolve. ‘Brittle’ and ‘beautiful’ are yoked by alliteration into a single property that a woman owns and can break, and nothing in the plot disproves the account — only Darcy’s money limits the damage.

quotations.text: Are the shades of Pemberley to be thus polluted?
quotations.speaker: Lady Catherine de Bourgh
quotations.context: In the Longbourn shrubbery, demanding that Elizabeth promise never to accept Darcy.
quotations.analysis: The objection has left the realm of income and become almost sacramental: a house has shades, and a marriage would defile them. It is the class argument in its purest and least answerable form, and the novel answers it by having the interview itself convince Darcy to propose again.

quotations.text: I am only resolved to act in that manner which will, in my own opinion, constitute my happiness, without reference to you, or to any person so wholly unconnected with me.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Refusing Lady Catherine the promise she has come for.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to define her own happiness and denies her interrogator any standing at all, and she does it in the flattest, least witty sentence she speaks in the book. The wit is dropped because this is not a duel; it is a jurisdictional claim.

quotations.text: For what do we live but to make sport for our neighbours, and laugh at them in our turn?
quotations.speaker: Mr Bennet
quotations.context: Reading Mr Collins’s letter aloud to Elizabeth, who cannot enjoy it.
quotations.analysis: It is the closest thing he has to a philosophy, and the novel has just finished showing what it costs: the daughter he did not watch has been retrieved with somebody else’s money. The rhetorical question assumes an answer that the last hundred pages have withdrawn.

quotations.text: I have been a selfish being all my life, in practice, though not in principle. As a child I was taught what was right, but I was not taught to correct my temper.
quotations.speaker: Mr Darcy
quotations.context: Walking with Elizabeth after the second proposal has been accepted.
quotations.analysis: The distinction between practice and principle is the same one Elizabeth reached in Chapter 36, and Austen gives the two confessions a matching shape so that the marriage is founded on a shared diagnosis. He blames an upbringing and does not use it as an excuse, which is the difference between him and Wickham.

quotations.text: I am the happiest creature in the world. Perhaps other people have said so before, but not one with such justice. I am happier even than Jane; she only smiles, I laugh.
quotations.speaker: Elizabeth Bennet
quotations.context: Writing to Mrs Gardiner, who had been at Pemberley with her.
quotations.analysis: She claims a superlative and then immediately audits it, which is exactly how she has argued all book. The comparison with Jane is not vanity but accuracy about temperament: the sister who thinks well of everyone smiles, and the one who has had to revise her judgements laughs.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Thomas Egerton, London, in three volumes, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility.

atAGlance.label: Earlier title
atAGlance.note: The 1796–97 draft; the discarded title names the novel’s central test more plainly than the published one.

atAGlance.label: Copyright
atAGlance.note: Austen sold the copyright to Egerton for £110 rather than publishing on commission, and so earned nothing from later editions.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The first proposal falls almost exactly at the centre of the book, and everything after it is re-reading.

criticalViews.position: A comedy of moral education
criticalViews.summary: The oldest reading takes the novel at the word of its discarded title: two people form wrong first impressions, gather better evidence, and are rewarded with each other. On this account the book’s subject is the discipline of judgement.
criticalViews.counter: It has to explain away how much of the reward is material, and why the plot is settled by Darcy’s chequebook rather than by anybody’s improved understanding.

criticalViews.position: An economic novel about women without money
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the entail reads the courtships as a survey of what is available to genteel women with no income: Charlotte’s bargain, Lydia’s disaster and Elizabeth’s luck are three outcomes of one predicament.
criticalViews.counter: Pressed hard it can make Elizabeth’s refusals look like bad economics rather than integrity, and it struggles with how funny the book is.

criticalViews.position: A study in narrative point of view
criticalViews.summary: Formalist and stylistic criticism has focused on Austen’s free indirect style, arguing that the novel’s real achievement is the reader’s induced error: we misjudge Darcy because we are reading through Elizabeth without being told so.
criticalViews.counter: The technique is not applied evenly — several chapters step away from Elizabeth entirely — so the effect may owe as much to withheld information as to style.

essayQuestions.question: How does Austen present the relationship between marriage and money?
essayQuestions.focus: Entail, income and the price of refusal
plan: Start with the entail as a legal fact, not a theme: Longbourn passes to Collins, and five daughters must therefore marry or be dependent.
Read the first sentence as a joke whose real subject is the mothers, then set Charlotte’s speech in Chapter 22 beside it as the same proposition without irony.
Compare the three completed bargains — Charlotte’s comfort, Lydia’s rescue, Elizabeth’s Pemberley — and note what each one cost and who paid.
Test the romantic reading against Chapter 47: Lydia’s ruin is averted by money, and the novel says so plainly.
Conclude on whether the ending endorses the system it has mocked, or simply gives one heroine an exemption from it.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The novel is about learning to read people.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Judgement, evidence and revision
plan: Establish the pattern of instant verdicts: the assembly in Chapter 3, Wickham’s history in Chapter 16, Mrs Bennet on Bingley’s income.
Show how Austen implicates the reader through free indirect style, so that Elizabeth’s misreadings arrive as narrative fact.
Make Chapter 35 the hinge: the evidence is written, it can be re-read, and nothing happens except a change of mind.
Use Pemberley in Chapter 43 to argue that the novel trusts long testimony and property over conversation and charm.
Weigh the counter-case: Jane reads everybody generously and is wrong about nobody’s character, only about their conduct.

essayQuestions.question: Examine Austen’s presentation of Mr Bennet.
essayQuestions.focus: Wit, detachment and paternal failure
plan: Open with the twenty-year joke about his wife’s nerves: the marriage as a settled comic arrangement.
Show the wit turned on his own children in Chapter 18, and on Elizabeth’s proposal crisis in Chapter 20, where it happens to help.
Trace the cost: Lydia goes to Brighton because refusing would have been tiresome, and the library is his habitual answer to every demand.
Read his line about making sport for our neighbours in Chapter 57 against the crisis that has just been paid for by Darcy.
Decide whether the novel forgives him, and what his brief self-reproach after Lydia’s flight is worth.

essayQuestions.question: How far does Pride and Prejudice challenge the class system it describes?
essayQuestions.focus: Rank, connection and the Gardiners
plan: Separate money from rank: the Bennets are gentry without capital, the Gardiners have capital without rank, and Darcy has both.
Track the objection as it hardens: Caroline Bingley’s sneers, Darcy’s first proposal, Lady Catherine’s shades of Pemberley.
Use the Gardiners as the novel’s counter-argument — the tradesman’s family are the most sensible adults in the book and the ones Darcy treats best.
Note the limits: no character crosses a class line without a fortune arriving to make it respectable, and Wickham’s rise is punished.
Conclude on the ending’s arithmetic, where affection is settled alongside incomes in the same sentences.

discussionQuestions: Charlotte Lucas asks only for a comfortable home. Does the novel think she is wrong?
Elizabeth changes her mind about Darcy after seeing his house. Is that a shallow reason or a sound one?
Mr Bennet is the funniest character in the book and arguably the most culpable. Can both be true at once?
Lydia’s elopement is settled with money and never with an apology. What does the novel want us to feel about that?
The book was first called First Impressions. Which title describes it better, and what does the change cost?

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: The seventh child of a Hampshire rector, in a household that read aloud and wrote for each other.

timeline.label: First Impressions drafted
timeline.detail: Written in 1796–97, in Austen’s early twenties. No manuscript of this version survives.

timeline.label: The manuscript is offered to Thomas Cadell
timeline.detail: Austen’s father wrote to the London publisher, who declined without asking to see it. The novel waited more than a decade.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Austen’s first published novel, issued anonymously, made a second Austen title commercially plausible.

timeline.label: Pride and Prejudice published
timeline.detail: Thomas Egerton issued it in three volumes on 28 January, credited to the author of Sense and Sensibility. A second edition followed the same year.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first of Austen’s novels written entirely after she had become a published author.

timeline.label: Emma published
timeline.detail: Issued by John Murray with an 1816 date on the title page.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: She was forty-one. Her name had still not appeared on a title page.

timeline.label: Northanger Abbey and Persuasion published together
timeline.detail: Issued in the last days of 1817 with 1818 on the title page, and carrying the biographical notice by her brother Henry that named her at last.

timeline.label: Richard Bentley reprints the novels
timeline.detail: Austen enters the cheap standard-novel market, and stays in print from this point on.

timeline.label: The Peacock edition
timeline.detail: George Allen publishes Hugh Thomson’s illustrated edition, whose gilt peacock binding became the novel’s most recognisable object.

timeline.label: MGM’s Pride and Prejudice
timeline.detail: Directed by Robert Z. Leonard, with Greer Garson and Laurence Olivier, and costumed with cheerful disregard for the Regency.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: Jennifer Ehle and Colin Firth in six episodes; the version against which most later screen Darcys are measured.

timeline.label: Joe Wright’s film
timeline.detail: Keira Knightley and Matthew Macfadyen, in a version that puts mud, livestock and noise back into Longbourn.

places.name: Hertfordshire
places.note: Longbourn, Meryton and Netherfield: a neighbourhood of twenty-four families, small enough that one new tenant changes everything.

places.name: Gracechurch Street, London
places.note: The Gardiners’ house, within sight of their own warehouses — the address that Caroline Bingley finds fatal and the novel finds respectable.

places.name: Kent
places.note: Hunsford parsonage and Rosings Park, where Charlotte’s bargain and Darcy’s first proposal are both inspected at close range.

places.name: Derbyshire
places.note: Pemberley and the village of Lambton, reached on a tour that Elizabeth undertakes only because the Lakes proved too far.

places.name: Brighton
places.note: The militia’s summer quarters, and the town Lydia is allowed to visit because refusing would have caused a scene.

places.name: Newcastle upon Tyne
places.note: Where Wickham’s new regiment is quartered after the marriage: far north, and paid for by Darcy.

related.why: Austen’s first published novel, and the same marriage market seen from the side of women who have already lost their income.
Another governess-adjacent heroine who refuses a proposal on principle, written thirty years later and with the comedy removed.
A hero who has to discover that his own judgement was bought for him, and that the money came from a source he despised.
The marriage market as farce, with the interrogation about income and connections played at full volume.
The opposite settlement of the same questions about property, rank and who may marry whom.

books.title: Richard II
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: England and Wales, 1398 to 1400, from the lists at Coventry to a cell at Pomfret
books.lengthNote: Around 2,800 lines, and not one of them in prose
books.openingLine: Old John of Gaunt, time-honour'd Lancaster, Hast thou, according to thy oath and band, Brought hither Henry Hereford thy bold son?
books.summary: A king who believes the crown was fixed on him by God seizes his cousin's inheritance to pay for a war in Ireland, and finds that the cousin comes home for the land and stays for the throne. Bolingbroke wins without a battle; Richard loses without a defeat. The play is written entirely in verse, so the man who cannot hold a kingdom can still out-speak everyone in it, and the deposition turns into an argument about what words a king is made of.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Richard II
