Her self-command is a duty she has taken on rather than a coldness, and Austen is careful to show the bill: four months of knowing about Lucy while listening to her sister complain that she does not feel enough.
characters.clue: She keeps another woman’s engagement secret for four months because she was told it in confidence, and is called cold-hearted for it by her own sister.

relationships.label: confided in, and quietly attacked by

characters.name: Marianne Dashwood
characters.summary: Everything but prudent, in the novel’s own phrase. Her mistake is not that she feels too much but that she treats shared taste as evidence of shared character, which makes her the ideal audience for a man performing sensibility at her.
characters.clue: She runs down a hill in the rain, is carried home by a stranger, and later asks her sister whether her own conduct has been blameless.

characters.name: Edward Ferrars
characters.summary: Diffident, without a profession, and held in place by an engagement he made at nineteen to a woman he no longer loves. His honour consists entirely of refusing to break a promise that has become a trap, which is both admirable and the reason he is nearly absent from his own love plot.
characters.clue: He is disinherited rather than break an engagement, and is released only when the woman he is bound to elopes with his richer brother.
traits: with no occupation to fill his time

characters.name: John Willoughby
characters.role: Heir to Allenham, of Combe Magna in Somersetshire
characters.summary: He reads the right poets, rides the right horses and agrees with Marianne about everything, which is exactly how a fortune-hunter would behave and also how a man in love behaves. Austen’s hardest decision is giving him a midnight scene in which his remorse is entirely genuine and entirely useless.
characters.clue: He carries a girl home through the rain, cuts her dead in a London drawing room, and turns up months later to explain himself to her sister while she lies ill upstairs.

characters.name: Colonel Brandon
characters.summary: Introduced as a joke about flannel waistcoats and old age, and revealed to be the only man in the book who has ever acted at real cost. The story of the two Elizas gives the novel its darker arithmetic: what happens to a woman with feeling and no protection.
characters.clue: Thirty-five, silent, and mocked for wearing flannel; he keeps a ward in the country and fights a duel he never mentions.

characters.name: Lucy Steele
characters.summary: Uneducated, sharp and the best tactician in the book. She turns a confidence into a weapon by making Elinor the one person who cannot repeat it, and she ends the novel richer than anybody except by abandoning the engagement she spent four hundred pages defending.
characters.clue: She tells her rival a secret in order to bind her to silence, and finally marries the brother with the money instead.
traits: illiterate on paper and expert in person

characters.name: Mrs Dashwood
characters.summary: She has her second daughter’s temperament and none of a mother’s caution, which is why nobody ever asks Marianne and Willoughby whether they are engaged. Her romantic delicacy is indistinguishable, in its effects, from neglect.
characters.clue: She refuses to ask her daughter a direct question about an engagement because asking would show a want of confidence.

characters.name: John Dashwood
characters.role: The sisters’ half-brother, owner of Norland
characters.summary: He means to keep his promise to his dying father and is talked out of it in one conversation without ever noticing that he has changed his mind. He is the novel’s demonstration that selfishness does not require a villain, only a wife with an argument and a husband who wants to be persuaded.
characters.clue: He promises his dying father to provide for his sisters, and reduces three thousand pounds to occasional presents of fish and game.

characters.name: Fanny Dashwood
characters.summary: She conducts the second chapter like a barrister, moving from three thousand pounds to five hundred to an annuity to nothing at all, and each step sounds more reasonable than the last. Austen gives her no soliloquy and no villainy — only impeccable argument in her own interest.
characters.clue: She observes that people always live for ever when there is an annuity to be paid them, and so the annuity is dropped.

characters.name: Mrs Jennings
characters.summary: Vulgar, inquisitive and the most practically kind person in the novel. She embarrasses both sisters constantly and is also the one who sits up with Marianne when she is dying, which is Austen’s way of separating manners from goodness.
characters.clue: She jokes relentlessly about beaux and conquests, and then nurses a girl she barely knows through a fever nobody else can face.

themes.name: Sense and sensibility
themes.summary: The title looks like a contest and the novel refuses to hold one. Elinor’s judgement leaves her carrying knowledge alone; Marianne’s candour makes her legible to a man who reads her for profit. Each sister ends the book holding something she learned from the other.
themes.development: Set up in Chapter 1 as a contrast of temperaments, tested through four months of silence, and settled in Chapter 46 when Marianne judges her own conduct by her sister’s standard.

themes.name: Money and inheritance
themes.summary: The plot is started by a will and finished by a settlement, and every important decision in between has a figure attached. Austen puts the numbers on the page — two thousand a year, five hundred pounds, a hundred a year — so that no reader can treat the feeling as separable from the income.
themes.development: From the second chapter’s reduction of a promise to nothing, through Marianne’s argument about competence in Chapter 17, to the livings and settlements distributed in the last chapters.

themes.name: Secrecy and silence
themes.summary: Almost every crisis in the book is caused by something withheld: an engagement kept for four years, an attachment never declared, a history told too late. Silence is variously honour, weapon and cowardice, and the novel distinguishes carefully between the three.
themes.development: Lucy’s disclosure in Chapter 22 loads the gun; Elinor’s four months of secrecy are detonated in Chapter 37; Brandon’s history and Willoughby’s confession arrive when they can no longer help.

themes.name: Dependence
themes.summary: The Dashwood women are not poor in any sense a labourer would recognise, and they have no power whatever over where they live, what they keep or whom they may marry. The novel’s interest is in that specific genteel powerlessness, which looks comfortable and forecloses everything.
themes.development: Begins with the entail of Norland, continues at Barton on a relation’s charity, and reaches its sharpest point in the two Elizas, who had feeling and no protection at all.

themes.name: Performance and sincerity
themes.summary: Willoughby’s great advantage is that he is genuinely charming, so the performance of sensibility and the thing itself cannot be told apart by taste alone. The novel keeps asking what evidence of character is admissible, and keeps answering: conduct over time, and nothing else.
themes.development: Established in Marianne’s first conversations with Willoughby about Cowper and dead leaves, and undone by the letter in Chapter 29 that he did not write.

themes.name: Illness and the body
themes.summary: Marianne’s fever is not a metaphor that arrives conveniently; it is caused by wet feet, twice, and nearly kills her. Austen lets grief have physical consequences so that the reckoning that follows is forced on a body rather than reasoned out at leisure.
themes.development: Wet grass at Cleveland, a putrid fever, a night when Elinor expects her sister to die, and a recovery that produces the novel’s only formal self-examination.

techniques.name: Free indirect style
techniques.definition: Narration that borrows a character’s idiom and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.bookDefinition: Narration that borrows a character’s idiom and assumptions without marking them as quotation.
techniques.inThisBook: The narration sits mostly with Elinor, so the reader is kept as ignorant as she is and as bound by her discretion; Marianne is largely observed from outside, which is why her feelings arrive as events.

techniques.name: Irony
techniques.definition: Wording that invites the reader to a judgement the speaker has not made.
techniques.bookDefinition: Wording that invites the reader to a judgement the speaker has not made.
techniques.inThisBook: The second chapter is conducted entirely in reasonable-sounding speech, and Austen never once says that John Dashwood is being mean; the arithmetic says it.

techniques.name: Letters
techniques.definition: Written documents used as plot, evidence and characterisation.
techniques.bookDefinition: Written documents used as plot, evidence and characterisation.
techniques.inThisBook: Marianne writes three unanswered notes and receives one cold reply that was dictated by another woman, and the physical returning of her letters and a lock of hair is what makes the break public.

techniques.name: Paired plots
techniques.definition: Running two versions of a situation side by side so that each measures the other.
techniques.bookDefinition: Running two versions of a situation side by side so that each measures the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Both sisters lose a man to a prior claim and a richer woman; one conceals it for four months and one collapses in a ballroom, and the novel refuses to declare a winner.

techniques.name: Embedded histories
techniques.definition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.bookDefinition: A second, older story told by a character to explain the present one.
techniques.inThisBook: Brandon’s account of the two Elizas supplies the consequences the main plot is too polite to stage, and turns Willoughby from a disappointment into a danger.

techniques.name: Dialogue as exposure
techniques.definition: Allowing characters to convict themselves in their own speech.
techniques.bookDefinition: Allowing characters to convict themselves in their own speech.
techniques.inThisBook: Fanny Dashwood argues her husband down from three thousand pounds to nothing in a single conversation, and every step she takes sounds more reasonable than the one before.

quotations.text: possessed a strength of understanding, and coolness of judgment, which qualified her, though only nineteen, to be the counsellor of her mother
quotations.context: The narrator’s first account of the eldest Dashwood sister.
quotations.analysis: A nineteen-year-old is described as her mother’s counsellor, which characterises the mother as much as the daughter. The nouns are all about control — strength, coolness, judgment — and the clause that follows insists she also has strong feelings, so the novel cannot later be read as praising numbness.

quotations.text: She was sensible and clever; but eager in everything: her sorrows, her joys, could have no moderation. She was generous, amiable, interesting: she was everything but prudent.
quotations.context: The narrator introducing Marianne, immediately after the account of Elinor.
quotations.analysis: Three compliments and then the single withheld word. ‘Everything but prudent’ concedes that she lacks only one quality and structures the whole plot around its absence, and the list of generous, amiable, interesting is exactly what Willoughby will find useful.

quotations.text: people always live forever when there is an annuity to be paid them; and she is very stout and healthy, and hardly forty. An annuity is a very serious business; it comes over and over every year, and there is no getting rid of it.
quotations.speaker: Fanny Dashwood
quotations.context: Persuading her husband out of the last version of his promise to his dying father.
quotations.analysis: The objection to an annuity is that the recipients will be so inconsiderate as to survive. Notice the shift from a moral question to a bookkeeping one: ‘a very serious business’ and ‘no getting rid of it’ are the phrases of a woman describing a liability, and nobody in the room corrects her.

quotations.text: I think very highly of him⁠—that I greatly esteem, that I like him.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Answering her mother and sister about her feelings for Edward Ferrars.
quotations.analysis: Three verbs in ascending order, each hedged, and none of them the one she means. It is not coldness but accuracy: she has no engagement and no declaration, so she claims only what she can defend — and her sister immediately treats the precision as an insult to love itself.

quotations.text: Esteem him! Like him! Cold-hearted Elinor! Oh! worse than cold-hearted! Ashamed of being otherwise. Use those words again, and I will leave the room this moment.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Bursting out at Elinor’s careful account of her feelings for Edward.
quotations.analysis: She repeats her sister’s two verbs as though quoting evidence at a trial, and the charge is not that Elinor feels nothing but that she is ashamed to say so. Forty chapters later Marianne will use the same word about her own conduct, and mean the opposite by it.

quotations.text: Oh! happy house, could you know what I suffer in now viewing you from this spot, from whence perhaps I may view you no more!⁠—And you, ye well-known trees!⁠—but you will continue the same.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Walking alone in front of the house on the family’s last evening at Norland.
quotations.analysis: She addresses a house and then a stand of trees, and both refuse to answer, which she takes personally. The apostrophe is her method in miniature: feeling counts as real only when it is performed aloud, and the complaint that the trees will continue the same is a complaint that grief has no witness.

quotations.text: with me a flannel waistcoat is invariably connected with aches, cramps, rheumatisms, and every species of ailment that can afflict the old and the feeble.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Rejecting Mrs Jennings’s suggestion that Colonel Brandon admires her.
quotations.analysis: A whole character is dismissed on the evidence of one garment, which is precisely the reasoning Marianne uses in the other direction about Willoughby. The novel remembers the joke: the last paragraph about her marriage returns to the flannel waistcoat, and by then the garment has stopped being funny.

quotations.text: with what transporting sensation have I formerly seen them fall! How have I delighted, as I walked, to see them driven in showers about me by the wind! What feelings have they, the season, the air altogether inspired! Now there is no one to regard them. They are seen only as a nuisance, swept hastily off, and driven as much as possible from the sight.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Told by Elinor that the walks at Norland are thick with dead leaves.
quotations.analysis: Three exclamations about her own past sensations, and then a grievance: the leaves are now swept up by people who do not feel them. Elinor’s one-line reply, that not everyone shares her passion for dead leaves, is the driest thing she says in the book, and it lands because Marianne has just claimed a monopoly on noticing.

quotations.text: What have wealth or grandeur to do with happiness?
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Objecting to Elinor’s remark about the uses of money.
quotations.analysis: A rhetorical question that the plot spends the next thirty chapters answering in detail. Within ten lines Marianne has priced her own competence at about two thousand a year, which is roughly the income of the man she is rejecting as too old.

quotations.text: Your competence and my wealth are very much alike, I dare say; and without them, as the world goes now, we shall both agree that every kind of external comfort must be wanting. Your ideas are only more noble than mine. Come, what is your competence?
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Turning her sister’s objection about money into a question with a number in it.
quotations.analysis: The trick is to let Marianne keep the nobler word and then ask her to define it. Austen’s characters argue about income the way other novels’ characters argue about virtue, and the scene ends with a figure rather than a principle.

quotations.text: We have been engaged these four years.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Telling Elinor about her engagement to Edward Ferrars, in a conversation Lucy has carefully arranged.
quotations.analysis: Six words, placed after a long approach designed to make Elinor ask for them. The disclosure is an act of aggression disguised as intimacy: once Elinor holds the secret as a confidence, she is the one person in England who cannot use it.

quotations.text: to be as solemnly engaged to him, as if the strictest legal covenant had bound us to each other.
quotations.speaker: Lucy Steele
quotations.context: Marianne, quoting her own understanding of her position with Willoughby after his letter arrives.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a legal instrument, which is exactly what she does not have. A private understanding, however sincere, leaves no document and no claim; Lucy Steele’s four-year engagement is equally unwritten and she treats it as property, which is why she wins.

quotations.text: For four months, Marianne, I have had all this hanging on my mind, without being at liberty to speak of it to a single creature; knowing that it would make you and my mother most unhappy whenever it were explained to you
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Telling Marianne, for the first time, how long she has known about Lucy’s engagement.
quotations.analysis: The unit is time, not feeling: four months, without liberty to speak, while being told repeatedly that she does not feel enough. The sentence also explains the novel’s structure — the reader has been kept inside Elinor’s silence too, and only now learns what it weighed.

quotations.text: I acknowledge that her situation and her character ought to have been respected by me. I do not mean to justify myself, but at the same time cannot leave you to suppose that I have nothing to urge⁠—that because she was injured she was irreproachable, and because I was a libertine, she must be a saint.
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: At Cleveland, at midnight, while Marianne lies dangerously ill upstairs.
quotations.analysis: He concedes the charge and then immediately reopens it, which is the pattern of the whole confession: an apology with a defence folded inside it. ‘Because I was a libertine, she must be a saint’ is a real argument about evidence, offered by a man who needs it not to be true.

quotations.text: I felt that she was infinitely dearer to me than any other woman
quotations.speaker: John Willoughby
quotations.context: Describing the effect of Marianne’s note, received in London after he had decided to marry Miss Grey.
quotations.analysis: The comparative is the problem: she is dearer than other women, and he has already worked out what she is worth against an income. Austen allows the feeling to be genuine precisely so that the novel cannot be read as saying that charming men are simply insincere.

quotations.text: My illness has made me think. It has given me leisure and calmness for serious recollection. Long before I was enough recovered to talk, I was perfectly able to reflect. I considered the past: I saw in my own behaviour, since the beginning of our acquaintance with him last autumn, nothing but a series of imprudence towards myself, and want of kindness to others.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Convalescent at Barton, setting out her own conduct to Elinor.
quotations.analysis: The self-examination is conducted in the vocabulary of accounting — a series, a beginning, a survey of behaviour since last autumn — which is how her sister thinks, not how she does. Note that she blames imprudence and unkindness to others, never the strength of her feelings.

quotations.text: I compare it with what it ought to have been; I compare it with yours.
quotations.speaker: Marianne Dashwood
quotations.context: Refusing Elinor’s attempt to excuse her conduct by comparing it with other people’s.
quotations.analysis: Two clauses, the second shorter and harder than the first. She adopts an absolute standard and then names a person as its measure, which is the precise reversal of Chapter 4, where the same sister’s behaviour was evidence of a cold heart.

quotations.text: I will be calm⁠—I will be mistress of myself.
quotations.speaker: Elinor Dashwood
quotations.context: Watching from the window as a horseman she takes to be Edward dismounts at the gate.
quotations.analysis: She states self-command as an intention rather than a fact, which is the closest the novel comes to admitting what it has cost her. Two chapters of evidence follow: when Edward’s news finally arrives she leaves the room and cries until she thinks she will never stop.

quotations.text: Marianne Dashwood was born to an extraordinary fate. She was born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions, and to counteract, by her conduct, her most favourite maxims. She was born to overcome an affection formed so late in life as at seventeen, and with no sentiment superior to strong esteem and lively friendship, voluntarily to give her hand to another!
quotations.context: The narrator summing up Marianne’s marriage to Colonel Brandon.
quotations.analysis: The mock-heroic opening promises a destiny and delivers a list of maxims disproved. ‘Born to discover the falsehood of her own opinions’ makes the second marriage a correction rather than a reward, and readers have argued ever since about whether the joke is affectionate or a shrug.

quotations.text: among the merits and the happiness of Elinor and Marianne, let it not be ranked as the least considerable, that though sisters, and living almost within sight of each other, they could live without disagreement between themselves, or producing coolness between their husbands.
quotations.context: The final sentence of the novel.
quotations.analysis: The book closes not on either marriage but on the relation between the sisters, and phrases their achievement in the negative — no disagreement, no coolness. After a plot driven by what one sister could not tell the other, the last thing the novel counts as happiness is two women living within sight of each other and still speaking.

atAGlance.label: First published
atAGlance.note: Printed for the author by C. Roworth and published by T. Egerton, Whitehall, in three volumes, ‘By A Lady’.

atAGlance.label: Financial risk
atAGlance.note: Austen carried the cost herself and kept the copyright, which is why this novel, unlike Pride and Prejudice, went on earning for her.

atAGlance.label: Earlier form
atAGlance.note: Family tradition remembers an earlier version, probably in letters. No manuscript survives.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: The engagement that drives the whole plot is disclosed to Elinor at the end of the first volume and to everyone else in the third.

criticalViews.position: A conduct-novel with a verdict
criticalViews.summary: One long-standing reading takes the title at face value: Marianne’s sensibility is a fashionable excess, Elinor’s judgement is the corrective, and the plot administers the lesson through illness and a second marriage.
criticalViews.counter: It has to ignore how much the novel charges Elinor for her self-command, and how carefully it refuses to say that Marianne’s feelings were themselves the error.

criticalViews.position: A novel about property and dependence
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the opening chapters treats the will, the entail and the annuity conversation as the real engine: the book is about what happens to women whose income is decided by a half-brother’s conscience.
criticalViews.counter: Pushed far, it reduces both sisters to case studies and has little to say about the comedy, which is where most of Austen’s precision actually lives.

criticalViews.position: A study in what may be said aloud
criticalViews.summary: A more formal reading attends to who knows what and when: the novel is organised around secrets, confidences and disclosures, and the reader is held inside Elinor’s silence as a technical device rather than a moral example.
criticalViews.counter: This can make the ending feel arbitrary, since the secret is dissolved not by anyone’s virtue but by Lucy Steele changing brothers.

essayQuestions.question: Does Sense and Sensibility side with Elinor?
essayQuestions.focus: The title as a contest, and the novel’s refusal to hold one
plan: Set out the Chapter 1 contrast precisely: strength of understanding and coolness of judgment against sensible, clever and everything but prudent.
Show what Elinor’s method costs in Chapter 37 — four months of silence, and the accusation of feeling nothing from her own sister.
Show what Marianne’s method costs at Cleveland, and note that the illness has a physical cause, not a poetic one.
Read Chapter 46 closely: Marianne adopts her sister’s standard, and Elinor in Chapter 48 has to announce self-command as an intention rather than possess it.
Conclude on the last sentence, which measures success by the sisters’ relation to each other rather than by either temperament winning.

essayQuestions.question: How does Austen use money in the novel?
essayQuestions.focus: Wills, annuities, competence and settlements
plan: Begin with Chapter 2 as a set piece: a promise reduced by stages, with every step argued in reasonable language.
Trace the sums that follow — five hundred pounds, a hundred a year, two thousand a year at Delaford — and note that Austen always gives the figure.
Use the competence exchange in Chapter 17 to show the sisters arguing about income in the vocabulary of virtue.
Show money deciding the plot rather than decorating it: Willoughby’s debts, Mrs Ferrars’s disinheritance, and Brandon’s gift of a living.
Weigh whether the ending criticises this economy or simply provides two escapes from it.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of Willoughby.
essayQuestions.focus: Charm, sincerity and the midnight confession
plan: Establish how his charm works: shared taste in poetry and music, treated by Marianne as proof of shared character.
Set the letter of Chapter 29 beside the man, and note that it was dictated by another woman — his cruelty is partly delegated.
Bring in Brandon’s history of the two Elizas, which converts a disappointing suitor into a demonstrable danger.
Read the Chapter 44 confession carefully: the apologies and the self-defences are interleaved, and the feeling is genuine.
Decide what the novel gains by refusing to make him simply insincere, and what it loses.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The novel is driven by what cannot be said.’ Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Secrecy, confidence and disclosure
plan: List the withheld information: Lucy’s engagement, Brandon’s history, Willoughby’s debts, Elinor’s own attachment.
Show that Lucy’s disclosure in Chapter 22 works as a weapon precisely because it is framed as a confidence.
Contrast Marianne, who conceals nothing and is ruined by having no written proof of anything.
Use Mrs Dashwood’s refusal to ask a direct question about an engagement as the novel’s sharpest criticism of delicacy.
Close on how the secret is finally dissolved — not by honesty, but by Lucy transferring herself to the richer brother.

discussionQuestions: Elinor keeps Lucy’s secret for four months because she was told it in confidence. Was she right to?
Marianne marries a man she once mocked for wearing flannel. Is the ending a reward, a compromise or a joke?
Fanny Dashwood is never punished and never in doubt. Why does Austen put her argument at the very front of the book?
Willoughby’s remorse is real. Does that make him better or worse?
Mrs Jennings is vulgar and kind; Mr John Dashwood is polite and cold. What is the novel saying about manners?

timeline.label: Jane Austen born at Steventon
timeline.detail: In the Hampshire rectory where she wrote the first versions of three of her six novels.

timeline.label: Elinor and Marianne
timeline.detail: Family tradition places an early version of this story in the mid-1790s, probably told in letters. No manuscript survives.

timeline.label: First Impressions offered to a publisher and refused
timeline.detail: The novel that became Pride and Prejudice was declined unseen, and Austen published nothing for another fourteen years.

timeline.label: The Austens settle at Chawton
timeline.detail: The move to a settled house in Hampshire begins the period in which every one of Austen’s novels was revised or written.

timeline.label: Sense and Sensibility published
timeline.detail: Printed for the author by C. Roworth, published by T. Egerton in three volumes, and advertised at fifteen shillings in boards.

timeline.label: The first edition sells out; a second follows
timeline.detail: In the same year Pride and Prejudice appeared as ‘by the author of Sense and Sensibility’, turning an anonymous debut into a commercial identity.

timeline.label: Mansfield Park published
timeline.detail: The first novel Austen wrote knowing that she had readers.

timeline.label: Austen dies at Winchester
timeline.detail: Aged forty-one, with none of her novels published under her own name.

timeline.label: Bentley’s Standard Novels reprint
timeline.detail: Sense and Sensibility re-enters the market in a cheap uniform edition, and Austen’s novels stop going out of print.

timeline.label: First BBC television adaptation
timeline.detail: The beginning of a long serial tradition that gives the social network around the sisters more room than a feature film can.

timeline.label: Ang Lee’s film, from Emma Thompson’s screenplay
timeline.detail: Thompson as Elinor, Kate Winslet as Marianne, Alan Rickman as Brandon; it won the Academy Award for Adapted Screenplay and the Golden Bear at Berlin.

timeline.label: Kandukondain Kandukondain
timeline.detail: Rajiv Menon’s Tamil-language film relocates the sisters, the prospects and the delayed recognition to an Indian setting.

timeline.label: BBC serial adapted by Andrew Davies
timeline.detail: A three-part version directed by John Alexander, which restores the seduction plot to its place near the front of the story.

places.name: Sussex
places.note: Norland Park, where the Dashwoods had been settled for generations and lived for a single year as guests of the heir.

places.name: Devonshire
places.note: Barton Cottage and Barton Park: a house taken on very easy terms from a relation, which is a polite name for charity.

places.name: London
places.note: Berkeley Street and the drawing rooms where Marianne waits for a reply, and is cut in public when it comes.

places.name: Somersetshire
places.note: Combe Magna, Willoughby’s own small estate, and Cleveland, where Marianne walks in wet grass until she is dangerously ill.

places.name: Dorsetshire
places.note: Delaford, Colonel Brandon’s property, with the living he gives away and the mulberry tree Mrs Jennings cannot stop describing.

places.name: Plymouth
places.note: Where the Steele sisters have their connections, and the town whose name is enough to place them socially the moment it is mentioned.

related.why: Written from the same drafts and the same decade, with the comedy pitched higher and the money kept just as visible.
Another dependent young woman with no property and a prior claim standing between her and the man she wants.
Marianne’s question about what feeling is owed to convention, asked again eighty years later and answered far more bleakly.
Sensibility taken to the point where it stops being a temperament and becomes a force that wrecks two households.
Fanny Dashwood’s arithmetic turned into farce, with incomes and connections interrogated out loud.

books.title: The Taming of the Shrew
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Padua and a country house on the road to Verona, framed by an English alehouse
books.lengthNote: Around 2,600 lines, of which the first 270 belong to a drunk who then disappears
books.openingLine: I'll pheeze you, in faith.
books.summary: A tinker is picked up drunk outside an alehouse and persuaded by a bored lord that he is a nobleman recovering from madness. The play performed for him is about a man who marries a woman for her dowry and then starves and contradicts her into agreement, and about a younger sister whose suitors buy their way into her house disguised as tutors. Shakespeare never returns to the tinker, so the audience is left holding a frame with nothing on the other end of it.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of The Taming of the Shrew
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The two Induction scenes are numbered 0.1 and 0.2 in the digital text used for checking, and are cited here as Induction 1 and Induction 2.

structure.label: Induction
structure.title: A tinker is told he is a lord
structure.summary: Christopher Sly is thrown out of an alehouse for breaking glasses and falls asleep. A lord returning from hunting decides, as a joke, to have him carried home, dressed in fine clothes and told that his old life was a fifteen-year delusion. Sly holds out for about a hundred lines and then accepts it, and a company of players is brought in to perform the Padua comedy for him.

scenes.title: The alehouse
scenes.summary: Sly refuses to pay for the glasses, passes out, and is found by a lord with an idea.

scenes.title: The bedchamber
scenes.summary: Sly is waited on, given a page dressed as his wife, and settles down to watch a play.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: One daughter unsellable, the other on the market
structure.summary: Baptista announces that Bianca may not marry until her elder sister is off his hands, which makes Katherina an obstacle before the audience has heard her speak twenty lines. Lucentio falls in love at first sight and swaps clothes with his servant so that he can enter the house as a tutor. Petruchio arrives from Verona and says plainly that he has come to marry money.

scenes.title: The condition
scenes.summary: Baptista sets his terms; Katherina is insulted in public; Lucentio and Tranio exchange identities.

scenes.title: The suitor from Verona
scenes.summary: Petruchio states his price, hears about Katherina's temper, and is undeterred; Hortensio disguises himself as a music master.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A courtship conducted at speed
structure.summary: Katherina has tied up her sister and is striking her when their father walks in, which is the one scene that shows what the household is actually like. Petruchio then meets her, matches her insult for insult for a hundred lines, tells her father they have privately agreed to marry, and settles the dowry. The wedding is fixed for Sunday before Katherina has consented to anything.

scenes.title: The wooing
scenes.summary: Katherina beats Bianca; Petruchio conducts a wit duel, declares a match, and bargains with Baptista; Tranio outbids Gremio for Bianca.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: A wedding treated as a piece of theatre
structure.summary: Two disguised suitors compete for Bianca's attention under cover of a Latin lesson and a music lesson. Petruchio arrives hours late for his own wedding in deliberately ridiculous clothes, behaves outrageously in church, and then removes his wife before the dinner, announcing that she is his property and pretending to rescue her from thieves.

scenes.title: The lessons
scenes.summary: Lucentio courts Bianca through a construed Latin sentence; Hortensio through a gamut; Bianca sets the terms.

scenes.title: The wedding
scenes.summary: Petruchio comes late and badly dressed, marries Katherina, and carries her off before the feast.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The taming, and a father invented
structure.summary: At Petruchio's house the food is sent back, the bed is pulled apart and a tailor is abused, all in the name of Katherina's comfort. Petruchio explains the method to the audience in falconry terms. On the road back to Padua he makes her agree that the sun is the moon; in Padua a passing pedant is recruited to impersonate Lucentio's father, and the real one arrives.

scenes.title: The country house
scenes.summary: Servants are beaten, the meat is thrown out, and Petruchio sets out his plan alone on stage.

scenes.title: Substitutions
scenes.summary: Hortensio gives up on Bianca and marries a widow; Tranio recruits a pedant to play Vincentio.

scenes.title: The cap and the gown
scenes.summary: Katherina insists on her right to speak; the tailor's work is destroyed; the journey is cancelled over the time of day.

scenes.title: The false father
scenes.summary: The pedant settles the marriage terms as Vincentio, and Lucentio and Bianca slip away to be married.

scenes.title: Sun and moon
scenes.summary: Katherina agrees that the sun is the moon, then greets old Vincentio as a budding virgin.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The wager
structure.summary: The real Vincentio meets his impostor and is nearly arrested; the secret marriage is revealed and forgiven. At the wedding feast the three husbands bet on which wife will come when sent for. Katherina comes, fetches the other two, and delivers forty-four lines on a wife's duty to a room of men who have just staked money on her behaviour.

scenes.title: Two Vincentios
scenes.summary: The impersonation collapses; Lucentio confesses the marriage; the fathers are reconciled.

scenes.title: The feast
scenes.summary: The wager is laid and won, and Katherina speaks on obedience before the company.

characters.name: Katherina
characters.summary: She is called a devil, a fiend and a shrew before she has done anything on stage except resent being auctioned second. Her wit is faster than anyone else's in Padua and she is never once allowed to use it without being punished for it, which is the strongest argument the play makes on her side.
characters.clue: The elder sister nobody will bid for, who ties up the younger one, matches a stranger joke for joke, and ends by telling a room of men to put their hands under their husbands' feet.

characters.name: Petruchio
characters.role: A gentleman of Verona, come to Padua to marry
characters.summary: He announces his financial motive in his first scene and never withdraws it, which makes him harder to sentimentalise than productions often allow. His method is entirely theatrical — arriving in absurd clothes, praising food he is about to throw away, insisting the sun is the moon — and he explains it to the audience in the language of hawking.
characters.clue: He comes to Padua to wive it wealthily, turns up to his own wedding in rags on a broken-down horse, and starves his bride in the name of kindness.

characters.name: Bianca
characters.summary: She is silent and obedient for as long as it is useful, and the moment she has tutors alone in a room she tells them she will learn as she pleases. By the last scene she has married in secret, refuses to come when sent for, and calls her husband a fool for betting on her — the play's quietest joke at the taming plot's expense.
characters.clue: Everyone's idea of a good daughter, who arranges her own marriage behind her father's back and then will not come when her husband calls.

characters.name: Baptista Minola
characters.role: A wealthy gentleman of Padua, father of both sisters
characters.summary: He runs his household as a market and says so: Bianca goes to the highest bidder, Katherina to anyone who will take her. He asks his elder daughter for her consent exactly once, receives an answer that is plainly not one, and proceeds anyway.

characters.name: Lucentio
characters.role: A student from Pisa, in love with Bianca
characters.summary: He arrives in Padua announcing that he has come for philosophy and falls in love before the end of his first speech. His solution is to become his own servant and teach Latin, which means the romantic lead spends most of the play pretending to be someone poorer than he is.

characters.name: Tranio
characters.summary: Given his master's clothes, he negotiates with Baptista, outbids a rich old man, hires an impostor father and keeps three deceptions running at once. The play's most competent social performer is a servant, and it lets him get away with all of it.
traits: better at being a gentleman than his master

characters.name: Hortensio
characters.role: A suitor to Bianca, disguised as the music master Litio
characters.summary: He disguises himself, is beaten over the head with his own lute, gives up on Bianca when he sees her flirting with a Latin tutor, and marries a widow out of pique. He then loses the wager in the last scene, which is the play's verdict on choosing a wife in a temper.

characters.name: Gremio
characters.role: An elderly, rich suitor to Bianca
characters.summary: He is the pantaloon of Italian comedy, bidding his plate and his hangings and his ships against a young man's invented inheritance. Beaten in the auction, he is left to report on the wedding — and his account of Petruchio in church is the only description of it the play gives.

characters.name: Grumio
characters.summary: He is beaten in the first scene for misunderstanding an instruction and spends the rest of the play as the taming's foot soldier: withholding food, describing the journey, playing along with a master he plainly finds frightening. His account of the ride to the country house is the closest the play comes to showing what the marriage looks like from outside.

characters.name: Christopher Sly
characters.role: A tinker, and the audience for the Padua play
characters.summary: He is talked out of his own identity in under a hundred lines by people who find it funny, which is the experiment the rest of the play repeats on a wife. Shakespeare's text drops him after the first act and never brings him back, and every production has to decide what to do about that.
characters.clue: A tinker who will not pay for the glasses he has broken, claims the family came in with Richard Conqueror, and wakes up being offered sack and a wife.

themes.name: Marriage as a market
themes.summary: Nobody in Padua marries without a negotiation. Baptista will not release Bianca until Katherina is sold, Gremio bids his tapestries against Tranio's imaginary ships, Petruchio states his price in his first scene, and the last act is a wager laid on wives. The romance is real but it is always conducted over a contract.
themes.development: Baptista's condition in 1.1, the dowry settled in 2.1, the auction for Bianca in the same scene, and twenty thousand crowns added as a second dowry in 5.2.

themes.name: Taming
themes.summary: The method is deprivation dressed as care: no food, no sleep, no clothes, every refusal delivered as concern for her comfort. Petruchio borrows the vocabulary of hawking to describe it, which is the play at its most disquieting — the language assumes a creature that can be reduced to obedience by hunger and then flown.
themes.development: Announced as an intention in 2.1, explained to the audience in 4.1, tested on the road in 4.5 and displayed as a finished result in 5.2.

themes.name: Disguise and substitution
themes.summary: A servant becomes his master, a master becomes a tutor, a suitor becomes a music teacher, a passing pedant becomes a father, and a tinker becomes a lord. Identity in this play is a matter of clothes and repetition, which is exactly the assumption the taming plot is built on.
themes.development: Lucentio and Tranio change places in 1.1; the false Vincentio is recruited in 4.2 and exposed in 5.1; Sly's transformation in the Induction sets the pattern for all of them.

themes.name: The obedience speech
themes.summary: Forty-four lines on a wife's duty to her lord, delivered in front of men who have just bet money on whether she would come when called. Nothing in the text settles the tone, which is why the speech has been played as surrender, as irony, as a private arrangement between two people and as a public humiliation.
themes.development: Katherina refuses to be silenced in 4.3, agrees to call the sun the moon in 4.5, and in 5.2 tells two other women that their lances are but straws.

themes.name: Naming and contradiction
themes.summary: Petruchio's chief weapon is insisting on his own version of the words: she is Kate, the food is burnt, the cap is a bauble, the sun is the moon. Katherina's resistance is equally verbal, and the marriage is settled not by force but by who gets to decide what things are called.
themes.development: The wit duel of 2.1 is fought on equal terms; by 4.5 one party is naming and the other assenting; the last speech is the naming done in her own voice.

themes.name: Who is watching
themes.summary: Almost everything in the play is performed for an onstage audience: Sly watches the comedy, Gremio reports the wedding, Hortensio spies on Bianca, and the obedience speech is delivered to a room of spectators who have money on it. The Induction makes watching a subject before the main plot has begun.
themes.development: The frame is set up in the Induction and abandoned after 1.1; the wager scene reinstates the same arrangement, with the husbands as the lord and Katherina as Sly.

techniques.name: The unclosed frame
techniques.definition: A story enclosed within another story, often several layers deep.
techniques.bookDefinition: A story enclosing another story, here left open at one end.
techniques.inThisBook: Sly is set up as the play's audience and then simply dropped. The related 1594 quarto A Shrew brings him back at the end, which is why eighteenth-century editors borrowed that ending and why modern directors still have to choose.

techniques.name: Disguise plot
techniques.definition: A character adopting another identity in full view of the audience.
techniques.bookDefinition: Comedy driven by exchanged and counterfeited identities.
techniques.inThisBook: Inherited from Gascoigne's Supposes, itself from Ariosto: a servant in his master's gown, two suitors as tutors and a stranger hired to play a father, all running at once and colliding in 5.1.

techniques.name: Falconry imagery
techniques.definition: Sustained comparison of a person to a hawk being trained.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sustained comparison of a person to a hawk being trained.
techniques.inThisBook: Petruchio's soliloquy in 4.1 uses the technical vocabulary exactly — sharp, full-gorged, lure, man my haggard, watch her — so the audience is told the method in the language of a manual rather than a metaphor.

techniques.name: Stichomythia
techniques.definition: Rapid exchange of single lines between two speakers.
techniques.bookDefinition: Rapid exchange of single lines between two speakers.
techniques.inThisBook: The wooing scene in 2.1 runs on it for over eighty lines: joined-stool, ass, jade, buzzard, each answer taking the previous line's word and turning it round. It is the only sustained conversation in which Katherina is a match for anyone.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, telling the audience what they are doing.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character alone on stage, telling the audience what they are doing.
techniques.inThisBook: Petruchio gets one and Katherina does not. His speech at the end of 4.1 hands the audience the whole strategy and then asks whether anybody knows a better way, which makes the spectators accomplices.

techniques.name: Wordplay
techniques.definition: Puns and quibbles used as attack and defence.
techniques.bookDefinition: Puns and quibbles used as attack and defence.
techniques.inThisBook: Kate, cate and Kates in 2.1; a cap that is a custard-coffin, a bauble and a silken pie in 4.3. The play keeps showing that whoever controls the joke controls the scene.

quotations.text: Ye are a baggage: the Slys are no rogues; look in the chronicles; we came in with Richard Conqueror.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: Outside the alehouse, refusing to pay for the glasses he has broken.
quotations.analysis: He defends his family's standing by appealing to a history book he has never read and getting the Conqueror's name wrong. The play's first words are therefore a man insisting on an identity he cannot support — which is exactly the trick the lord is about to play on him from the other direction.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, Induction 1, lines 3-4 (numbered 0.1.3-4 in the digital text)

quotations.text: Come, madam wife, sit by my side and let the world slip: we shall ne'er be younger.
quotations.speaker: Sly
quotations.context: The last thing Sly says before the Padua play begins.
quotations.analysis: He has accepted the lordship, the wife who is a page in a dress, and the play about to be performed for him, all within a scene. These are almost his final words in the text: the character who has just learned to let the world slip is himself allowed to slip out of the comedy without explanation.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, Induction 2, lines 143-144 (numbered 0.2.143-144 in the digital text)

quotations.text: To see fair Padua, nursery of arts
quotations.speaker: Lucentio
quotations.context: Arriving in the city to study.
quotations.analysis: The play he has walked into is not about arts but about prices, and he will abandon the university within forty lines for a disguise and a marriage. Padua's reputation is set up in the second line of the main plot precisely so that everything that follows can ignore it.

quotations.text: Her eldest sister is so curst and shrewd That till the father rid his hands of her, Master, your love must live a maid at home;
quotations.speaker: Tranio
quotations.context: Explaining the household's rules to Lucentio.
quotations.analysis: Katherina is introduced to the audience as a problem of logistics: a thing the father must be rid of before the real business can proceed. 'Curst' and 'shrewd' are both technical terms of abuse for women rather than descriptions, and they are applied by a servant who has seen her once.

quotations.text: I come to wive it wealthily in Padua; If wealthily, then happily in Padua.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Telling Hortensio what kind of wife he is looking for.
quotations.analysis: The couplet makes wealth the condition of happiness in so many words, and the repetition of 'in Padua' turns the city into a marketplace with a location. Nothing later in the play retracts this; the love, if it is there, arrives after the terms have been agreed.

quotations.text: What, will you not suffer me? Nay, now I see She is your treasure, she must have a husband; I must dance bare-foot on her wedding day And for your love to her lead apes in hell.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: To her father, who has just sent Bianca out of the room after Katherina struck her.
quotations.analysis: The violence of the scene is real and so is the grievance underneath it: she is describing, accurately, a household in which one daughter is the treasure and the other the obstacle. Dancing barefoot at a younger sister's wedding and leading apes in hell were both proverbial fates of the unmarried, so she is naming the future arranged for her.

quotations.text: Asses are made to bear, and so are you.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: In the middle of the wit duel, after Petruchio invites her to sit on him.
quotations.analysis: She takes his innuendo and returns it as an insult in the same number of syllables, which is what the whole scene consists of. His reply — 'Women are made to bear, and so are you' — changes bearing weight into bearing children, and the exchange shows the two of them evenly matched at the only game either of them is playing.

quotations.text: Thus in plain terms: your father hath consented That you shall be my wife; your dowry 'greed on; And, Will you, nill you, I will marry you.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Ending the wooing scene, before her father returns.
quotations.analysis: Three clauses, and her consent is not among them: the father has agreed, the money has been agreed, and the remaining matter is announced rather than asked. 'Will you, nill you' — whether you are willing or not — is the plainest sentence in the play about how the marriage is made.

quotations.text: For I am he am born to tame you Kate, And bring you from a wild Kate to a Kate Conformable as other household Kates.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Immediately before Baptista comes back to hear how the wooing went.
quotations.analysis: The pun runs through wild cat, Kate and cates, which were delicacies laid on a table — three meanings of a name she has already told him she does not use. Renaming is the first move of the taming, and it is done here in front of her while she is being told what she will become.

quotations.text: Why, gentlemen, you do me double wrong, To strive for that which resteth in my choice: I am no breeching scholar in the schools; I'll not be tied to hours nor 'pointed times, But learn my lessons as I please myself.
quotations.speaker: Bianca
quotations.context: To her two disguised suitors, who are arguing about who teaches her first.
quotations.analysis: The obedient daughter, alone with two men and out of her father's hearing, says that the choice rests with her and sets the timetable herself. A breeching scholar is a schoolboy still young enough to be whipped, and she is refusing the position the whole household has assigned her.

quotations.text: To me she's married, not unto my clothes:
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Refusing to change out of the ridiculous outfit he has worn to his wedding.
quotations.analysis: It is a good argument, and it is made by a man who has spent the morning proving the opposite: the clothes are the entire point of the performance, as the Induction has already demonstrated on a tinker. He will use the same principle in reverse in 4.3, when a cap and a gown become grounds for ruining a tailor.

quotations.text: I see a woman may be made a fool, If she had not a spirit to resist.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: At the wedding, being told she will not be staying for the dinner.
quotations.analysis: It is the clearest statement of her position in the play, and it is made in public at her own wedding feast. The conditional is doing the work: she is not saying she has resisted successfully, only that resistance is the one thing standing between her and being made ridiculous — and four lines later she is carried out of the door.

quotations.text: I will be master of what is mine own: She is my goods, my chattels; she is my house, My household stuff, my field, my barn, My horse, my ox, my ass, my any thing;
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Removing Katherina from her own wedding feast, pretending to defend her from thieves.
quotations.analysis: The list descends from buildings to livestock to 'my any thing', and the legal terms are accurate: a wife's goods did pass to her husband. What makes the speech theatre rather than doctrine is the pantomime around it — he draws a weapon on an imaginary gang in order to carry her off as a rescue.

quotations.text: My falcon now is sharp and passing empty; And till she stoop she must not be full-gorged, For then she never looks upon her lure.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: Alone on stage at the country house, after the food has been thrown away.
quotations.analysis: Every word is technical: a sharp hawk is hungry, stooping is the dive to the lure, full-gorged is fed. The audience is being handed a working method rather than a metaphor, and the calm of the vocabulary is what makes the speech disturbing — this is a man describing standard practice.

quotations.text: This is a way to kill a wife with kindness; And thus I'll curb her mad and headstrong humour. He that knows better how to tame a shrew, Now let him speak: 'tis charity to show.
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: The end of the same soliloquy.
quotations.analysis: The phrase now used to mean overwhelming someone with affection is invented here to describe starvation and enforced sleeplessness carried out in the name of care. The closing invitation to the audience is the sharpest thing in the play: he asks a theatre full of husbands whether anyone has a better method, and waits.

quotations.text: Why, sir, I trust I may have leave to speak; And speak I will; I am no child, no babe: Your betters have endured me say my mind, And if you cannot, best you stop your ears.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: When the cap she has asked for is taken away from her.
quotations.analysis: She claims the right to speak rather than the cap, and the argument she makes is about who has authority over her tongue. Her next lines say that if her heart conceals its anger it will break — a physiological claim, not a rhetorical one, and the strongest case in the play for reading the last speech as something other than a change of mind.

quotations.text: Then, God be bless'd, it is the blessed sun: But sun it is not, when you say it is not; And the moon changes even as your mind.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: On the road to Padua, after agreeing that the sun is the moon and being contradicted again.
quotations.analysis: She gives him the answer he wants and then explains the rule she has worked out: truth is whatever he last said. The third line is not obedience but a description of his behaviour, and productions that play the scene as a shared joke and productions that play it as defeat are both working from the same words.

quotations.text: Marry, peace it bodes, and love and quiet life, And awful rule and right supremacy; And, to be short, what not, that's sweet and happy?
quotations.speaker: Petruchio
quotations.context: When Katherina goes to fetch the other two wives.
quotations.analysis: Peace, love and quiet life are listed in the same breath as awful rule and right supremacy, as though they were the same thing rather than its price. 'Awful' here means awe-inspiring, which makes the sentence a definition of the household he thinks he has built.

quotations.text: The wager thou hast won; and I will add Unto their losses twenty thousand crowns; Another dowry to another daughter, For she is changed, as she had never been.
quotations.speaker: Baptista
quotations.context: After Katherina comes when sent for.
quotations.analysis: A father watches his daughter obey and responds by paying out: the transformation is priced at twenty thousand crowns and described as producing a different daughter altogether. It is the last word of the marriage market that opened the play, and it makes the obedience speech that follows a piece of after-sales demonstration.

quotations.text: Thy husband is thy lord, thy life, thy keeper, Thy head, thy sovereign; one that cares for thee, And for thy maintenance commits his body To painful labour both by sea and land,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Instructing Bianca and the Widow on a wife's duty.
quotations.analysis: The argument is contractual: he labours by sea and land, she keeps warm at home, and obedience is the payment due. It is also a description of a marriage that is not hers — Petruchio has been at no sea, and the man who earned his wife by refusing her food is standing in the room while she says it.

quotations.text: My mind hath been as big as one of yours, My heart as great, my reason haply more, To bandy word for word and frown for frown; But now I see our lances are but straws,
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: Near the end of the obedience speech.
quotations.analysis: The past tense is doing something the rest of the speech does not: she tells the other women that she was their equal in mind and their superior in reason, and then says the weapons were never real. 'Bandy word for word' is an exact description of what she did to Petruchio in 2.1, so the speech remembers the wit duel even as it disowns it.

quotations.text: Then vail your stomachs, for it is no boot, And place your hands below your husband's foot: In token of which duty, if he please, My hand is ready; may it do him ease.
quotations.speaker: Katherina
quotations.context: The last lines of the speech, and almost her last in the play.
quotations.analysis: Everything hangs on 'if he please' and on what the actor does with a hand that is offered rather than placed. The gesture is conditional, the token is symbolic, and Petruchio's reply is not thanks but a summons to bed — after which Katherina says nothing at all for the remaining eleven lines of the play.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: Usually placed among the earliest comedies; no document fixes the year.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: There is no quarto of Shakespeare's Shrew before the First Folio; a 1631 quarto was set from the Folio text.

atAGlance.label: The other Shrew
atAGlance.note: A Pleasant Conceited Historie, called The taming of a Shrew was printed in quarto — closely related, differently worded, and still unexplained.

atAGlance.label: Chief source
atAGlance.note: The Bianca plot comes from Gascoigne's 1566 translation of Ariosto; the taming plot has analogues but no single source.

criticalViews.position: The play as farce
criticalViews.summary: One long tradition treats the taming as broad comic business in the manner of commedia dell'arte: exaggerated, unreal and not to be examined for a theory of marriage.
criticalViews.counter: The falconry soliloquy is not farcical in tone, and the deprivation it describes is precise rather than cartoonish.

criticalViews.position: The play as ironic
criticalViews.summary: A widespread modern reading takes the obedience speech as performance: Katherina has learned Petruchio's own game of saying what the occasion requires, and is playing it in public for the couple's joint profit.
criticalViews.counter: Nothing in the text marks the irony, and the reading relies on staging decisions the words do not require; it can also make a very long speech into a wink.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of coercion
criticalViews.summary: A third position takes the Induction seriously: a man is talked out of his identity for other people's amusement, and the play then repeats the experiment on a wife, with a wager at the end to confirm the result.
criticalViews.counter: It has to account for the comedy actually working in performance, and for Bianca and the Widow, who refuse to come when called and are not punished for it.

essayQuestions.question: How should Katherina's final speech be played?
essayQuestions.focus: Obedience, irony and the evidence in the text
plan: Set out the staging facts first: forty-four lines, delivered in public, to two women, in a room where money has just changed hands on her conduct.
Trace her earlier language — the refusal to be silenced in 4.3 and the account of his changing mind in 4.5 — as the material an actor has to build on.
Read the speech's own past tense: my mind hath been as big as one of yours, my reason haply more.
Test the ironic reading against 'place your hands below your husband's foot', and the sincere reading against the wager that produced it.
Conclude with what follows: Petruchio's reply, Lucentio's last line about froward women, and Katherina's silence.

essayQuestions.question: What does the Induction do to the rest of the play?
essayQuestions.focus: Frames, spectatorship and the missing ending
plan: Describe what happens to Sly: an identity dismantled and replaced by repetition, clothes and other people's insistence.
Show that the Padua plot repeats the method on a wife, and that Petruchio's technique is the lord's technique.
Note that the Folio never returns to Sly, and that the 1594 A Shrew does — and that editors once borrowed that ending.
Consider the wager scene as a reinstated frame: husbands watching, a woman performing, money on the outcome.
Decide whether a production that cuts the Induction is playing a different play.

essayQuestions.question: 'Every courtship in the play is a negotiation.' Discuss.
essayQuestions.focus: Money, contracts and consent
plan: Begin with Baptista's condition in 1.1, which makes one daughter's marriage the price of the other's.
Use Petruchio's 'wive it wealthily' and the settlement of the dowry in 2.1 before any consent is sought.
Set the auction for Bianca — plate, hangings, an argosy — against the romance Lucentio believes he is conducting.
Examine what Bianca actually does: takes the tutor, marries in secret, and refuses to come when called.
Close on 5.2, where a second dowry is paid for a change in behaviour.

essayQuestions.question: How does disguise work in the play, and what does it prove?
essayQuestions.focus: Identity, clothes and the Supposes plot
plan: List the disguises and note how many of them are of social rank rather than sex: servant as master, gentleman as tutor, stranger as father.
Connect the machinery to Gascoigne's Supposes, and to the comic tradition of substitution the audience would have recognised.
Show that Tranio is better at being a gentleman than Lucentio, and ask what the play does with that.
Set the disguises against Petruchio's wedding clothes and his claim that she is married to him and not to his clothes.
Return to Sly, whose transformation is achieved with nothing but a gown and a consistent story.

discussionQuestions: Christopher Sly never comes back. Should a production invent an ending for him?
Petruchio asks the audience directly whether anyone knows a better way to tame a shrew. What is that question doing in a comedy?
Bianca and the Widow refuse to come when their husbands send for them, and nothing happens to them. Does that undercut the taming plot or confirm it?
Katherina and Petruchio are evenly matched in the wooing scene of Act II. Is anything of that match left by Act V?
The play is still funny in performance. Is that a problem, and for whom?

timeline.label: Gascoigne's Supposes performed at Gray's Inn
timeline.detail: An English version of Ariosto's I Suppositi, and the source of the Bianca plot's disguises and substituted fathers.

timeline.label: Supposes printed
timeline.detail: Its availability in print is what makes the borrowing traceable.

timeline.label: The Taming of the Shrew probably written
timeline.detail: Usually placed around 1590-92 among the earliest comedies; nothing fixes the year.

timeline.label: A Pleasant Conceited Historie, called The taming of a Shrew printed
timeline.detail: A closely related play with different names and wording, reprinted in 1596 and 1607. Source, memorial report, adaptation or early draft: the question is still open.

timeline.label: Fletcher's The Woman's Prize, or The Tamer Tamed
timeline.detail: Usually dated around 1609-11. Petruchio remarries after Katherina's death and is resisted by a second wife, which shows the play was being answered within its own generation.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The first secure printed text of Shakespeare's Shrew, with the Induction and no return to Sly.

timeline.label: A quarto printed from the Folio text
timeline.detail: Not an independent witness; it confirms that the Folio was the version in circulation.

timeline.label: John Lacy's Sauny the Scot
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation in prose that expanded Grumio into a Scottish servant and made Petruchio harsher.

timeline.label: Garrick's Catharine and Petruchio
timeline.detail: Three acts, no Sly, almost no Bianca — and the version most audiences saw for well over a century.

timeline.label: Sam Taylor's film with Mary Pickford and Douglas Fairbanks
timeline.detail: Widely cited as the first sound Shakespeare film; Pickford's wink during the last speech became part of the play's argument with itself.

timeline.label: Kiss Me, Kate opens on Broadway
timeline.detail: Cole Porter's musical puts the play inside a backstage quarrel — a twentieth-century replacement for the abandoned Sly frame.

timeline.label: Michael Bogdanov's RSC production
timeline.detail: Sly disrupted the auditorium before the Padua story began, treating the taming plot as a problem rather than a farce.

timeline.label: Justin Audibert's gender-reversed RSC production
timeline.detail: Set in a matriarchal Elizabethan England, with Petruchia and Katherine, so that the hierarchy itself became visible as a construction.

places.name: Padua
places.note: Baptista's city, described as a nursery of arts and run as a marriage market.

places.name: Verona
places.note: Petruchio's home, which he leaves in the first scene of Act I to find a wealthy wife.

places.name: Pisa
places.note: Lucentio's city, and Vincentio's — the identity a passing pedant is hired to counterfeit.

places.name: Venice
places.note: Where Petruchio goes for rings and fine array between the betrothal and the wedding.

places.name: Mantua
places.note: The pedant's home, and the city he is told it is dangerous to have come from.

places.name: Barton-on-the-Heath
places.note: Sly's Burtonheath: a Warwickshire village a few miles from Stratford, where Shakespeare had relatives by marriage.

related.why: Beatrice and Benedick are the later, kinder version of a courtship conducted entirely through insult.
Another early comedy of disguise, servants and travel between Italian cities, with an ending readers have argued about for as long.
The other early play built out of mistaken identity and substitution, taken from Roman comedy rather than from Ariosto.
Disguise used to court on someone else's behalf, with the consequences taken seriously.
A comedy in which a woman directs her own courtship, and speaks the epilogue herself.

books.title: Tess of the d’Urbervilles
books.author: Thomas Hardy
books.setting: Hardy’s Wessex: the Vale of Blackmoor, the Var valley, the uplands at Flintcomb-Ash, and Stonehenge
books.lengthNote: Fifty-nine chapters gathered into seven named phases
books.openingLine: On an evening in the latter part of May a middle-aged man was walking homeward from Shaston to the village of Marlott, in the adjoining Vale of Blakemore, or Blackmoor.
books.summary: A parson tells a haggler on a Dorset road that he is descended from knights, and the boast costs his daughter everything. Hardy tracks Tess Durbeyfield through four employers, two men and one dead child, and arranges the novel so that every disaster arrives through ordinary machinery: a horse on a dark road, a letter under a carpet, a threshing engine that will not stop. The subtitle is an argument, and the book is built to win it.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of Tess of the d’Urbervilles
sourceText.note: Chapters are numbered continuously in Roman numerals from I to LIX across the seven phases; references below give the phase as well, since the phases are the divisions Hardy himself named.

structure.label: Phase the First
structure.title: The Maiden
structure.summary: A chance meeting on the road tells John Durbeyfield he is a d’Urberville, and the family’s drunken celebration puts Tess in charge of the horse. Prince is killed, the family loses its living, and Tess is sent to claim kin from a household that bought the name.

scenes.title: The name
scenes.summary: Parson Tringham’s antiquarian civility turns a haggler into a knight, and the club-walking gives Angel Clare his first, unused sight of Tess.

scenes.title: Prince
scenes.summary: Tess takes the beehives to market at night, falls asleep, and the mail-cart kills the horse; the guilt sends her to Trantridge.

scenes.title: The Chase
scenes.summary: Alec installs her in the poultry farm, follows her through the fog after the dance at Chaseborough, and the novel’s central assault is narrated in the dark and in the dark of the prose.

structure.label: Phase the Second
structure.title: Maiden No More
structure.summary: Tess walks home, refuses Alec’s offer of support, and works the harvest with her child at the field edge. Sorrow is baptised by his mother when the parson is refused and buried in the unconsecrated corner with the drunkards and the stillborn.

scenes.title: The return
scenes.summary: She goes back to Marlott and asks her mother why she was never warned.

scenes.title: Sorrow
scenes.summary: The harvest scene, the home baptism, the refused burial, and the two years of silence that follow.

structure.label: Phase the Third
structure.title: The Rally
structure.summary: At Talbothays the work is skilled, the valley is fertile and Tess is briefly an employee rather than a victim. Angel Clare, learning dairying before emigrating, watches her across three months of summer and decides that she is Nature itself, which is the beginning of the trouble.

scenes.title: The Var valley
scenes.summary: A larger landscape, real skill at the milking, and the harp heard across the garden.

scenes.title: Summer
scenes.summary: The dairy’s three other milkmaids love Angel too, and the novel keeps them in view; Angel declares himself in a cart full of milk.

structure.label: Phase the Fourth
structure.title: The Consequence
structure.summary: Tess refuses Angel repeatedly and then accepts, tries four times to tell him, and finally writes it down. The letter goes under the carpet as well as under the door, and the confession she owes is postponed to the wedding night, where he makes his own first.

scenes.title: The engagement
scenes.summary: Angel’s family, his brothers’ respectability, and the ride to the station where Tess begins and abandons her history.

scenes.title: The letter
scenes.summary: The note that is never read, the wedding at last, and Angel’s confession of his own forty-eight hours in London.

structure.label: Phase the Fifth
structure.title: The Woman Pays
structure.summary: Angel hears the same offence he has just confessed and finds it a different thing entirely. He leaves for Brazil; Tess sends money home, is turned away from dairy work, and ends at Flintcomb-Ash pulling swedes in the rain and feeding a threshing machine.

scenes.title: The rejection
scenes.summary: The confession, the sleepwalking, the coffin, and the separation dressed as a temporary arrangement.

scenes.title: Flintcomb-Ash
scenes.summary: The starve-acre farm, Marian and Izz, and the walk to Emminster that ends with Tess overhearing the Clare brothers and turning back.

structure.label: Phase the Sixth
structure.title: The Convert
structure.summary: Alec reappears as a ranting preacher and abandons the pulpit within a fortnight of seeing her again, telling her the backsliding is her fault. He follows her to the rick, offers to keep her family, and waits for her father’s death to do the arguing for him.

scenes.title: The preacher
scenes.summary: The conversion, the pursuit across the uplands, and the confrontation on the threshing rick.

scenes.title: Lady Day
scenes.summary: The unanswered letter, John Durbeyfield’s death, the loss of the cottage, and the night in the churchyard at Kingsbere.

structure.label: Phase the Seventh
structure.title: Fulfilment
structure.summary: Angel comes back from Brazil thin and altered, and finds Tess installed in a boarding house at Sandbourne under another man’s protection. She kills Alec, the two of them walk north for five days, and the police take her at dawn on the stone at Stonehenge.

scenes.title: Sandbourne
scenes.summary: The return, the landlady’s staircase, and the spreading stain on the ceiling below.

scenes.title: Stonehenge and Wintoncester
scenes.summary: The empty house in the New Forest, the sleep on the altar stone, the arrest at sunrise, and the black flag over the city gaol.

characters.name: Tess Durbeyfield
characters.role: A field-woman, sixteen at the opening
characters.summary: Hardy gives her the intelligence of a National-school education and the position of an unskilled labourer, and the gap between the two is where the novel lives. She is judged by everyone she meets on evidence she was never allowed to present, and the subtitle exists because Hardy expected his readers to join in.
characters.clue: She baptises her own child with a jug of water because the parson will not come, and names him for a word out of the Bible.

relationships.label: assaulted, pursued and finally killed by her hand

characters.name: Alec d’Urberville
characters.role: Son of a Stoke family that purchased the name
characters.summary: His ancestry is bought and his power is entirely current: money, a gig, a poultry farm, a mother who cannot see. He converts, preaches, relapses and proposes with the same unembarrassed energy, and blames Tess for each turn.
characters.clue: He drives too fast downhill, feeds a girl strawberries she has not asked for, and later preaches in a barn about the sin he committed.

characters.name: Angel Clare
characters.role: A parson’s youngest son, learning farming
characters.summary: He has rejected his father’s church and kept every one of its judgements. The cruelty of the wedding night is not hypocrisy in the ordinary sense — he has genuinely convinced himself that the woman in front of him is a different person from the one he proposed to.
characters.clue: He confesses forty-eight hours of dissipation, is forgiven in a sentence, and cannot manage the same for a confession he has just been given.

characters.name: Joan Durbeyfield
characters.summary: She sends her daughter to claim kin in a clean dress and never explains why a clean dress might matter. Hardy is precise about the gap between them: the mother’s world is ballads and a fortune-telling book, the daughter’s is the Sixth Standard, and two hundred years lie between the two.
characters.clue: She keeps a fortune-telling book in the thatch because she will not have it in the house at night.

characters.name: John Durbeyfield
characters.summary: He is given a title and no money, and spends the rest of his short life being carried home. His death is the event that empties the cottage, because the lease was on his life: the novel’s cruellest joke is that the ancestry which ruined his daughter also fails to house her.
characters.clue: Told on the road that he is descended from knights, he immediately orders a carriage to take him the rest of the way home.

characters.name: Marian
characters.role: A dairymaid at Talbothays, later at Flintcomb-Ash
characters.summary: She loves Angel, loses him without resentment, and is the one who finds Tess work when nobody else will. Her drinking at the starve-acre farm is treated as a fact about the work rather than a fault in her.
characters.clue: The stoutest of the three milkmaids who lie awake listening for a man’s footstep, and the one who later writes to warn of a danger she cannot name.

characters.name: Izz Huett
characters.summary: Asked by Angel to come to Brazil with him, she agrees, and then tells him the truth about how much Tess loved him, which ends the proposal. It is the most disinterested act in the book and nobody thanks her for it.
characters.clue: She is offered a passage to Brazil and talks the man out of it by telling him what another woman would have done for him.

characters.name: Liza-Lu
