quotations.context: Her first words in the play, watching the wreck from the shore.
quotations.analysis: She knows at once that the storm is her father's doing, which tells the audience more about the household than any description could. The conditional 'if' is politeness rather than doubt, and the sentence ends in an imperative: the only person on the island who gives Prospero orders is fifteen.

quotations.text: What seest thou else In the dark backward and abysm of time?
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Testing how much Miranda remembers of her life before the island.
quotations.analysis: 'Backward' is used as a noun, which is not ordinary English then or now; the phrase makes the past a place you could fall into. He is checking the extent of her ignorance before deciding how much of it to repair, and the grandeur of the image conceals a piece of information management.

quotations.text: Hell is empty And all the devils are here.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Reporting how Ferdinand leapt from the burning ship.
quotations.analysis: Ariel is quoting a terrified boy, so the most famous line in the first act belongs to a character who never says it again. The joke underneath it is theological: the devils on this island are a spirit doing as it is told and a man who was once a duke.

quotations.text: Is there more toil? Since thou dost give me pains, Let me remember thee what thou hast promised, Which is not yet perform'd me.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: After performing the storm, before being sent out again.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is contractual rather than emotional: work has been done, a promise was made, the promise is outstanding. Prospero's answer is to recite the rescue from the cloven pine, which is the standard reply of an employer who would rather discuss gratitude than terms.

quotations.text: This island's mine, by Sycorax my mother, Which thou takest from me.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Answering Prospero's summons, before the quarrel about his attempt on Miranda.
quotations.analysis: The claim is made in the language of inheritance law — by his mother, therefore his — which is exactly how Prospero would argue for Milan. Nobody on stage disputes the facts; they change the subject to his conduct, and the play never returns to settle the question of title.

quotations.text: You taught me language; and my profit on't Is, I know how to curse. The red plague rid you For learning me your language!
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: The end of his argument with Prospero and Miranda about his education.
quotations.analysis: The complaint is delivered in fluent blank verse, which quietly contradicts it: he has plainly got more from the lessons than curses. 'Profit' is a merchant's word, and 'learning' here means teaching — the exchange is being audited, and the pupil finds it a bad bargain.

quotations.text: Full fathom five thy father lies; Of his bones are coral made; Those are pearls that were his eyes: Nothing of him that doth fade But doth suffer a sea-change Into something rich and strange.
quotations.speaker: Ariel
quotations.context: Sung invisibly to Ferdinand, who believes his father has drowned.
quotations.analysis: The song tells a lie — Alonso is alive — in the gentlest possible form, turning a corpse into jewellery so that grief arrives already consoled. 'Sea-change' enters English here, and the whole lyric is an argument that loss can be transformation, which is the claim the last act will have to make good.
quotations.source: Globe/Moby text, 1.2.461-466; sung by Ariel within Ferdinand's scene

quotations.text: I' the commonwealth I would by contraries Execute all things; for no kind of traffic Would I admit; no name of magistrate;
quotations.speaker: Gonzalo
quotations.context: Imagining what he would do if he were king of the island.
quotations.analysis: The speech follows Florio's translation of Montaigne closely enough that the borrowing is visible, and Shakespeare stages it as a joke: Antonio and Sebastian point out that a commonwealth with no sovereignty has just been proposed by a man who began by saying he would be king of it. The mockery does not dispose of the idea, and the contradiction is the play's own.

quotations.text: And by that destiny to perform an act Whereof what's past is prologue, what to come In yours and my discharge.
quotations.speaker: Antonio
quotations.context: Persuading Sebastian to murder the sleeping Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The line is now quoted as though it were wisdom about history; in the play it is a murderer's argument that the past is merely the warm-up and the killing is the real performance. 'Prologue' and 'act' are theatre words, put into the mouth of the man whose plot competes with Prospero's for control of the island's plot.

quotations.text: Be not afeard; the isle is full of noises, Sounds and sweet airs, that give delight and hurt not.
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Reassuring Stephano and Trinculo, who have heard Ariel playing on an invisible pipe.
quotations.analysis: The drunkards are frightened and the so-called monster is the one who knows the island is safe. Shakespeare gives the play's most delicate verse to the character everyone on stage calls a beast, three minutes after he has explained how to drive a nail into a man's skull.

quotations.text: Remember First to possess his books; for without them He's but a sot, as I am, nor hath not One spirit to command
quotations.speaker: Caliban
quotations.context: Instructing Stephano on how the murder of Prospero must be done.
quotations.analysis: It is the most accurate piece of political analysis in the play, and it comes from the servant: the power is not in the man, it is in the library. Prospero lost Milan to his books and now holds the island by them, and the only character who understands the mechanism is the one with no share in it.

quotations.text: I am your wife, if you will marry me; If not, I'll die your maid: to be your fellow You may deny me; but I'll be your servant, Whether you will or no.
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: Proposing to Ferdinand at the log-pile, with Prospero watching unseen.
quotations.analysis: She proposes, sets out the alternatives and closes off the last of them: the grammar moves from a condition to a refusal to accept one. Having been given no information about her own life for twelve years, she takes the single decision available to her without consulting the man who arranged the meeting.

quotations.text: Our revels now are ended. These our actors, As I foretold you, were all spirits and Are melted into air, into thin air:
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Breaking off the wedding masque on remembering Caliban's conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: He is apologising to his son-in-law for a cancelled entertainment, and the apology grows into the play's largest statement about existence within eight lines. Note that he says 'as I foretold you': the consolation is that the disappearance was always in the design, which is true of a masque and is what he needs to believe about a dukedom.

quotations.text: We are such stuff As dreams are made on, and our little life Is rounded with a sleep.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The close of the same speech, before he admits his mind is troubled.
quotations.analysis: 'Made on' means made of, so human beings are built out of the same material as the vanished spirits — not that life resembles a dream but that it is cut from it. 'Rounded' can mean surrounded or finished off, and the line declines to choose, which is why it can be read as consolation or as the bleakest sentence in the play.

quotations.text: A devil, a born devil, on whose nature Nurture can never stick; on whom my pains, Humanely taken, all, all lost, quite lost;
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Alone, immediately after breaking off the masque.
quotations.analysis: The verdict is delivered by a man who has just spent years teaching the creature he says cannot be taught, and the repetitions — 'all, all lost, quite lost' — are those of someone arguing with himself. It is also the play's clearest statement of the position Miranda's existence contradicts.

quotations.text: Though with their high wrongs I am struck to the quick, Yet with my nobler reason 'gaitist my fury Do I take part: the rarer action is In virtue than in vengeance
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Immediately after Ariel says that he would pity the charmed courtiers if he were human.
quotations.analysis: The decision that ends twelve years of planning is made in four lines and prompted by a spirit. 'Rarer' means both more unusual and finer, which concedes that mercy is the less natural response; and the reason he gives is not that they deserve it but that it is the better piece of work.

quotations.text: But this rough magic I here abjure, and, when I have required Some heavenly music, which even now I do, To work mine end upon their senses that This airy charm is for, I'll break my staff, Bury it certain fathoms in the earth, And deeper than did ever plummet sound I'll drown my book.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Ending the long invocation of the elves of hills, brooks and groves.
quotations.analysis: He renounces the art in the middle of using it: the sentence that abjures magic also orders up the heavenly music that will disarm his enemies. The staff is broken, but the book is drowned deeper than any sounding line can reach, which is a peculiar precaution against an object he says he no longer wants.

quotations.text: How beauteous mankind is! O brave new world, That has such people in't!
quotations.speaker: Miranda
quotations.context: On seeing the assembled courtiers for the first time.
quotations.analysis: The people she is admiring include the two men who set her adrift to die and a third who tried to murder his brother two days ago. Prospero's reply — three words, 'Tis new to thee — is the most economical piece of irony in Shakespeare, and it is the last thing he says to his daughter in the play.

quotations.text: Two of these fellows you Must know and own; this thing of darkness! Acknowledge mine.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: Presenting the three conspirators to Alonso.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built to balance: two servants belong to the king, one belongs to me. 'Acknowledge' is doing a great deal of work — it can mean simply claiming a possession, or admitting a kinship, and the entire modern performance history of the play turns on which of those an actor decides to play.

quotations.text: As you from crimes would pardon'd be, Let your indulgence set me free.
quotations.speaker: Prospero
quotations.context: The last two lines of the epilogue, spoken alone to the audience.
quotations.analysis: The man who has spent the play releasing or refusing to release other people ends by asking to be released himself, and the currency is applause. 'Indulgence' was also the word for a remission of punishment granted by the Church, so the audience is being asked to perform an absolution that the play's own theology could not quite supply.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: After reports of the 1609 Sea Venture wreck reached London, and before the recorded court performance of November 1611.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto exists. The First Folio prints it first in the volume, at the head of the comedies.

atAGlance.label: Sources
atAGlance.note: Shipwreck pamphlets, Florio's Montaigne, Ovid and the court masque, combined rather than adapted.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Act I Scene 2 alone runs to about a third of the play.

criticalViews.position: The play as Shakespeare's farewell
criticalViews.summary: The oldest popular reading takes Prospero's renunciation of magic as the dramatist laying down his own art, and the epilogue as a retirement speech.
criticalViews.counter: It sits badly with the facts of the career: Shakespeare went on to collaborate on at least two more plays, and the epilogue is a conventional appeal for applause of a kind other plays also make.

criticalViews.position: The play as a colonial document
criticalViews.summary: Read beside the Bermuda pamphlets and the Virginia venture, the island becomes a place with an inhabitant, a claim and an occupation, and Caliban's case is the one the drama cannot dispose of.
criticalViews.counter: The Mediterranean geography is insistent — Milan, Naples, Tunis, Algiers — and a reading built entirely on the Atlantic has to work around it.

criticalViews.position: The play as a study of service
criticalViews.summary: A third approach puts Ariel rather than Caliban at the centre and reads the island as a workplace: promised wages, deferred release, labour that is invisible because it is magical.
criticalViews.counter: It risks flattening the difference between a spirit who is freed in the last scene and a man whose future the play never mentions.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The Tempest endorse Prospero's rule of the island?
essayQuestions.focus: Authority, service and the limits of art
plan: Begin with the fact that the audience is shown the storm before it is told who made it, so the first experience of his power is as a catastrophe.
Set Ariel's petition in 1.2 beside Caliban's claim in the same scene: two servants, two grievances, two completely different answers from the same master.
Use the breaking of the masque in 4.1 to show that his control is dependent on his attention, and collapses the moment he remembers a threat.
Weigh the decision in 5.1: mercy chosen freely, but only after a spirit has had to describe what pity is.
Close on the epilogue, where a man who has ruled everything asks an audience for the power to leave.

essayQuestions.question: 'The most eloquent character in the play is its slave.' Discuss Caliban.
essayQuestions.focus: Language, dispossession and sympathy
plan: Establish what Caliban actually claims in 1.2 and note that nobody on stage denies the history, only changes the subject.
Examine the verse of 'the isle is full of noises' and ask why Shakespeare gives this speech to this character at this point in a conspiracy scene.
Balance the sympathy against 1.2 and the attempt on Miranda, which the play states plainly and does not excuse.
Compare his understanding of Prospero's power — take the books first — with the courtiers' failure to understand anything.
Finish with 'this thing of darkness', and with the play's silence about what becomes of him.

essayQuestions.question: What is the effect of staging the masque in Act IV and then interrupting it?
essayQuestions.focus: Spectacle, form and control
plan: Describe what a Jacobean masque was for: blessing, order, flattery of the ruler who paid for it.
Show how the Ceres and Juno masque fits that description exactly, down to the banishing of Venus and Cupid from the betrothal.
Identify the interruption as the only point where Prospero's plan is affected by something outside it.
Read the 'revels' speech as an attempt to convert a failure of stage management into a philosophy.
Consider the staging consequences: how a production makes the spirits vanish determines how seriously it takes the speech.

essayQuestions.question: Is the ending of The Tempest a reconciliation?
essayQuestions.focus: Forgiveness, silence and what is left unresolved
plan: List what is settled in 5.1: the dukedom restored, the marriage arranged, Ariel freed, the ship repaired.
Set against it what is not: Antonio says nothing, Sebastian jokes, Caliban's future is never mentioned.
Look closely at Miranda's 'brave new world' and Prospero's reply as a test of how much the audience is being asked to believe.
Use Gonzalo's summary at 5.1.235-241 — all of us found ourselves when no man was his own — and ask whether the play has earned it.
Decide what the epilogue changes: a character stepping out of the fiction to ask for pardon from people who have not been wronged.

discussionQuestions: Prospero forgives his enemies before any of them apologises. Does that make the forgiveness stronger or emptier?
Ariel and Caliban are both unfree. Why does the play release one and say nothing about the other?
Miranda has been told nothing about her own history until the day the play begins. What does her father gain from that?
The conspiracy of the drunkards repeats the conspiracy of the courtiers almost exactly. Why is one funny?
If a production cuts the epilogue, what is lost?

timeline.label: Florio's translation of Montaigne published
timeline.detail: The English 'Of the Cannibals' behind Gonzalo's commonwealth speech becomes available.

timeline.label: The Sea Venture wrecked on Bermuda
timeline.detail: Bound for Virginia, the ship broke up on the reefs; the survivors reached Jamestown the following year.

timeline.label: Jourdain's A Discovery of the Barmudas printed
timeline.detail: One of the pamphlets that turned the wreck into a London story of storm, survival and abundant islands.

timeline.label: Performed before James I at Whitehall on 1 November
timeline.detail: The Revels record is the earliest firm evidence that the play existed and was being acted.

timeline.label: Played at court during the festivities for Princess Elizabeth's marriage
timeline.detail: One of a group of plays given by the King's Men that winter for the betrothal and wedding celebrations.

timeline.label: First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text, and the volume opens with it — unusually well printed, with full stage directions and a cast list.

timeline.label: Dryden and Davenant's The Enchanted Island
timeline.detail: A Restoration rewriting that gave Miranda a sister and Caliban a mate, and held the stage for well over a century.

timeline.label: Peter Brook directs John Gielgud as Prospero
timeline.detail: At the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre; remembered for a Prospero of severity rather than serenity.

timeline.label: Jonathan Miller's colonial production
timeline.detail: Casting made the island's politics explicit, and helped establish a reading British theatre has not since put down.

timeline.label: Peter Greenaway's Prospero's Books
timeline.detail: A film that takes the library rather than the island as the centre of the play.

timeline.label: Julie Taymor's film, with Helen Mirren as Prospera
timeline.detail: Changing the magician's sex reorganises the play's questions about parenthood, exile and authority.

places.name: Milan
places.note: The dukedom Prospero lost to his brother while he studied.

places.name: Naples
places.note: Alonso's kingdom, and the wedding party the shipwrecked court was returning from.

places.name: Tunis
places.note: Where Claribel was married, and the voyage home from which the storm interrupts.

places.name: Algiers
places.note: Argier in the text: the city from which Sycorax was banished to the island.

places.name: Bermuda
places.note: The still-vex'd Bermoothes of Ariel's speech, and the site of the 1609 wreck behind the play's storm.

places.name: Whitehall Palace, London
places.note: Where the first recorded performance was given before James I on 1 November 1611.

related.why: The other late play in which a ruler's damage is repaired after years, though there the miracle is a statue rather than a storm.
Written at about the same time, and equally willing to let romance conventions do work that tragedy would refuse.
Shipwreck, a lost daughter and reunion at sea: the pattern The Tempest compresses into one afternoon.
More's island commonwealth stands behind the tradition Gonzalo is drawing on, and being mocked for.
The earlier play of spirits, spells and interrupted entertainments, with the magic used for comedy rather than government.

books.title: The Woman in White
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.setting: Cumberland, London and a decaying estate in Hampshire, between 1849 and 1851
books.written: Begun 15 August 1859; the manuscript finished 26 July 1860, with the serial still running
books.lengthNote: Three Epochs, assembled out of eleven separate narratives by nine hands
books.openingLine: This is the story of what a woman’s patience can endure, and what a Man’s resolution can achieve.
books.summary: A drawing master meets a frightened woman on the Finchley Road at midnight and learns afterwards that she has escaped from an asylum. Her resemblance to the heiress he is about to teach turns out to be the whole machinery of a conspiracy: two women can be exchanged if the documents say so, and a marriage settlement supplies the motive. Collins tells it as a file of statements by different hands, so that the reader assembles the case as a jury would, out of testimony that nobody has cross-examined.

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The Woman in White
sourceText.note: References give the epoch, the narrator and the chapter number within that narrative, since the novel numbers its chapters afresh for each new hand.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Hartright
structure.title: The road, Limmeridge and the likeness
structure.summary: Walter Hartright takes a post teaching drawing in Cumberland, having met a woman dressed entirely in white on the Finchley Road and helped her into a cab. At Limmeridge he finds his pupil’s face is the same face, falls in love with an engaged woman, and is quietly removed from the household.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Gilmore
structure.title: The settlement
structure.summary: The family solicitor takes over the narrative and the story becomes a document. Sir Percival’s lawyer refuses to protect Laura’s twenty thousand pounds, Mr Fairlie will not exert himself to object, and Gilmore signs a settlement he says no daughter of his would have been married under.

structure.label: The First Epoch — Marian’s diary
structure.title: The marriage agreed
structure.summary: Marian’s diary begins, and with it the novel’s most immediate voice: dated, unrevised and written by somebody who does not know what happens next. Laura tells Sir Percival the truth about her feelings and he marries her anyway.

structure.label: The Second Epoch — Blackwater Park
structure.title: Fosco, surveillance and a diary interrupted
structure.summary: The couple return with Count and Countess Fosco, and Blackwater Park becomes a place where letters are read and servants are managed. Marian climbs onto the verandah roof in the rain to hear the two men plan, and writes down what she has heard until the fever takes the pen out of her hand.

structure.label: The Second Epoch — other hands
structure.title: The substitution, told by the people who were there
structure.summary: Mr Fairlie, the housekeeper Eliza Michelson, a cook, a doctor and a headstone carry the story through the exchange. Anne Catherick dies in London under Laura’s name; Laura is taken to the asylum under Anne’s, and every step is attested by somebody who saw only a fragment.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — Hartright returns
structure.title: A living woman and her own grave
structure.summary: Walter comes back from Central America to find a stone with Laura’s name on it and a woman nobody will identify. The investigation turns into a search for dates: what is needed is not a confession but proof that the journey to London happened after the death on the certificate.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — Mrs Catherick and Fosco
structure.title: Two confessions, neither of them penitent
structure.summary: Mrs Catherick’s letter explains the vestry, the forged register and the secret Sir Percival died trying to burn. Fosco, writing at pistol point, gives the conspiracy as a piece of intellectual autobiography and awards himself the credit for it.

structure.label: The Third Epoch — the conclusion
structure.title: Identity restored, on paper
structure.summary: Fosco is killed in Paris by the Brotherhood he betrayed, the false inscription is cut away from the stone, and Laura’s name is publicly restored in front of the tenants at Limmeridge. Walter closes the file he has spent the novel assembling and hands the last word to Marian.

characters.name: Walter Hartright
characters.role: A teacher of drawing, later the editor of the whole narrative
characters.summary: He is the novel’s hero and also its archivist, which are two different kinds of power. He collects, orders and introduces every other statement in the book, so the reader’s impression of Marian, Fosco and Laura has already passed through his hands before it arrives.
characters.clue: He is walking back to London at midnight when a hand touches his shoulder, and he spends the rest of the book assembling the paperwork that follows.

characters.name: Marian Halcombe
characters.summary: She is introduced through a description that admires her figure and recoils from her face, and then proceeds to do everything the plot requires: investigate, climb, travel, negotiate and remember. The novel gives her no money, no legal standing and the best prose in the book.
characters.clue: She takes off her shoes, crawls out over a verandah roof in a downpour and writes down what she hears until the fever takes the pen away.
traits: without any legal power at all

characters.name: Laura Fairlie
characters.role: Heiress of Limmeridge, later Lady Glyde
characters.summary: She is the object the conspiracy moves around, and Collins gives her almost no narrative of her own: her testimony is the one thing the plot establishes is legally worthless. What is stolen from her is not money but the acknowledged fact of being herself.
characters.clue: Her name is on a gravestone in Cumberland while she is alive in London, and for a whole epoch nobody in authority will say otherwise.

characters.name: Anne Catherick
characters.summary: She is dressed in white because a kind woman once praised her in it, shut up in an asylum because she knew a secret she did not understand, and killed by the conspiracy because her heart gives out at the right moment for it. She gives the novel its title and almost nothing else of her own.
characters.clue: She asks a stranger on the road whether he knows many men of the rank of Baronet, and will not say which one she means.

characters.name: Sir Percival Glyde
characters.summary: Charming for exactly as long as the settlement takes to sign, and after that a man locking doors. His secret is smaller and more frightening than the plot implies: he has no title at all, only a page added to a parish register, which makes him a forgery rather than a villain.
characters.clue: He dies in the vestry of a country church, trying to burn the book that proves he was never entitled to his own name.
characters.firstAppearance: The First Epoch, Vincent Gilmore’s narrative

characters.name: Count Fosco
characters.role: An Italian exile, Sir Percival’s friend
characters.summary: Enormous, silent-footed, fond of white mice and pastry, and the only character in the novel who thinks in terms of systems. He is also the one who writes his own confession and cannot resist making it a lecture; his vanity is what eventually kills him.
characters.clue: He keeps canaries and white mice, flatters his enemy in her own diary, and is found in the Paris Morgue with a mark cut into his left arm.

characters.name: Frederick Fairlie
characters.role: Laura’s uncle, master of Limmeridge House
characters.summary: A collector of etchings and coins who has made his own nerves into a full-time occupation, and whose refusal to be troubled is what allows every stage of the conspiracy to proceed. Collins hands him a narrative of his own so that he can convict himself in his own voice.
characters.clue: He asks visitors to speak more quietly and to put the tray of coins back themselves, and calls himself a bundle of nerves dressed up to look like a man.

characters.name: Mrs Catherick
characters.summary: She sold her silence for respectability and has spent twenty years collecting it in instalments: a house, a clock, and the clergyman’s bow every Sunday. Her narrative is the coldest thing in the book, because she is not ashamed of any of it.
characters.clue: She sits at her window each Sunday to be bowed to by the clergyman, and counts that bow as the price of what she did in a vestry.

characters.name: Vincent Gilmore
characters.summary: He writes the second narrative and supplies the novel’s legal spine: the marriage settlement, the twenty thousand pounds, and the clause that makes Laura worth more dead than alive. He sees exactly what is coming and signs anyway, because his client will not be bothered.
characters.clue: He records, twice and in the same words, that no daughter of his would have been married under the settlement he was compelled to draw up.

themes.name: Identity and documents
themes.summary: A person in this novel is whatever the paperwork says. A gravestone, a doctor’s certificate and a parish register are enough to kill a living woman and to make a commoner a baronet, and no amount of embodied self-knowledge will overturn any of them.
themes.development: Anne’s white dress and Laura’s face set up the resemblance; the inscription in Limmeridge churchyard executes it; and the counter-attack, when it comes, is made of dates rather than recognition.

themes.name: Testimony and the record
themes.summary: The book is arranged as evidence in a trial that never takes place, and the arrangement is itself the argument: no single witness sees enough, and the person who compiles them holds the real power. Walter says so in the preamble and then exercises it for six hundred pages.
themes.development: From Hartright’s opening statement of method, through Marian’s dated diary and Mr Fairlie’s self-serving deposition, to Fosco’s written confession extracted at gunpoint.

themes.name: Marriage, money and the law
themes.summary: The conspiracy needs no magic, only a settlement. Laura’s twenty thousand pounds passes to her husband if she dies first, and the whole plot is an attempt to bring that clause forward by about fifty years.
themes.development: Drafted in Gilmore’s narrative, refused correction by an indolent guardian, and executed at Blackwater Park by a man who needs the money before his creditors arrive.

themes.name: Confinement and the asylum
themes.summary: Two women are shut up in this novel and neither is mad. Private asylum admission needed certificates and somebody willing to sign them, and Collins builds his most frightening scenes out of that ordinary administrative fact rather than out of anything Gothic.
themes.development: Anne escapes in the first chapters, Laura is admitted under her name in the second epoch, and the rescue depends on a nurse being bribed rather than on any doubt being raised.

themes.name: What women are allowed to do
themes.summary: The preamble divides the world into a woman’s patience and a man’s resolution, and the novel immediately disobeys it. Marian does the investigating, the climbing and the remembering; Laura’s own word about who she is counts for nothing in law.
themes.development: Stated as a formula in the first paragraph, contradicted throughout Marian’s diary, and quietly restored at the end when the record is closed by Walter and the estate passes to his son.

themes.name: Rank, name and forgery
themes.summary: Sir Percival’s secret is that his rank is a forgery, and the novel treats this as worse than the conspiracy it produced. A title, like an identity, turns out to be a line of writing in a book kept in a badly locked cupboard.
themes.development: Hinted by Anne’s question about men of the rank of Baronet, investigated through the marriage register at Old Welmingham, and settled by a fire in a vestry.

techniques.name: Multiple narrators
techniques.definition: Telling one story through a sequence of first-person accounts by different people.
techniques.bookDefinition: Telling one story through a sequence of first-person accounts by different people.
techniques.inThisBook: Eleven narratives by nine hands, from a solicitor and a housekeeper to a cook, a doctor and a headstone; each witness speaks only of what they saw, and the differences between their voices carry the class comedy as well as the evidence.

techniques.name: Documentary form
techniques.definition: Building a novel out of objects that would exist in the world it describes.
techniques.bookDefinition: Building a novel out of objects that would exist in the world it describes.
techniques.inThisBook: Diaries with dates, letters, a marriage settlement, a death certificate, a parish register and a carved inscription are not illustrations of the plot; they are the plot, and altering one of them is the crime.

techniques.name: Doubling
techniques.definition: Two characters constructed so that one can stand in for the other.
techniques.bookDefinition: Two characters constructed so that one can stand in for the other.
techniques.inThisBook: Anne and Laura are half-sisters without knowing it, share a face and a childhood dress, and the conspiracy consists simply of letting the world act on the resemblance.

techniques.name: Serial suspense
techniques.definition: Shaping instalments so that each ends where a reader cannot stop.
techniques.bookDefinition: Shaping instalments so that each ends where a reader cannot stop.
techniques.inThisBook: Collins was writing weekly while the novel was appearing, and the seams show in the best way: narratives break off mid-crisis, and Marian’s diary simply stops in the middle of a sentence.

techniques.name: Dates as evidence
techniques.definition: Making the exact timing of events the decisive fact in a plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Making the exact timing of events the decisive fact in a plot.
techniques.inThisBook: The conspiracy is not overturned by anyone recognising Laura but by proving that she travelled to London after the date on her own death certificate.

techniques.name: Reading faces
techniques.definition: Treating physical appearance as evidence of character, in the manner of Victorian physiognomy.
techniques.bookDefinition: Treating physical appearance as evidence of character, in the manner of Victorian physiognomy.
techniques.inThisBook: Walter grades Marian’s figure and then her face in two consecutive paragraphs, and the novel spends the rest of its length disproving the second reading with her conduct.

quotations.text: This is the story of what a woman’s patience can endure, and what a Man’s resolution can achieve.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: The first sentence of the preamble.
quotations.analysis: Two virtues, two sexes, and the capital letters fall on Man and not on woman. The book then reverses the assignment without ever amending the sentence: it is Marian who acts and Walter who spends years waiting for a date to be proved, and the formula stands at the front of the file like an uncorrected heading.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Hartright, Chapter I

quotations.text: the story here presented will be told by more than one pen, as the story of an offence against the laws is told in Court by more than one witness⁠—with the same object, in both cases, to present the truth always in its most direct and most intelligible aspect; and to trace the course of one complete series of events, by making the persons who have been most closely connected with them, at each successive stage, relate their own experience, word for word.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: The preamble, setting out how the narrative to follow has been assembled.
quotations.analysis: The comparison is to a court, and it promises the reader a jury’s job. What the sentence does not mention is the person who chose the witnesses and set them in order; ‘word for word’ guarantees the accuracy of each statement and says nothing about the selection.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Hartright, Chapter I

quotations.text: There, in the middle of the broad bright high road⁠—there, as if it had that moment sprung out of the earth or dropped from the heaven⁠—stood the figure of a solitary woman, dressed from head to foot in white garments, her face bent in grave inquiry on mine, her hand pointing to the dark cloud over London, as I faced her.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: On the Finchley Road at the end of a July night, the moment a hand touches his shoulder.
quotations.analysis: The repeated ‘there’ holds her in place for a whole clause before the sentence admits what she is, and the two alternatives offered — out of the earth or down from the heaven — are both supernatural. She is described entirely by her clothes and her gesture; the novel will spend six hundred pages establishing that she also has a name.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Hartright, Chapter IV

quotations.text: Done! She has escaped from my asylum. Don’t forget; a woman in white. Drive on.
quotations.speaker: The proprietor of the asylum
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Called down from a chaise to a policeman on the Finchley Road, minutes after Walter has put the woman into a cab.
quotations.analysis: Four sentences, and the only description offered is a colour. The policeman asks what she has done and is answered with a word that means the opposite of an offence, which is the novel’s first demonstration that a certificate does the work a charge would otherwise have to do.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Hartright, Chapter IV

quotations.text: She left the window⁠—and I said to myself, The lady is dark. She moved forward a few steps⁠—and I said to myself, The lady is young.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter VI
quotations.context: Meeting Marian Halcombe for the first time, before she turns round.
quotations.analysis: Two clauses of movement, each answered by a verdict, as though a face were arriving in instalments. The syntax is a piece of physiognomy in action, and the paragraph that follows — swarthy, masculine, almost a moustache — shows the method failing on the one person in the book most worth reading correctly.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Hartright, Chapter VI

quotations.text: I am nothing but a bundle of nerves dressed up to look like a man.
quotations.speaker: Frederick Fairlie
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Frederick Fairlie’s narrative
quotations.context: Asked by his servant how he is, on the morning Fosco’s messenger arrives.
quotations.analysis: He describes himself as an assemblage rather than a person, and does it with obvious pleasure. Collins gives him his own narrative precisely so that this self-portrait can be volunteered rather than reported: the man whose refusal to be troubled costs his niece her name is allowed to explain himself, and does.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, Frederick Fairlie’s narrative

quotations.text: Seriously and sorrowfully I repeat here the parting words that I spoke at Limmeridge House:⁠—No daughter of mine should have been married to any man alive under such a settlement as I was compelled to make for Laura Fairlie.
quotations.speaker: Vincent Gilmore
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Vincent Gilmore’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Closing his narrative, having failed to persuade Mr Fairlie to protect Laura’s twenty thousand pounds.
quotations.analysis: He puts his objection on the record, draws the document anyway, and then quotes himself in the past tense at the end of his own statement — which is what a professional man does when he expects to be asked about it later. It is the most accurate picture of legal helplessness in the novel: he sees the clause, names it, and signs.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Gilmore, Chapter IV

quotations.text: No man under heaven deserves these sacrifices from us women. Men! They are the enemies of our innocence and our peace⁠—they drag us away from our parents’ love and our sisters’ friendship⁠—they take us body and soul to themselves, and fasten our helpless lives to theirs as they chain up a dog to his kennel.
quotations.speaker: Marian Halcombe
quotations.reference: The First Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s diary, Chapter II
quotations.context: To Laura, who has just said that she means to go through with the marriage for her father’s sake.
quotations.analysis: The simile is domestic and brutal: a wife is a dog chained to a kennel, and the verbs — drag, take, fasten — are all transitive with women as their object. It is the most explicit political statement in the novel, and Collins gives it to a woman writing privately in a diary she does not expect anyone to read.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The First Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s diary, Chapter II

quotations.text: The fool’s crime is the crime that is found out, and the wise man’s crime is the crime that is not found out.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: At Blackwater Park, arguing after dinner that crimes cause their own detection is a piece of claptrap.
quotations.analysis: The antithesis is perfectly balanced and completely circular: the only evidence of a wise crime is that you have never heard of it. Fosco is describing the plan he is about to execute, out loud, to the woman who will try to stop him, and the pleasure of saying it is what he cannot forgo.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe, Chapter III

quotations.text: English Society, Miss Halcombe, is as often the accomplice as it is the enemy of crime.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter III
quotations.context: Continuing the same argument, having just accused John Bull of finding other people’s faults faster than his own.
quotations.analysis: The foreigner is given the outsider’s privilege of describing the host country’s machinery, and the sentence turns out to be a plot summary: the conspiracy works because respectable people accept a certificate. Collins puts his own thesis in the villain’s mouth, which is a cheap trick that works.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe, Chapter III

quotations.text: Women can resist a man’s love, a man’s fame, a man’s personal appearance, and a man’s money, but they cannot resist a man’s tongue when he knows how to talk to them.
quotations.speaker: Marian Halcombe
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Chapter V
quotations.context: In her diary, after an evening in which Fosco has deliberately charmed the table.
quotations.analysis: She writes the sentence as a general law and includes herself in it, which is the honesty that makes her diary worth reading. The list ascends from love to fame to appearance to money and then breaks the pattern: the irresistible thing is not a possession at all but a technique.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe, Chapter V

quotations.text: The illness of our excellent Miss Halcombe has afforded me the opportunity of enjoying an unexpected intellectual pleasure.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, postscript
quotations.context: Written at the foot of Marian’s diary, which breaks off mid-sentence when the fever takes her.
quotations.analysis: The violation is done entirely in the register of a compliment, and the reader discovers it at the same moment as the page is turned. It is also a formal outrage: the novel’s most private document is annotated by its antagonist, which tells you exactly how safe any of these testimonies are.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, Marian Halcombe’s narrative, Postscript by a Sincere Friend

quotations.text: Sacred to the Memory of Laura, Lady Glyde, wife of Sir Percival Glyde, Bart., of Blackwater Park, Hampshire, and daughter of the late Philip Fairlie, Esq., of Limmeridge House, in this parish. Born March 27th, 1829; married December 22nd, 1849; died July 25th, 1850.
quotations.reference: The Second Epoch, the narrative of the tombstone
quotations.context: The inscription on the Fairlie monument in Limmeridge churchyard, given as a narrative in its own right.
quotations.analysis: Collins lets a piece of carved stone take a turn as narrator, and it is the only witness in the book that cannot be cross-examined. Three dates — born, married, died — are all it offers, and the last of them is the lie on which everything depends and, eventually, the thing that breaks the case open.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Second Epoch, The Story Continued in Several Narratives

quotations.text: Dead to her uncle, who had renounced her; dead to the servants of the house, who had failed to recognise her; dead to the persons in authority, who had transmitted her fortune to her husband and her aunt; dead to my mother and my sister, who believed me to be the dupe of an adventuress and the victim of a fraud; socially, morally, legally⁠—dead.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter I
quotations.context: Opening the Third Epoch, standing in a world where the woman beside him is officially buried.
quotations.analysis: Four clauses, each beginning with the same word and each naming a different authority — a guardian, the servants, the officials who transferred her fortune, and his own family. The three adverbs at the close rank the kinds of death from softest to hardest, and it is the legal one the rest of the novel has to attack.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Hartright, Chapter I

quotations.text: she must have started on the twenty-sixth, and must have come to London one day after the date of her own death on the doctor’s certificate. If we can prove that date, we prove our case against Sir Percival and the Count.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IV
quotations.context: Working out with Marian what evidence would actually overturn the conspiracy.
quotations.analysis: The rescue turns on a single day. Nobody needs to recognise Laura, and nobody’s word about her is worth anything; what is required is a document showing she travelled after she died. Collins makes the emotional climax of his novel an argument about a calendar, which is the most Victorian thing about it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Hartright, Chapter IV

quotations.text: I was struck by the insecurity of the place in which the register was kept. The door of the press was warped and cracked with age, and the lock was of the smallest and commonest kind. I could have forced it easily with the walking-stick I carried in my hand.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s narrative, Chapter IX
quotations.context: In the vestry at Old Welmingham, as the clerk produces the marriage register.
quotations.analysis: A baronetcy is kept in a warped cupboard behind a lock that a man could break with a walking-stick, and Collins gives us the exact means to hand. The register is the same kind of object as the gravestone and the death certificate: a piece of writing that makes a person, kept somewhere nobody guards.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Hartright, Chapter IX

quotations.text: Chemistry especially has always had irresistible attractions for me from the enormous, the illimitable power which the knowledge of it confers. Chemists⁠—I assert it emphatically⁠—might sway, if they pleased, the destinies of humanity.
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Count Fosco’s narrative
quotations.context: Opening his written confession, composed at Walter’s dictation and at his own leisure.
quotations.analysis: Asked for a confession, he delivers a prospectus. The dash before ‘I assert it emphatically’ is the sound of a man who cannot let a sentence go without applauding it, and this vanity is exactly what Walter has counted on: the document he needs is produced because Fosco cannot bear to write a dull one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Fosco’s narrative

quotations.text: That conception involved nothing less than the complete transformation of two separate identities. Lady Glyde and Anne Catherick were to change names, places, and destinies, the one with the other⁠—the prodigious consequences contemplated by the change being the gain of thirty thousand pounds, and the eternal preservation of Sir Percival
quotations.speaker: Count Fosco
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Count Fosco’s narrative
quotations.context: Describing the moment he first understood what could be done with the resemblance.
quotations.analysis: He calls it a conception, as though it were a piece of composition, and prices it in the same clause: thirty thousand pounds and a secret kept. The three nouns he exchanges — names, places, destinies — go from the trivial to the absolute without a change of tone, which is the whole character in one list.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Fosco’s narrative

quotations.text: I passed on my way the terrible dead-house of Paris⁠—the Morgue. A great crowd clamoured and heaved round the door. There was evidently something inside which excited the popular curiosity, and fed the popular appetite for horror.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter II
quotations.context: In Paris, walking towards Notre Dame, some days after Fosco has left England.
quotations.analysis: The Count’s death is delivered as a piece of tourism: a crowd, a queue and an overheard conversation. Collins refuses his villain a scene, and the body is identified by a mark cut into the arm — another inscription, in the one place where a name could not be forged.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter II

quotations.text: The long, happy labour of many months is over. Marian was the good angel of our lives⁠—let Marian end our Story.
quotations.speaker: Walter Hartright
quotations.reference: The Third Epoch, Walter Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter III
quotations.context: The last sentences of the novel, after Marian has held up the child who is the heir of Limmeridge.
quotations.analysis: The labour of months is the writing, not the living, so the book ends by announcing that a file has been closed. He calls Marian the good angel and hands her the last word in a sentence he himself is writing, which is generosity and editorial control performing the same gesture.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, The Third Epoch, Hartright’s conclusion, Chapter III

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: Weekly in Dickens’s All the Year Round from 26 November 1859, and simultaneously in Harper’s Weekly in New York.

atAGlance.label: Book edition
atAGlance.note: Three volumes in 1860; Collins then prepared a revised one-volume text, with a dated preface, in 1861.

atAGlance.label: Written to deadline
atAGlance.note: Collins began on 15 August 1859 and finished the manuscript on 26 July 1860, with instalments appearing throughout.

atAGlance.label: Shape
atAGlance.note: Hartright, Gilmore, Marian’s diary, Mr Fairlie, the housekeeper, a cook, a doctor, a gravestone, Mrs Catherick and Fosco — and Hartright decides the order of all of them.

criticalViews.position: The founding sensation novel
criticalViews.summary: The standard literary-historical reading places the book at the head of a 1860s genre that put crime, bigamy and false identity inside respectable English houses rather than in Italian castles, and made the newspaper rather than the Gothic its source.
criticalViews.counter: Treating it as the origin of a genre can flatten what is odd about it, particularly the decision to tell the whole thing as a bundle of legal statements.

criticalViews.position: A novel about the law of married women’s property
criticalViews.summary: Criticism attentive to the settlement reads the plot as an argument about legal disability: Laura’s money, her testimony and her liberty all belong to somebody else, and the conspiracy only has to use powers that the law already grants.
criticalViews.counter: The novel’s resolution restores her by the same legal machinery it has just exposed, which makes it hard to read as a reforming book.

criticalViews.position: A book that cannot decide about Marian
criticalViews.summary: Feminist criticism since the 1970s has focused on the gap between what Marian does and how the novel frames her: she is the intelligence of the plot and is introduced through a description of her face that treats her as a physiological joke.
criticalViews.counter: Defenders point out that the description is Walter’s rather than the narrative’s, and that the structure allows Marian’s own prose to answer it at length.

essayQuestions.question: What does Collins gain by telling the story through many narrators?
essayQuestions.focus: Form, evidence and the power of the editor
plan: Begin with the preamble’s own claim: a court, several witnesses, and each speaking only of what they saw.
Show the method producing suspense — Marian’s diary breaking off, Mr Fairlie’s account arriving after the damage is done.
Show it producing class comedy and range, from a solicitor’s professional prose to a housekeeper’s careful self-defence and a cook’s few sentences.
Turn the argument: Walter selects and orders every document, so the novel about distributed testimony has one author inside it.
Test the case with Fosco’s confession, which is extracted under threat and is still the most self-satisfied writing in the book.

essayQuestions.question: How does the novel present the relationship between identity and documents?
essayQuestions.focus: Certificates, registers, inscriptions
plan: Set out what the conspiracy actually requires: a death certificate, a gravestone, a reception at an asylum, and nobody willing to look twice.
Show that recognition fails repeatedly — servants, an uncle and a village all decline to identify a living woman.
Use the register at Old Welmingham to show the reverse case: a forged page makes a commoner a baronet.
Read the counter-attack as an argument about dates, not about faces, and ask what that says about the novel’s idea of proof.
Conclude on the restoration scene, in which Laura is made herself again by a public reading and a new inscription.

essayQuestions.question: Examine the presentation of Marian Halcombe.
essayQuestions.focus: Capability, appearance and the limits placed on her
plan: Start with the two-paragraph introduction, where the figure is admired and the face is recoiled from in consecutive sentences.
Track what she actually does: investigates, negotiates, climbs the verandah in the rain, and keeps the only dated record of the conspiracy.
Examine what she cannot do — hold property, give testimony that counts, or prevent a marriage settlement.
Read Fosco’s postscript as a violation that is also a tribute, and consider why Collins gives her admirer to the villain.
Weigh the ending: she is called the good angel and given the last word, in a book whose last word is written by somebody else.

essayQuestions.question: ‘The conspiracy needs no villains, only institutions.’ How far do you agree?
essayQuestions.focus: Marriage law, private asylums and respectability
plan: Set out the legal position: the settlement, the twenty thousand pounds, and the clause Gilmore objects to and signs anyway.
Show private asylum admission as an administrative act requiring certificates and a willing signature.
Use Fosco’s after-dinner argument about English Society as the accomplice of crime, and check it against the plot that follows.
Test the counter-case: Sir Percival’s violence and Fosco’s ingenuity are not reducible to procedure.
Decide whether the novel wants these institutions reformed or merely finds them frightening.

discussionQuestions: Walter compiles every statement in the book. How much should we trust the arrangement?
Laura is the centre of the plot and is given almost no narrative of her own. Is that a failure or a point being made?
Fosco writes his own confession and cannot resist showing off. Does that make him more or less frightening?
Sir Percival’s secret is a forged entry in a parish register. Why does the novel treat that as worse than the conspiracy it caused?
Marian does the work and Walter gets the marriage. What would have to change for the novel to end differently?

timeline.label: Wilkie Collins born in London
timeline.detail: Son of the landscape painter William Collins, and trained for the law before he gave it up for fiction.

timeline.label: Collins meets Dickens
timeline.detail: An amateur theatrical brings them together, and Dickens’s magazines become Collins’s main platform for the next decade.

timeline.label: Composition begins
timeline.detail: Collins started writing on 15 August at Broadstairs, with no complete manuscript and a serial slot already booked.

timeline.label: Serialisation starts
timeline.detail: The first instalment appeared on 26 November in All the Year Round and, the same week, in Harper’s Weekly in New York.

timeline.label: The manuscript is finished
timeline.detail: Collins completed it on 26 July, while the serial was still running; the British serial ended on 25 August.

timeline.label: First English book edition
timeline.detail: Three volumes, in the expensive format that circulating libraries preferred.

timeline.label: The revised one-volume text
timeline.detail: Collins corrected the chronology and added a dated preface; this is the text most modern editions follow.

timeline.label: The Moonstone
timeline.detail: Collins uses the same method again — a case assembled from the statements of people who each saw one part of it.

timeline.label: Collins’s own stage version
timeline.detail: He dramatised the novel himself, part of a long effort to keep control of a story that was being adapted without him.

timeline.label: Collins dies
timeline.detail: He had published more than twenty novels, and the sensation novel had long since been absorbed into the detective story.

timeline.label: Warner Bros. film
timeline.detail: Directed by Peter Godfrey, with Eleanor Parker in the double role of Laura and Anne, which is how the cinema usually solves the resemblance.

timeline.label: BBC television serial
timeline.detail: A serial version with room to keep the narrators separate, which is how the novel’s documentary structure survives adaptation.

timeline.label: BBC television film
timeline.detail: A single-film adaptation that compresses the eleven narratives into one line of action, as most screen versions do.

places.name: Cumberland
places.note: Limmeridge House and its churchyard: where Walter is engaged, where the false inscription is cut, and where Laura’s name is finally read out to the tenants.

places.name: London
places.note: Clement’s Inn, the Finchley Road at midnight, the asylum, and the poor lodgings where Walter, Marian and Laura hide while the case is built.

places.name: Hampshire
places.note: Blackwater Park, with its stagnant lake and dilapidated wing, and Welmingham, where Mrs Catherick sits at her window collecting respectability.

places.name: Paris
places.note: The Morgue by the river, where Fosco’s body is displayed to a crowd and identified by a mark on his left arm.

places.name: Liverpool
places.note: The port Walter sails from with the expedition to Central America, and the passenger lists that later help fix the dates.

places.name: Honduras
places.note: Where Walter lands with the archaeological expedition, and spends the months in which the conspiracy is carried out at home.

related.why: Collins doing the same thing again eight years later: a case assembled from statements by people who each saw one part of it.
A confined woman, a husband with a secret and a country house with a wing nobody visits, written thirteen years earlier.
Another novel built entirely out of diaries, letters and transcripts, with a group assembling evidence against something official channels will not credit.
Serialised in the same magazine a year later, and equally interested in what documents, settlements and hidden benefactors do to an identity.
The other great case of a narrative handed to the reader as a document, with the reliability of the narrator left as the real question.

books.title: Twelfth Night
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.setting: Illyria: Orsino's court, Olivia's house and garden, and a stretch of coast
books.lengthNote: Around 2,500 lines, with more songs than any other Shakespeare comedy
books.openingLine: If music be the food of love, play on;
books.summary: A girl washed up in a country she has never heard of puts on her drowned brother's kind of clothes and goes to work for a duke. Everything that follows comes from that one decision: a messenger who is loved by the wrong person, a household that turns a joke into an imprisonment, and a recognition scene that has to give two people back a twin before anybody can marry.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Twelfth Night
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering, which counts the prose scenes continuously. Modern editions vary.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: A shipwreck, a mourning house, and a borrowed name
structure.summary: Orsino is in love with the idea of being in love; Olivia has sworn off company for seven years to mourn a brother. Viola, believing her own brother drowned, takes service with the duke as a boy called Cesario and is sent within three days to court the woman her master wants — a job she does well enough to be loved for it herself.

scenes.title: Music
scenes.summary: Orsino calls for a strain, tires of it in eight lines, and hears that Olivia will see nobody.

scenes.title: The coast
scenes.summary: Viola asks what country this is, is told her brother may have survived, and decides to serve disguised.

scenes.title: Late drinking
scenes.summary: Sir Toby introduces Sir Andrew as a suitor and as a source of income.

scenes.title: Three days in
scenes.summary: Cesario is already the duke's favourite and is sent to Olivia; Viola admits she wants the master.

scenes.title: The veil
scenes.summary: Feste talks his way back into favour; Olivia unveils for the messenger and falls in love with him.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: A ring, a night of songs, and a forged letter
structure.summary: Olivia sends a ring after Cesario on a pretext, and Viola understands her own position exactly: she loves Orsino, Orsino loves Olivia, Olivia loves a disguise. In the same act Malvolio interrupts a drinking party, and Maria answers him with a piece of handwriting designed to fit the fantasy he already has.

scenes.title: Sebastian lives
scenes.summary: Antonio, who has saved him from the sea, follows him into a city where he has enemies.

scenes.title: The ring
scenes.summary: Viola works out what Olivia has done and leaves the knot to time.

scenes.title: Cakes and ale
scenes.summary: A catch, a quarrel with the steward, and Maria's plan for the letter.

scenes.title: Patience on a monument
scenes.summary: Orsino discourses on men's constancy; Viola answers with a sister who never spoke.

scenes.title: The box-tree
scenes.summary: Malvolio reads the letter aloud while three men hide and provide the commentary.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Yellow stockings, a duel and the wrong twin
structure.summary: Olivia abandons discretion and declares herself; Viola can say only that she is not what she is. Malvolio arrives smiling and cross-gartered in front of a woman in mourning and is taken for mad. Sir Toby arranges a duel between two people equally unwilling to fight it, and Antonio walks into the middle of it and is arrested.

scenes.title: Not what I am
scenes.summary: Feste on the abuse of words, and Olivia's open declaration to Cesario.

scenes.title: Sir Andrew's challenge
scenes.summary: Sir Toby dictates a letter so incoherent he decides to deliver the challenge by mouth.

scenes.title: The Elephant
scenes.summary: Antonio gives Sebastian his purse and arranges to meet him at an inn.

scenes.title: Madness
scenes.summary: The stockings, the dark room, the duel, and Antonio mistaking Viola for her brother.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: A beating, a betrothal and a dark room
structure.summary: Sebastian is attacked in the street by people who think they know him, is proposed to by a woman he has never met, and accepts. Malvolio, shut in the dark, is visited by Feste pretending to be a curate, who tells him the room is full of light. The comedy and the cruelty are running in the same scene.

scenes.title: Mistaken
scenes.summary: Sebastian fights Sir Andrew and Sir Toby; Olivia stops it and takes him home.

scenes.title: Sir Topas
scenes.summary: Feste in a false beard argues that there is no darkness but ignorance.

scenes.title: The chantry
scenes.summary: Sebastian, sure he is not mad, agrees to be betrothed at once.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: Both twins on stage at once
structure.summary: Everything converges: Antonio's accusation, Olivia's claim to a husband, Orsino's threat to kill the boy he loves, and then Sebastian walks on. The knot unties itself in fifteen lines. Malvolio is released, reads his letter out, learns the truth and leaves promising revenge, and Feste is left alone to sing about rain.

scenes.title: Recognition
scenes.summary: The twins meet, three marriages are arranged, Malvolio exits vowing revenge, and the clown sings.

characters.name: Viola
characters.role: A shipwrecked gentlewoman, disguised as Cesario
characters.summary: She invents Cesario as a practical measure and then finds the disguise doing things she did not intend: it makes her the confidant of the man she loves and the object of the woman she is sent to persuade. She is the only character who sees the whole situation and the only one who can do nothing about it.
characters.clue: Washed ashore in a country she has never heard of, she dresses as her drowned brother's sort of young man and is sent to woo on behalf of the man she wants for herself.

relationships.label: courts for another, and is loved by

characters.name: Olivia
characters.summary: Her seven-year mourning is a position, and it lasts until somebody argues with her. Once she falls, she is the most decisive person in the play: she declares herself, sends after the messenger and marries a stranger within three days of meeting his face on somebody else.
characters.clue: She vows to weep for a brother for seven years, and is engaged to a man she has spoken to twice — and who is not the man she thinks.

relationships.label: loves, believing her a young man

characters.name: Orsino
characters.summary: He opens the play calling for music and stops it within eight lines, which is his whole character in one gesture. He has never spoken to Olivia; what he loves is the condition of loving, and the play transfers him to Viola with an ease that has troubled readers ever since.
characters.clue: He orders up music as an appetite to be killed by excess, courts a woman he never meets, and proposes to his own page in the last scene.

characters.name: Malvolio
characters.summary: Humourless, ambitious and correct about the drinking, which is what makes him unbearable. The trick works because the letter tells him what he already believes; the punishment goes far beyond the joke, and the play lets him leave without being forgiven or forgiving.
characters.clue: A steward who practises behaviour to his own shadow, appears before a woman in mourning in yellow stockings, and is shut in a dark room for smiling.

characters.name: Feste
characters.summary: He is paid by both households and belongs to neither, which lets him say things nobody else can. He sings the play's best songs, performs the curate who torments Malvolio, and is left alone at the end to sing about a world where it rains every day.
characters.clue: He is licensed to say anything, takes money from two rival houses, plays a priest in a false beard, and has the last word after everyone else has gone in to dinner.

characters.name: Sir Toby Belch
characters.summary: He lives in his niece's house at her expense and funds his drinking by keeping a rich fool on the premises. He is the engine of the misrule and the first to tire of it: when the duel goes wrong and he is bloodied, he turns on Sir Andrew and marries Maria offstage.
characters.clue: He keeps a foolish knight in the house for his money, argues that virtue does not abolish cakes and ale, and discards his friend the moment he gets hurt.

characters.name: Sir Andrew Aguecheek
characters.role: A foolish knight, Olivia's supposed suitor
characters.summary: He is being robbed in plain sight and is happy about it. Shakespeare gives him one line of real pathos — that he was adored once too — and then has him beaten by a stranger and cast off by the man who has been living on his money.
characters.clue: He is kept in the house as a suitor and a source of funds, is frightened into a duel he cannot fight, and says quietly that he was adored once.

characters.name: Maria
characters.summary: She writes the letter, and the letter is a piece of character analysis: she knows exactly what Malvolio wants to hear because she has watched him practise it. Her reward is marriage to Sir Toby, which happens offstage and is reported in a line.
characters.clue: She can imitate her mistress's hand closely enough to ruin a man, and her wages for it are a knight, announced in half a sentence.

characters.name: Sebastian
characters.summary: He arrives late, is given money by a man who loves him, and spends his scenes being greeted by strangers who know his name. His response to being handed a countess is not to question it but to check that he is not mad, and to marry her within the hour.
characters.clue: Everyone in the city seems to know him, one of them hits him and another proposes marriage, and he concludes that the air and the sun are at least real.

characters.name: Antonio
characters.summary: He risks arrest in a hostile city because he cannot stand to be parted from Sebastian, and says so in terms no other character in the play uses about anybody. He is arrested, believes himself betrayed, and at the end is neither punished nor paired: he simply stops speaking.
characters.clue: He follows a young man into a city where he is a wanted enemy, hands over his purse, and is left standing at the end with nothing settled.

themes.name: Desire and the imagined lover
themes.summary: Orsino has never met Olivia, Olivia falls for a messenger she sees for ten minutes, and Malvolio builds a marriage out of a letter with no name on it. The play's joke is that every one of them is in love with something they have made up, and that being right about the object is not what makes the feeling real.
themes.development: Orsino's abstract appetite in 1.1 becomes a proposal to a servant in 5.1, and the play does not stop to explain the transfer.

themes.name: Disguise and identity
themes.summary: Viola's costume is a practical solution that turns into a trap: it earns her the intimacy she wants and makes the declaration impossible. On a stage where the women were played by boys, a boy playing a girl playing a boy is not a complication but a machine for saying true things under cover.
themes.development: She calls disguise a wickedness in 2.2, tells Olivia in 3.1 that she is not what she is, and never removes the clothes — the play ends with Orsino still calling her Cesario.

themes.name: Mourning and its uses
themes.summary: Two households are organised around a dead brother. Olivia's grief is public and performed for seven years; Viola's is private and she goes to work. The play is quietly interested in the difference between grief you can display and grief you have to earn a living through.
themes.development: Both brothers turn out to be a matter of report — Sebastian is not dead, and Olivia's mourning ends the moment something more interesting arrives.

themes.name: Festivity and cruelty
themes.summary: Twelfth Night was the end of the Christmas misrule, and the play tests what happens when the licence runs on too long. The gulling of Malvolio is funny, then uncomfortable, then a man shut in the dark being told by a fake priest that the room is light.
themes.development: A catch sung at midnight in 2.3 leads by 4.2 to an imprisonment, and the household's response in 5.1 is that he brought it on himself.

themes.name: Service, rank and ambition
themes.summary: Almost everybody in Illyria works for somebody. Malvolio's offence is wanting to cross the line upward; Maria crosses it successfully by marrying Sir Toby, and nobody objects. The play punishes the ambition it finds humourless and rewards the one that makes people laugh.
themes.development: The letter's promise that some have greatness thrust upon them is quoted back at Malvolio by the fool in the last scene, after it has cost him everything.

themes.name: Time, patience and endings
themes.summary: Viola hands the knot to time because she can see no other way through, and time duly unties it by producing her brother. The comedy's resolutions are not earned by anybody's cleverness, which is part of why the last act feels both magical and slightly arbitrary.
themes.development: From 'O time! thou must untangle this' in 2.2 to the whirligig of time bringing in its revenges in 5.1, the play keeps handing responsibility to the calendar.

techniques.name: Song
techniques.definition: Sung lyric used to carry mood, comment or structure rather than plot.
techniques.bookDefinition: Sung lyric used to carry mood, comment or structure rather than plot.
techniques.inThisBook: There are more songs here than in any other Shakespeare comedy, and they go in one direction: from 'O mistress mine' through 'Come away, death' to a closing ballad about wind and rain that undoes the happy ending.

techniques.name: Speaking under disguise
techniques.definition: A character telling the literal truth in a form the listener cannot decode.
techniques.bookDefinition: A character telling the literal truth in a form the listener cannot decode.
techniques.inThisBook: Viola's account of her father's daughter who never told her love is autobiography delivered to the man it is about, and he takes it as a story.

techniques.name: The gulling scene
techniques.definition: A trick staged in front of hidden observers who supply the running commentary.
techniques.bookDefinition: A trick staged in front of hidden observers who supply the running commentary.
techniques.inThisBook: The box-tree scene puts three men on stage interrupting a fourth as he reads, so that the audience laughs at the victim and at the watchers' inability to keep quiet.

techniques.name: Identical twins
techniques.definition: A plot device by which one actor's part is doubled by another body.
techniques.bookDefinition: A plot device by which one actor's part is doubled by another body.
techniques.inThisBook: The device is old, but Shakespeare makes the twins brother and sister, so the resemblance depends on clothes rather than on nature — which is the play's point about gender rather than a mechanical convenience.

techniques.name: The fool's licence
techniques.definition: A professional entertainer permitted to say what others may not.
techniques.bookDefinition: A professional entertainer permitted to say what others may not.
techniques.inThisBook: Feste's wordplay on corruption and sentences is a job rather than a temperament; Olivia defends him by saying there is no slander in an allowed fool, and he uses the permission to torment the one man who cannot laugh.

techniques.name: Prose and verse
techniques.definition: Movement between unmetered and metered speech as a signal of register or state.
techniques.bookDefinition: Movement between unmetered and metered speech as a signal of register or state.
techniques.inThisBook: The kitchen plot is almost all prose and the court scenes almost all verse; Malvolio's ruin is that he reads a prose letter as if it were a prophecy and then tries to talk like the people upstairs.

quotations.text: If music be the food of love, play on; Give me excess of it, that, surfeiting, The appetite may sicken, and so die.
quotations.speaker: Orsino
quotations.context: The first lines of the play, to his musicians.
quotations.analysis: He is not asking for music because he enjoys it; he wants to overeat until he is sick of the feeling. The metaphor treats love as an appetite that can be killed by indulgence, and eight lines later he stops the music because it is not as sweet as it was — an attention span the whole play measures him by.

quotations.text: What country, friends, is this?
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Her first line, on the coast, having just survived the wreck.
quotations.analysis: Five words that establish everything: she has no idea where she is, no standing, and no information. The Captain's answer, 'This is Illyria, lady', is the last time anybody in the play addresses her as a woman until the final scene.

quotations.text: Whoe'er I woo, myself would be his wife.
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: An aside, having agreed to carry Orsino's suit to Olivia.
quotations.analysis: A single rhymed line closing the scene, and the first statement of the play's central knot. Three days into her employment she is already in the position the rest of the comedy depends on, and she tells the audience rather than anybody on stage — which is where she will keep it for four acts.

quotations.text: Oh, you are sick of self-love, Malvolio, and taste with a distempered appetite.
quotations.speaker: Olivia
quotations.context: Rebuking her steward for sneering at Feste's wit.
quotations.analysis: The diagnosis is delivered in the same appetite imagery Orsino used in the first scene, so the play's two kinds of self-absorption are made to rhyme. It is also the reason the forged letter will work: his mistress has told him publicly what his weakness is, and Maria is listening.

quotations.text: Make me a willow cabin at your gate, And call upon my soul within the house; Write loyal cantons of contemned love And sing them loud even in the dead of night;
quotations.speaker: Viola
quotations.context: Answering Olivia's question: what would you do if you loved as your master does?
quotations.analysis: Asked what she would do, she describes a courtship nobody in the play is actually conducting — noisy, sleepless, unembarrassed — and it is the moment Olivia falls. The irony is exact: the speech is convincing because Viola means it, and she means it about somebody else.

quotations.text: Disguise, I see, thou art a wickedness, Wherein the pregnant enemy does much.
quotations.speaker: Viola
